ATHEISM. (Written in a sleeping-berth of the yacht "Santa Maria.") The sun shines on the waters; and the waters to the

wall Of my poorcabin, narrow, dark, and small, Fling a perpetual unpurposed flow Of luminous pulses dancing to and fro; And from the wall the many-flickering show Shoots to my eye, Far-travelled from its fountain in the sky. Suppose me born and bred in such small home, Cabin and cribbed, with never a look outside Into toe heaving tide, Or upward to the bright expansive dome Which men call Heaven, what should I say of LIGHT? Pd say, belike, it was a tangled maze Of freakish rays, Flitting about to feed my wondering gaze, Redeemed such-wise from Chaos and old Night, A bright confusion without law or rule. And for the Stn. the glorious lord of day, . And his all-permeant, all-plastic ray, For that I knew no Sun, mayhap I'd say, There is no sun in Heaven—and be a fool, As Atheists are—blind guides who go to school 7 With outward sense, and what mere sense compels Alone believe. Be wiser thou, and know, Behind all shadowy show A causeful Substance dwells, Behind all tangled maze Of crowded things that try the wondering gaze In air, in water, and in teeming sod, A Reason works, which wisely men:call GOD. —Cassell's Magazine. _ "Who was the straightest man in the Bible ?" "Joseph?' "Why 9" "Because Pharaoh made a ruler of him?' Believe nothing against another but upon good au- thority; nor report what may hurt another unless it be a greater hurt to others to conceal it. She—" I don't like my bonnet now that I've got it. Circles are praised, not that abound In largeness, but the exactly round: So life we praise that does excel Not in much time but living well.—Waller. An author was boasting of a comedy he had written, and appealed to a friend, to whom he had read it, to con- firm his own estimate of its excellence. The friend gravely said—" Your come ly is a great work—a very serious work—a work that is by no means to be laughed at ! " _ _ .

Solicitous friend: " That's an awful cold you've got, my dear boy! Now, what you want to do is to go right home and take—" Victim : "Just jot it down in this book, please. I've got one hundred and forty-six recipes already, and I expect to meet enough friends before night to bring it up to two hundred." The other day a journal, hitherto without a spot on its character, inquired with well feigned innocence—" How can five persons divide five eggs so that each man will receive one, and still one remain in the dish?" After several hundred people went two;-thirds distracted in the mazes of this proposition, the journal meanly says—" One takes the dish with the egg." It is said that Dr. Chalmers once entertained a dis- tinguished guest from Switzerland, when he asked if he would be helped to kippered salmon. The foreign divine asked the meaning of the uncouth word kippered, and was told that it meant preserved. The poor man in a public prayer soon after, offered up a petition that the distinguished divine might long be "kippered to the Free Church in Scotland." Young housekeeper: "I am sorry to have to say, Mr. Grazer, that your meat has not been good lately." Mr. Grazer: " Beggin' your panting, marm, but if you will choose the joints yourself, and trust to your amatoor in- stead of my professional judgment, what can you ex- pect ?" Young housekeeper: "But the weight is always light." Mr. Grazer: "Dear me, marm, dear me! Still you must bear in mind that my charges ain't heavy." (And she left, feeling quite small.) We all know how a few words hastily uttered led to the death of Thomas a Becket. Something of that kind happened the other day to a petulant woman, who acci- dentally broke the handle of a china cup, and rashly Q7C- claimed that she wished none of them had handles. Later on it became necessary for the servinglmaid to explain matters, and she proceeded to do so by saying, " Indade, marm, and ye said ye'd prefare to hey the hanthles all off, and ye see I have done it rale noice." THri THREE WISHES.—Three merry wights sat together at dinner in the Lamb at Kehl on the Rhine. After they had finished they each drank a bottle of Klingenberger, and began to talk of all kinds of things. At last they fell to wishing, and it was agreed among them that he 'who wished the most extravagant wish should have his expenses for the rest of their journey paid by the others. The first said, "I wish that all the moats of all the fort- resses of Strasburg and Kehl were full of needles, and for every needle a tailor, who should work for a whole year makirfg flour bags, and if I had all the sacks full of doubloons I should be satisfied." The second said, "I wish the Strasburg Cathedral, from floor to roof and up to the very top of the tower, were full of bills of ex- change written on the finest note-paper, and accepted by substantial people, and that each bill were made out to my order and for the full amount contained in all your sacks put together." The third said, "I wish both of you had your wishes, and that you departed this life both in one night and left me as your heir and successor." The third companion went scot-free. VEGETARIANISM AND TEMPERANCE.—Spices, wines, and spirits destroy delicacy of taste, and deprive us of the means of pleasure which it affords, which must thence- forward be derived from the quantity instead of the quality of food and beverages; including the sottish in- dulgence of repletion and intoxication. This leads me to make a few remarks on food and beverages, which I cannot do better than derive from my own experience: —Being early impressed with the notion that the breed.- ing of animals for slaughter was a remnant of the savage state of mankind, and, in the highest degree, wasteful of the food resources which the earth offers to man, bru- -talising to many besides the butcher ; and being at the same time disgusted at the idea of chewing the flesh, the fat, the humours, the sores, and injured parts of animals, which are often besides in a state of general disease, I abandoned the use of flesh as food, and I abstained from it for six months. At the end of this time the mere odour or smell of cooked meat became inexpressibly disgusting to me, and it, extended my distaste to all other animal productions. For the following twelve months I there- fore used only bread, water, and occasionally, though very seldom, a bit of fruit ; nor during that period did I break the practice in a single instance. To truth I must submit, and to humanity I must declare, that under this diet my strength was unabated; besides which the clearness, freedom, and vigour of my mind was greatly increased. With regard to beverwies, I ought to observe that, happening in subsequent life to get into the habit of drinking wine and water after dinner, though always in such moderation that I was not once tipsy, I yet began to feel that a second glass was more desirable than the first, and this result alarmed me. I clearly foresaw the steps by which even men who are not -.especially prone to such indulgence do ultimately beccme drunkards. At the same time an idea impressed me that, during the time of this practice I had done less work than formerly, and after a. strict' examination I found such really was the case; and further, on closely obser- ving the operations of my mind, I discovered that I really had not the same love of intellectual pursuits as formerly, and that in particular I shrank from such as reuuired the greatest activity of mind. This was, of course, enough. In spite of the suggestion that sociabi- lity would be sacrificed (a lying suggestion in which selfishness and sensuality seek their apology), I " dashed down the cup of wine," and took up that of coffee in- se,ad. MY stomach, deprived of its usual stimulant, soon became satisfied. I had scantier excretions, a clearer mouth, and a clearer head. Intellectual objects resumed their influence over my mind, and sociability was enhanced a thousandfold.—" Walker, on the Nervous System." sAninsTEßs—whnFe prof4seortal labours necessitate long In- tervals trqween mPa's—uothing will be found 90 exhilarating, comfortin4, and car able of imstainin4 exhausted natu 13 as CaviburrN Coma. guaranteed absolutely pure. BEFORE You MARRY.—Of one thing girls may be sure, and that is that the young men who make the best sons and brothers will also make the best husbands. And young men may be equally sure that these girls who are the best daughters and sisters will also, as a rule, be the best wives. If the young man, before he is married, is destitute of those affections and principles which come out in filial obedience, courtesy, and a controlling sense of duty, he will be equally destitute of them after he is married. The mere fact of wedlock will not change the fundamental principles of his nature. He will be essen- tially the same human being after marriage—or, at least, after the honeymoon—that he was before it. The same principles hold true with regard to women. She who is selfish and vain and idle and deceitful as a girl, will be pretty apt to be the curses of the man who marries her; while the girl who is dutiful to her parents, and in- dustrious and unselfish and truthful, will be almost certain to be a blessing to him who gets her for a wife. THE BACHELOR'S SCREEN IN CHURCHES.—In the olden times it appears to have been customary to regard the unmarried men of a parish as a distinct body. We have bachelors' balls in our own day, and to this day in some parishes there is a field called Bachelor's Acre, where the single men once held their games. In churches it was the custom for the sexes to occupy different parts of the church, and in later times a separate place was provided for the bachelors. Shakspere makes Beatrice say of St. Peter in "Much ado •about Nothing"" He shows me where thebachelors sit" (in heaven). In the church of Thorp-le-Soken, in the county of Essex, is an ancient wooden screen formerly situated towards the east end of the north aisle, but now removed to the west end of the south aisle, in the centre of the upper part of which, on a scroll borne by angels, is the following inscription in black letters This cost is the bachelors made by ales Jhesu be tiler med, which means—" This cost (the expense of this screen) is defrayed by the single men of the parish by collections made for that purpose. • Jesus be their mode (reward)." The ales were social meetings at which collections were made. It appears, then, that the money which was re- quired for the erection of the screen in question was contributed on such occasions by the single men of the parish, and it is probable that the screen was placed in front of that portion of the church in which the bache- lors sat. CHILDREN -AND SWEET MEATS.—In the current 7 number of a religious monthly, the Rev. J. NV. Horsley, late chap- lain of the recently abolished Clerkenwell Prison, calls attention to an unsuspected cause of infantile depravity. "The perverted taste for lollipops." he says, "caused chiefly (because not prevented) by mothers, is a large— very large—cause of juvenile crime ; and, from a prison point of view, there is far more justification for an Anti- Lollipop League than for an anti-tobacco one." With- out going into the question of the connection between the craving for sweetmeats and juvenile vice—a ques- tion upon which Mr. Florsley's experience gives some weight to his opinion—it may be pointed out that there is nothing immoral or unwholesome in the gratification, within reasonable limits, of the saccharine tastes of children and women. On the contrary, the appetite is a far more natural one than that for tobacco, bitter beer, and very dry wines, so characteristic of manhood, and is certainly not more injurious. Of course, excess in sweets—as in any article of food—is calculated to cripple the digestive functions, and debilitate the constitution; and it is an unquestionable fact that many children, especially among the poorer classes, are permitted to in- dulge to a disgusting extent in the ingenious messes of the confectioner. There can be little doubt, however, that much of this infantile debauchery is due rather to sheer hunger, than to any pervers!on of appetite. So long as there are parents who fail to realise the fact that a rapidly growing child requires to be as well and as wisely fed as an adult, whose bones and tissues merely need to be kept in repair, so long will children be found ready to spend their uttermost farthing in cakes and lollipops.—British Medical Journal. THE SPECIAL AND THE ELEPHANTS.—With the elephant Mr. O'Shea, the well-known special correspondent, has more than a distant acquaintance. On one ocoasion he submitted to enthronement in a howdah in a Lord Mayor's show; on another he rode an elephant: across a tight rope for a bet, on the stage of Sanger's Hippo- drome. Of the character of the elephant he has not formed a high opinion; but the following anecdote shows that he was not ,fraid to put it to the test :—" A yoursg friend asked me once to show him some elephants in undress, and I took him along with. me, having first borrowed an apron, and filled it with oranges. This he was to carry whilst accompanying me in the saddle, but the moment we reached the door the herd set up such a trumpeting—they had scented the fruit—that he dropped the apron and its contents, and scuttled off like a scared rabbit. There were eight elephants, and when I had picked up the oranges I found I had five-and-twenty. I walked deliberately along the line, giving one to each. When I got to the extremity of the narrow stable I turned, and was about to begin tile distribution again, when I suddenly reflected that if elephant No. 7 in the row saw me give two oranges in succession to No. 8 he might imagine he was being cheated, and give me a smack with i his Iproboscis—that s where the elephant falls short of the thuman being,—so I went to the door and began de novo:as before: Thrice I went along the line, and then I was [in -a fix. I had one orange left, and I had to get back to the door. Every elephant in the herd had his greedy gaze focussed on that onsnere. It was as much as my life was worth to give it to any of them. What was Ito do? I held it up conspicuously, coolly peeled it, and sucked it myself. It was most amusing to notice the way those elephants nudged each other, and shook their pon- derous sides. They thoroughly entered into the humour of the thing."—Spectator. WIIY BABIES LOOK WISE.—In the Nineteenth Centuru appears ars'article on "Precocity and Genius," from the pen of Mr. Jas. Sully. The Daily News, commenting upon it, says every parent is interested in "Infant Phe- nomena," because in every family there is found at least one phenomenon among the infants. Now, what the father and mother of the wondrous child wants to know is, " Will this child live up to her or his amazing youth- ful genius?". !What are the odds against the miracle of six developing into the Mirandola of six-and-twenty? Putting aside music and mathematics, who is to decide on the reported merits of precocious children? In un- civilised races one man is 'commonly about as good as another in painting on the Walls of caves and scratching ornaments on clubs, and all can produce decorative effects which would baffle the•ordinary European. In the same way, most children will be drawing, and their attempts often seem wonderful and precocious to pleased parents forgetful of their own youth. The talent is rarely developed by instruction; it is allowed to die out, and, considering the vast crowds of mediocre artists, this can hardly be regretted. Mr. Sully says, with truth, that "it may turn out that the majority of great men have been remarkable as children." We could go further and maintain, without paradox, that the majority of human beings have been astonishing—as babies. Every mother—still more every grandmother—will agree with this opinion. Nor is their assent to be explained as mere fondness. Look at any baby and observe his astonish- ing appearance of wisdom and how much speculation dwells in Isis. eyes as he "takes notice." The truth is that the contrast between his personal feebleness and in- experience and his vast stores of accumulated inherited experience make a baby the most remarkable of living beings. He knows potentially all that has ever been known. His little brain—so big for the size of his body —contains all the impressions that have ever been made on human consciousness. They may never waken into conscious life, but there they are, and no wonder he looks strangely sagacious.

An American cattle breeder of experience says that a Galloway bull will sire more blacks than an Angus bull will, when crossing other breeds; the latter gives too many browns and brindles. The number of horses exported during the four months ending April 30 was 1,506, compared with 2,078 last year. Of these 373 went to Belgium, 164 to France, 350 to the United States, 14 to British North America, and,6os to other countries.

The popularity of the Clydesdale breed of horses in America is evidenced by the fact that a member of a Kansas firm has just purchased from a Paisley horse-• dealer 56 Clydesdale stallions at a figure which is said to be only very little short of £15,000. CALF-FEEDING.—" M. 0." asks whether hay-tea, given with an equal quantity of new milk, is a good and safe food for calves three weeks old. Might they be expected to thrive upon eight quarts of such mixture daily. At what age may linseed cake in small quantities be given? Unquestionably! Hay-tea has been often proved a capital displacer of milk for calves. A selection from the Westacre stud of Shire horses, belonging to Mr. Anthony Hammond, was sold recently by Mr. G. M. Sexton. The highest price was 90gs., for the mare "Mistress Mary," by "Honest Tom," which had gained prizes at the North Waltham and Lynn shows. Mr. Hudson gave the highest price for stallions (86gs.), for "Viceroy," by " Drayman " (665), dam " Westscre Lively." AMERICAN DEMAND FOR DRAIIUHT HORSES.—Within the past few years a powerful stimulus to breed draught horses of exceptionally high class has been created by the demand for such animals in the American and Cana- dian markets. Buyers from the Western Continent are now turning their attention to the English Shire horse. The efforts of the Shire Horse Society, and the influence of its annual exhibition of pedigree horses, have already done so much to establish the English horse to recogni- tion as one of specific and particular breed, that it may . _ _

be safely anticiPated in the iinmediate future that buyeis for the foreign markets will pronounce still more in favour of the Shire horse. STOCK SALES.—At the sale of Mr. Jefferson's herd of shorthorns at PPreston Flows, seventy-four animals averaged £l6 11s. Mr. Anthony Hammond's fifty-two shorthorns, sold at Westacre by Mr. John Thornton, averaged £2B 19s. At the draft sale of Bates shorthorns, the property of the Marquis of Exeter, Burghley Park, near Stamford, prices were very low; twenty-five cows and heifers averaged £23 6s. 2d. and six bulls £l5 6s. 3d. The herd of longhorns at Calke Abbey, Derbyshire, was dispersed by Messrs. Lythall, Mansell, -nd Walters. The forty-one cows and heifers averaged £22 75.; four two-year-old heifers, £l9 3s. 3d.; four yearling heifers, £l9 13s. 9d.; two heifer calves, £8 Bg.; and six bulls. £26. The oxen and steers, some of which were cross- breds, made good prices. _ _

_ LAMBS WITH SORE MOUTHS.—" S.S." writes :—" I have several with sore mouths, lips swelled and sore. Others have blotches on feet and near the eyes. One of the rams used last autumn has the same on his legs. They have a run of several fields, and hay-chaff in winter. Would your vet, or any practical man name the disease, cure, and preventive ?"—Your lambs are suffering from aphtha (probably a contagious form), to which they may be constitutionally predisposed by the use of a ram whose system was liable to become affected ,with dis- eases of this kind. The fact of sores existing on their limbs can readily be accounted for by the lambs rubbing their lips, &c., on these parts, either when lying down or standing (the hind limbs when in the former position). A few dressings with carbolate of zinc lotion, of the strength of ten grains to an ounce of water, and occa- sional applications of glycerine or olive oil, will soon effect a cure. Keep all affected animals away from the others, and have a fresh ram this season.

INFERIOR BurrEm.—Frequently the cause of butter being inferior arises from the presence of noxious plants in the meadows where the cows graze. 'There is more inferior butter made in the month of May than in any other, attributable to that being the period when these plants are most abundant. It is by no means uncom- mon to find a middling meadow for butter alongside of a good one, as very much depends on- the quality and sweetness of the grass. Where there are aquatic grasses and plants in the pastures it is seldom that really nice butter is made. Perhaps querist's meadow grov:rs coarse, sour herbage. If so, I should recommend his cutting the coarse part, and making hay or ensilage of it:; the cows will afterwards have more grazable land and sweeter grass than grows at present. It is notrgood management to let sheep feed along with dairy cows, as the former can graze closer to the ground than cows, and so eat the choice grasses, the cows getting only what they have left. Sheep also stain the grass, and leave it so that cows do not much care to graze after them.— Henry D.

SHEEP SHEARING.—In becoming a successful sheep- shearer, the first and most important essential to success is the position in which the animal is held. When this difficulty is overcome, practice, with a determination to do the work properly, will bring success. A sheep not properly held will be uncomfortable and restless, will kick its fleece into confusion, and gets many cuts and knocks into the bargain, entailing upon the shearer greatly increased labour, and rendering it impossible for him to do satisfactory work. The details of shearing can best be acquired by practice under the teachings of an experienced workman—one who will show the learner just how and where to open the fleece, and the proper position of the shears while so doing; how to avoid cut- ting the skin on the one extreme, or leaving too much wool on the other; how to keep the fleece during the progress of the work so as to preserve its form for con- venience in rolling and tying and assorting into its several grades when passing into the hands of the manu- facturer; how to keep the shears in order, and how to become proficient in the other details which go to make up the accomplishments of the expert shearer. Among , sheep-shearers, as among men in every other calling, there are many good workmen and many who are the I reverse. To the flock owner the good ones are worth all they ask for their labour; the' inferior ones will prove dear at any price. More discrimination on the part of the employers will be nothing more than justice to the former class, and will doubtless bring about some im- provement among the latter. SWINE FEVER AND ITS STARTING POINTS.—For some months past the county of Lancashire has had perhaps a larger proportion of cases of swine feverf than any other county in the North. The following remarks on the disease from Mr. H. Humfer. Abingdon, will be read i with interest :—" Corn damaged with salt water, or' heated and then mildewed, is found to be a very fruitful source of danger. It gets the animals into a low, fever- ish way through eating it; and then the doubly noxious vapours from the manure bespeak actual fever as a pro- bable result. Of course, such food has to be made the best of, and the safest plan to do so would seem to be to feed it in a large, open space, and to give the pigs a chance to run out part of their time; and during this change into pure air, give them a change also of pure food and clean water. Under these conditions, with this daily opportunity of righting themselves, it is astonish- ing what they can stand in the way of upinvitin, food and impure surroundings. Even in common single stys, bad drainage and imperfect ventilation are very danger- ous things. I will give the details of a case that came under my notice a few years ago. I mention it because there were three cases of fe-yer originated in the sty at intervals; they did not all occur during the same occu- pation; the last case was since the appointment of County Inspectors, and immediate slaughter was ordered. The farm has since changed hands, and the present occu- pier has moved the stys. Still a description of them may give some idea of what we lay ourselves open to by disregarding sanitary precautions in the very simplest I of our stys and stock yards. It was a double sty of the plainest description, the "house part was a lean-to against the end of a barn, and facing south-west, covered with blue slate, the ends closely walled up and not the slightest ventilation ' • the, outside yard was close-fenced, with open-paled doors. An under- ground drain starting near a stable and taking the runnings from the cattle yard as well, ran through the open yards of the stys with a grating in the centre of each, and emptied some distance down away from the stys. The consequence was an unfailing supply of foul air from this common sewage up through the gratings; then a hot sun and a slight current of air through the paled doors gave the pigs in the close houses the full benefit during their afternoon nap. The chances are that if these animals could have had a three hours' run in a meadow or large open yard daily they would have passed through the danger without fever; when they have sound lungs and are otherwise healthy, it is only a continuance of foul air that seems to overcome them. The sty itself, as I have described, is one of the most common that could be found, and without these draw- backs would have been fairly healthy. Amongst the many thousands of stys in the country that would have general features almost identical with this one, it would be interesting to know how many have the same disad- vantages. I notice this case in the hope that any source of danger of the same kind may be recognised. Altera- tions made at the instigation of an inspector would never go on so pleasantly as when the owner and occu- pier have the sole arrangement. And yet there seems an unaccountable discrepancy between this treatment of fever and that in the case of a human being suffering from the same disease. In the one case we do every- thing possible to cure the patient, and condemn every- thing doubtful in the way of closets, drainage, and ven- tilation; in the other, we condemn the animal to imme- diate slaughter, and allow the suitability of the stys for receiving other occupants to remain almost unques- tioned."

FOOTBALL COMPETITION AT ST. HELENS. VICTORY OF WARRINGTON. The semi-final and final ties in the seven-a-ide feotball contest, arranged in connection with the annual sports of the St. Helens Cricket Club, were played off on the ground at Denton's Green-lane, on Saturday night. .They had been postponed from the previous Saturday, when the four clubs left in were the St. Helens No. 1 and No. 2 teams, Warrington, and Southport Olympic. There was a fairly large attendance of spectators, and daring the matches, con- siderable excitement was manifested. BT. HELENS (No. 2) V. WARRINGTON.—The first couple to step into the field were the St. Helens No. 2 team and Warrington, and the players were as follows :—St. Helens : J. Dearden, full back; H. Pennington (captain) and C. Anders, three-quarter backs; D. McLoughlin, T. Finney, C. Ross, and W. Arnold, forwards. Warrington : J. Au- derton (Wigan), full back; W. Speakman and J. Buxton, tlree-quarter backs; H. Ashton (captain), T. Davies, W. Povey, and C. Unsworth, forwards. Having won the toss, Warrington chose to play with the sun at their backs, and Pennington kicked off for St. Helens. Arnold followed well up, but Ashton cleverly collared him. The subsequent scrimmaging was in the visitors' quarters, and the home lot infused some energy in the game. Buxton ultimately relieved with a short run and kick to the centre, where Speakman made a good attempt to score, but Anders collared him and threw him to the floor; the ball going into touch. Anderten, who played brilliantly throughout, next dis- tinguished himself by a clever run, and notwithstanding Pennington collared him on the line be struggled and se- cured a try. Buxton failed at the place-kick, making a bad attempt to secure the major point. Almost immediately afterwards Ashtcai rushed down the field, but Pennington enther luckily upset him. Just before ends were changed the home team secured a dead ball, and at half-time War- rington led by four points (a try) to one. On resuming Anderton rushed in St. Helen's quarters but be was collared, and Pennington in attempting to relieve had his jersey stripped from his back. For a few minate3 the play was even, but Warrington afterwards premed thefr opponents, tile defence of the Warringtouians being splendid, while the forwards dribbled and kicked well. After the visitors had secured a minor point, some desperate scrimmages in the St. Helens quarters ensued, resulting in Anderton securiug a try amid applause. From the place kick Anderton kicked a beautiful goal (8 points), and this placed Warrington ahead by 13 points to one. No other score was registered, and Warrington thus won by the points mentioned. Sr. HELENS (No. 1) v. :-...OIITHpORT OLYILPIC.—The tie between these was very exciting, and the players were:— St. Helens: A. Tickle, full-back; E. Foreman and A. Borth- wick, three-quarter backs; W. James, J. Halton, J. Basnett, and W. Grice forwards. Southport: J. Barnes, full back; W. Lund and P. Booth, three-quarter backs; Summers, Moorfield, Robinson, and Gill, forwards. The 'visitors won the toss, and Borthwick kicked off. Booth made a good re- turn, and while rushing with the ball Tickle collared him, and both fell heavily to the ground. From a scrimmage in the visitors' quarters Borthwick made an attempt at drop- ping a goal, but failed. Lund next eluded Borthwick and Tickle, and by a splendid run obtained a try (four points), straight between the posts. Gill was entrusted with the place kick—one of the easiest possible positions—but he made a miserable attempt, which evoked derisive laughter from the spectators. No other noticeable incident was wit- nessed before half-time. On the resumption there were cries of "Play up, St. Helene," and the home team at once carried the ball into the visitors' quarters. From a throw in Foreman touched the ball, and knocked it about a yard forward, but he caught it before it fell, and rushing forward he grounded the leather behind the posts, claiming a try. The referee (Mr. Vicars) disallowed the point on a claim by Southport, on the ground that the oval had been thrown forward. This decision gave rise to hooting from the sup- porters of the local team. Southport subsequently had the best of the scrimmaging, but St. Helens secured a minor point. The StaHelens team afterwards played with despera- tion to stave off the threatening defeat, and in the last four minutes Borthwick threw in splendidly to Tickle, who by a beautiful drop kicked a goal (six paints) amid prolenged cheers. In the remaining few minutes the visitors tried hard to secure an equalising point, but they failed to do so, and St. Helens won by seven points to four. FINAL TIE: WARRINGTON v. Sr. HELENS (No. 1).— The final tie was played, after a short interval, between the Warrington and St. Helens No. 1 teams, and was un- doubtedly the most exciting and fiercely contesttd tie in the contest. Anderton started the ball for Warrington, and a good follow-up was made, the scrimmaging resulting in a minor for Warrington. After a few minutes loose play in the centre of the field, the ball was kicked towards the St. Helens 25, and Buxton securing, eluded Tickle and made a try. Anderton took the place kick, and though it was from rather a difficult position, he landed a beautiful goal (eight points) amid some applause. Though Warrington had now a good lead their opponents pliyed hard, and Foreman, in the course of a spleudid run was only luckily stopped by Speakman, who was his last opponent. Unsworth next ap- peared to advairage for Warrington, but Foreman collared him amid cheers when crossing the goal line. The play was afterwards of a rough character, and while Anderton mani- fested signs of lameness, Grice received an injury to his face, causing blood to flow profusely from his nose. No further point was scored before half time, when Warrington led by nine points to nil. The second half was very exciting, and St. Helene had by far the best of the play Borthwick resumed by kicking the ball forward, and after some scrimmage Basnett nearly scored a try, but Speakman collared him on the goal line. Basnett again distinguished himself after a pass by Tickle, and he gained a try, which wae disallowed on a claim of "off-side." Playing well to- gether the home forwards pressed Warrington, and Basnett. Grice, and Foreman passed splendidly, but, Buxton and Anderton were almost impassible. One or two minors were notched, and during the play Speakman received an injury to his ankle which compelled his retirement from the field. Thus weakened the visitors played a defensive game, but amidst cheers Foreman gained a clever try (four points.) This was from a difficaelt position, and it was no surprise that Borthwick failed to secure the major point. The score now stood: Warrington 9 points, St. Helens 7 points. Amid increasing excitement St. Helens secured another minor two minutes from the finish, but they could do no more, and Warrington thus won the first prize (L 7 by .9 points to 8 pointe.
THE HOME RULE QuEsroN. IRISH MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
On Monday evening a meeting of Irishmen was held in the National League Hall, Warrington. The chair was taken by Mr. Loughlin and there was a crowded attendance.

Tbe CHAinerele said they were there that evening to sup• port Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule proposals. (Hear, hear.) They could not that night give a vote in the House of Commons in favour of those proposale, but they could pass a resolution which would go to swell the number of propo- sale that had been passed up and down the land, and they could help to swell the mighty chorus which had risen in every clime and every land where Irishmen do dwell, and further than that they could promise that their words of that evening should be turned into action at the -very earliest opportunity. (Applause.) The resolutions they passed that night would be changed into votes as soon as they had the opportunity. While on that subject of the election— which, if they might believe the press, was not far distant —he might say they in Warrington were in a very fortu- nate position, because he believed the contest would be a fair stand-up fight. (Hear, hear.) EN did not anticipate that they should have thrust upon them any of those so- called Unionist candidates, and consequently the issue will be clearly Home Rule or no Home Rule—to be or not to be. (Hear. hear.) They were also fortunate in having a candi- date, Mr. John Crosfield—(applause)—who had promised in public that he would support Mr. Gladstone and his propo- sals for Ireland through thick sad thin. (Applause.) He was sere his countrymen would forgive him if he took upor himself to say to Mr. Croefield that if he intended to do that they also would support him through thick and thin. (Loud applause.) And let his fellow countrymen remem- ber that they held in this town the balance of power and decided the fate of parties, and if those who held Liberal principles remained true to those principles at the next election they need have no hesitation in saying that the election was as good as fought and woo, and that the gentleman whom he bad named would be sent to the House of Commons to give a vote for Englana. for Ireland, and for Mr. Gladstone. (Loud applause.) As to the merits or demerits of the measure then before Parliament he did not profess himself to be a judge, but he would remind them that the leaders of the Irish people had accepted this measure as one calculated to satisfy the just aspiration of the Irish ' people, and claiming as they did to be loyal followers of these leaders they could not but do the same. The opponents of the measure, and he was sorry to say they were sadly too many all predicted terrible and dire calamities should it pass. It was to lead to the disruption of the Empire, the repeal of the Union, 1 and he knew not what, whilst it was to be injurious to Eng- land and disastrous to Ireland. Well, he thought it was drawing too strongly on their credulity when they were asked to believe that Ireland could be worse governed by a native Parliament than by an alien one. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was of opinion that if this measure passed the gulf which had existed between the two countries would be bridged over, and the relationship between England and Ireland would be better and firmer than ever in the past. (Applause.) The differences which it was now proposed to settle had kept Englishmen and Irishmen who lived in Eng- land apart, but he honestly believed that if this bone of contention was removed Irishmen would then settle down and, looking at things from an English point of view, would join shoulder to shoulder to bring about those grett and necessary reforms that had been too long kept in the beckgreund. (Applause.) There was one thing particu- larly edifying about the discussion en the Home Rule pro- posals during the last two months, and that was the educa- tional effect it was havines on the English people. Irish- men had said over and over again that Ireland had been oppressed and coerced simply because the people were igno- rant of the needs, the aspirations, and the desires of the Irish people, and that as soon as the English people were educated as to what Ireland needed then oppression would be removed and Ireland would get her rights. (Applause.) Therefore they were delighted because they felt that a system of education was going on at the present time. The measure might be now lost, but he believed it would never die. (Hear, hear.) The Irish people had fought so long for it that they might be surd they would not now give up the battle when they had behind them the words of an Eng- lish statesman second to none that this century had pro- duced—the memorable words of Mr. Gladstone when he said " I am not offering, nor will I be a party to offering, Ireland any measure that she will not accept." (Applause.) These were the grandest wo:ds an English statesman ever offered to Ireland and they were words that would live as long as history existed and words that deserved, and he (the chairman) knew would receive, the eternal gratitude of the Irish people the world over. (Loud applause.) Mr. KEAN moved, "That we recognise in Mr. Crladstone's Home Rule proposals an honest attempt to settle the Irish question, and we pledge ourselves to give them all the sup- port in our power, and furthermore we offer to the right hon. gentleman our hearty and sincere thanks for this his message of peace to our long misgoverned country." (Loud applause.) Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Kean said, like others had to get educated on this Irish question, but when once Mr. Gladstone saw that Ireland had been wrongly managed he had turned to a different course, and set himself about doing all he could to remedy the mistakes of the past, and it was their business to second him in that. (Applause.) Mr. DONLAN aeconded the proposal, and said that Irish- men were unanimous all the world over that nothing abort of self government would bring peace and contentment to the Irish people. (Hear. hear.) It might be asked who were against the present measure. First of all, of course, there were the prophets, but Mr. Grattan said you could not argue with a prophet—von could only disbelieve him. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) That was the best way they could deal with them. Then there others who told them that all the educated and intellectual people of England were against the measure. Well, before they labelled them all intellectual they should allow them to be weeded a bit. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He had read in an English paper that only two English speakers bad treated the Irish question from the historical point of view, and these were Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Morley. (Loud aoplause.) Mr. Clarke, in his speech, said Ireland had not a Parliament of its own in 1796, and repeated that again and again until Mr. Dillon turned round and said to him "You may be an excellent lawyer, but you have let to learn the rudiments of Irish history." (Laughter.) Mr. Clarke then sat down, and they heard no more of him. Another opponent of the bill, a Mr. Fisher, asserted that one of the first things the Irish would do would be to elect John Mitchell to the Irish Senate, and one of the Irish members had to get up and tell him that John Mitchell was dead and buried long since. (Loud laughter.) He had heard of dead men voting in Warrington in the election of 1868, but he had never known a dead man to be elected to represent any constitu- ency in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The time had now come when the democracy of England and Ireland should join together and give the indolent classes a taste of Adam's doctrine—that they had to earn their bread by the sweat of their brow. (Applause.) Re- ferring to the disclosures in the House of Commons as to arrangements made between Tories and Parnellites at the last election, Mr. Donlan said that Mr. T. P. O'Connor had let a young cat out of the beg—(laughter)—and he was greatly mistaken if Mr. Parnell did not let the old one out that night. He did not know whether their chairman could let a cat out or not, but if he couldn't let a cat out he could let fly a pigeon. (Loud laughter and applause.) The resolution was then carried unanimously amidst applause. Mr. Fox proposed "That we pledge our confidence once more in Mr. Parnell and the Irish Parliamentary party, and resolve to hold ourselves in readiness to vote at the next election as he in the interests of Ireland may indicate." (Cheers) They had, he said, every reason for placing con- fidence in Mr. Parnell and the Irish party, because they have been tried and found faithful. When Mr. Parnell took the leadership of the Irish party Ireland was indeed at a low ebb, and the people were at the feet of the tyrants of Irishmen. Mr. Parnell's first work was to relieve to some extent the weight that oppressed the people of Ireland, and since he became leader the rents of the people had been re- duced by about 20 per cent., and their miserable coulition bad been greatly ameliorated. The people of Ireland would at one time have been satisfied with very little, but now they wanted the power to manage their own affairs and exscute their own laws. As far as they could judge that power would he given them. In the present Parliament the Irish race scattered throughout the world was represented, and if England would grant the moderate demands of Ire- land the whole Irish question would be solved, the people of England and Ireland would join in the bands of fellow- ship, separated only by the silver streak of the Irish chan- nel, and the British Empire would make more progress and grow to greater strength and power. (Applause.) He should not like to picture of consequence of a refusal of the , demands, because there was not an Irishman with a spark of patriotism in his nature, but would feel dissatisfied if the moderate request of the Irish representatives was refused— they would look upon it as a black and hateful and detes- table act. Irishmen, he claimed, had never been hostile to the English, and there had, he said, never been a movement for the improvement of Englishmen and the establishing of their rights that Irishmen had not been ready to join. They had every confidence in the Irish Parliamentary party, and only awaited their comhsa.nds. They would not say for what party they would vote, but he must express gratitude at the conduct of Mr. Gladstone and his followers at the present time. Mr. Tuolterrote briefly seconded the resolution, which was carried without dissent.

Mr. SWEENEY, organiser for the North of England said that in Warrington at the last e!ection the Irish achieved a signal triumph in putting the Conservative candidate in, and, if thry should be asked to evict the Tory candidate and elect Mr. Crosfield in his place they had power to do so. (applausf..) Mr. Cox (Manchester) also addressed the meeting, which was brought to a conclusion at about half-past ten o'clock, with the customary votes of thanks.

To carry the business of life you must have surplus power. Be fit for more than the thing you are now doing. Let every one know that you have a reserve in yourself, that you have more power than you are r,tow using. If you are not too large for the place you occupy you are too small for it. Oh! if you could only witness the terrible struggles passing in the heart of that friend whose vivacity annoys you, whose fickleness provokes you, whose faults sometimes even make you blush. If you saw the tears that are shed in secret, the vexation felt against self (perhaps on your account), you would indeed pity them. Love them; make allowances for them; never let them feel that you know their failures.

The Duke of Devonshire has granted to the tenantry on his Chatsworth estate a remission of 15 per cent. on theil' rents for the last half-year. -SUP-POSED POISONING AT A SHTON.—By order of the Home Secretary, the bodies of Thomas Rritland and his daughter Elizabeth Ann, were exhumed on Thursday morn- ing at Dukinfield Cemetery. As already reported, the wife of the deceased man is in custody on the charge of mur- dering Mary Dixon, by administering vermin killer, and is suspected of causing the death of her husband and daugh- ter as well. All three persons died after a few hours ill- ness, and the post-mortem examination revealed strychine in Dixon's stomach. He fixed himself up at his very best, hair parted in the centre, perfumed handkerchief, very broad cuffs, very high collar, very shiny silk hat, very large seal ring, very I striped pants, and an overcoat that swung open, show- ing delicate-coloured silk lining. He was going down town to apply for a situation m a commission house. Entering the office with abundant assurance: "Good morning, sir. I understand there is a vacancy—" "Never fill a vacancy with a vacuum here, sir! Good morning." The merchant measured him with one look. WHY HI3 DID NOT CONSULT HElL—Counsel (to wit- ness): Was your wife with you on the occasion referred to ?—Witness: No, sir.—Counsel: You are sure? Re- member you are on: oath.—Witness. I am quite sure.— Counsel: Was she present with anyone else ?—Witness: No, sir.—Counsel : Did you tell her that night ?—Wit- ness: No, sir.—Counsel: Or at any subsequent time ? Witness : No, sir.--Counsel: You said nothing to her whatever ?—Witness: Not a word.—Counsel (getting angry) : Now, state to the Court the reason or reasons why you did not consult with your wife regarding the I important events which occurred on the occasioh men- tioned.—Witness: Because I haven't got a wife.

div.p: HOUSE COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the House Comm-lase expressed a wish that the admission notes sent by the relieving officer to the workhouse master be duly filled up as to the inmate's char- acter, religion, and, in the case of children, legitimacy, so that the classification might be correctly recorded.—Mr. Baowis moved the adoption of these(lminutes, and said there were certain books provided for the master to fill up, and it was supposed the master would get the requisite in- formation from some source. The committee thought there WAS no source so likely to afford it as the officer who sent the inmate to the house, and this was not an uhreasonable request to make ef the officers, and it was something that had been done before —The CLERK pointed out that the duties of the relieving officers were defined by law, and all he was required to do was to fill up an order form to authorise the admittance of the person to whom it referred. He advised that it would be a proper thing for the officer to voluntarily undertake the daty referred to when he could do so, hut he did not think it desirable to pass a resolution directing the relieving officers to do what they were not legally required to do. Lliear, hear. )—Some discussion having taken place on the point, Mr. Brown agreed to withdraw the minute in question, and the rest of the minutes were then passed. THE SURCIIAROB ON THE WORKHOUSE MASTER.

With regard to the surcharge on the workhouse master made by the district auditor at his last audit of the Union accounts of the cost of 271bs. of tea alleged to have been used in the workhouse in excess of the authorised quantity, Mr. VOISEY moved, "That a letter be addressed to the Local Government Board suggesting as to the surcharge of 271 be. of tea by the auditor on the workhouse waster-1. That the auditor be called upon to state in formal shape) exactly how be creates that deficiency, and into the state- ment made by Mr. Mackay of the manner in which he has supplied that deficiency in making a deficiency in milk. 2. That he carefully go through the whole dietary scale, so far as it affPcts the supply of milk, to ascertain what milk should have teen supplied during the six months, and how far the supply has been short of what the scale warranted. 3. That he then ascertain how the 2711,3. deficiency of the tea has been supplied to meet the deficiency of milk so as- certained."—This proposal was agreed to, and the Clerk directed to forward it to the Local Government Board in le- ply to their communication on thct subject.

THE SCHOOLS. The minutes of tbe Padgate Schools CotriTeittee stated that the doctor bad reported that the general health of the children was very good.—On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, the minutes were adopted.

SCHOOL FErg. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been granted in 61 cases, 49 of which were old and 12 new c4ses —On the motion of Mr. Braciuitresr, seconded by Mr. Jomon-, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: 7.11 E WORKHOUSE.
div.p: 7.11 E WORKHOUSE.
The Master of the Workhouse reported that the Local Government Board Tnspector, Mr. Stevens, had visited the house, and found everything in good order.
RESIGNATION OF DR. JOSEPH.

A letter was read from Dr. Joseph, Bo1(17r-street, Warring- ton, resigning his position as medical officer of No. 1 dis- trict, a position which he had held since January, 1879. The resignation was accepted, and the Clerk was instructed to advertise for a successor. VACCINATION IN EARLESTOWN. • Mr. CLARKE said that a few weeks ago he visited a child that had been vaccinated named Savage, whose parents live in Legh-street, Eirlestown, and found that it had eight distinct marks on its right arm. He then wrote to the Local Government Board about it, because the Act of Parliament only allowed four vaccination marks to be made. He wished to know if the officer at Newton who vaccinated the child had gone outside the law on this occasion.—Mr. BRoWN thought that notice of a question like that ought to have been given. They could not answer a question like that off hand.—The 'CHAIRMAN said that perhaps Mr. Clarke would give notice that he would ask the question at the next meeting of the Board.--Mr. CLARKE said he would do SO, and also that he would furnish the clerk with a copy of the letter ho had sent to the Local Government Board in order that the clerk might write to Dr. Watkins for an ex- planation.—The subject then dropped.

WALLING DAY. On the motion of Mr. W. HOUGHTON, it was agreed that the railway fares of the Padgate School children, when attending the Walking Day procession in Warrington,should be defrayed by the Board. The relief cases were then proceeded with.
Prosperity shines on different persons much in the same way that the sun shines on different objects. Some it hardens like mud, while others it softens like wax. _ .

"I am just as much opposed to tippling as anybody," said Fenderson ; "but nevertheless liquor rightly used is a blessing to humanity. When I was ill last winter, I actually believe it saved my life." Fogg—" Very likely; but how does that prove that liquor is a blessing to humanity?" INQUISITIVE INQUIRIES.—What is the length of a broad hint? Would going up in a balloon be the best way to have a high time? Does a ship suffer from tight lacing when in stays? Does a cutting proverb remind you of a saw? Are dead walls ever buried? If a barrel manu- facturer is ill does he go to the country to stave off his illness and recooperate? Would it be cheek to kiss a lady on the side of the face?

A learned Berlin professor has given to the world the information of what makes a "merry twinkle." It is caused by a peculiar abrillar-like movement of the lids, the orbiufilarius palpebrarum and the parts around the nose. The new reading of "Twinkle, little star," would then be :—" Abrillar-like movement of the lids, the orbiu- filarius palpebrarum and the parts around the nose diminutive satellite."

The queru- lous tones and pale faces give place to cheerful words and the rose-hue of health; or possibly the grave will have hidden them from your sight for ever. THE GREEK QUESTION.—RA,ISING OF THE "PACIFIC BLOCKADE." AmtENs, MoNraY.—The representatives of Great Bri- tain, Austria, Germany, Italy, and Russia met at the Rus- sian Legatioa at noon to-day, and signed a Note formally announcing the raising of the blockade. The Greek Government has sent a note acknowledging the receipt of the above, and has telegraphed to all the Greek ports noti- Roation of the raising of the blockade. ATHENS, TEESDNY.—The Greek prisoners were formally aerrendered to-day by the Turkish military authorities, There was an animater debate in the Chamber to-day on the bill for electoral reform. M. Leviths strongly condemned tile measure and also spoke in condemation of the attitude ot the King 'during the recent crisis. His remarks elicited booting and other signs of disapprobation from the occu- Pants of the public gallery, which was cleared by order of the President. Finally the first reading of the first section of the bill, providing for reduction in the number of Depu- ties, was carried lw a majority of 27. The result was re- ceived with loud applause in the public gallery. the bill Nating to officers of the army seeking election was also read a first time.

AFFAIRS IN BURMAH. Camel:rm., SIIIIDA.Y.—The condition of the united provin- ces continues far from sltisfactorv. Public opinion in In- dia is all but unanimous in pointina. to Sir Charles Ber- nard as the mrs an primarily responsible and, as far as I Can gather, the same op;laion is h.ld in Burmah. ANTI-AUSTRIAN DEMONSTRATIONS. ROME. SIINDA.Y.—Violent anti-Austrian demonstrations are announced to have taken place at Padua on the occa- tien of the recent Garibaldi demonstrations. A conflict °c- entred between the police and the rioters, of whom many Were students. Several of the latter were wounded, and 53 Were arrested. MONDA.Y.—R.rIeWed diStnrhAnCeS, caused by a fresh demonstration against General Janskv, occurred here , 'Ast night. Although the streets were blocked by detach. Ciente of troops, many shop windows were broken by the rioters, who wets, however, prevented from assembling in rest force at any particalar point. Several persans were Wounded, and Si arrests were made. EXPULSION OF THE FRENCH PRINCES.—LETTER FROM PRINCE NAPOLEON. PARIS, SATURDAY —The Council of Ministers to-day re- jected the recommendation of the committee on the Expul- °toe Bill that the measure should be general and compul- sory, and adopted the proposal providing for the immediate exPulsion of the Legitimist or Bonapartist pretenders in the direct line, and empowering the Government to expel the Other Princes if considered necessary. The committee on the Expulsion Bill to-day heard the explanation of M. de Freycinet, and elected as its reporter M. Maret, who is op- posed to expulsion in any shape. PARIS, MONDAY —Prince Napoleon has addressed a letter to the members of the Chamber of Deputies protesting against the exile with which he is threatened, not, he says, as a pretender, for he is no pretender, but as chief of the family of the Napoleons. The Prioce,.while declaring that be would willing.y accept exile should it tend to the country's good, points out that tbe*perils to the Republic trise rather from the vices of its monarchical Constitution and the bad policy of the country's rulers. The exile of the Princes, will, moreover, involve the proscription of eitizens, the revival of the reign of terror, and finally of civil war. The letter conelu lee by expressing the bone that the people will shortly see who are its true friends. 'he committee on the Expulsion Bill has rejected the re- Port prepared by M. Maret, and has finally adopted the pro- -Poaal that the Legislature should pass a bill banishing all the Princes, without distinction. M. Pelletan was elected the new reporter. ILLNESS OF EX-PRESIDENT ARTHUR. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY.—General Arthur's state of health is now such as to cause alarm to his friends, and grave doubts of his recovery are entertained. The General Was unable to take his usual drive yesterday. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN.' CAIRO, WRDNESDAY.—The Conference on the Soudan question between the Kbedive, Fir H. D. Wolff, and Ahmed ' caukbtar Pasha was resumed at the Abdin Palace last night, When it was decided to instruct the Ebedival delegate at Wady Haifa that it was impossible to permit the entire re- cloening of trade with the Soudan so long as disturbances continued and an advance of the insurgents was threatened. The delegate 'will, however, be authorised to allow the Kab- babish tribe, in recognition of their friendly attitude, to ob- tain provisions through Wady Haifa. • VOLCANIC ERUPTIONS IN NEW ZEALAND. It is stated from Wellington that there has been a terri ble eruption of the Tarawera Volcano, accompanied by Shocks of earthquake. Great loss of life is reported among the natives, and some Europeans are also stated to have Perished. FIGHTING ON THE WEST COAST OF AFRICA.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT._
ROUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his set shortly after 4-0. The Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Bill was read a second time. THE MURDER BY MOONLIGHTERS.—The Earl Of LIMERICK asked for information concerning the murder of Patrick Tagney, near Kilarney.—Earl SPENCER stated that the motive for the murder was supposed to be that the deceased had taken steps to allow men from outside to get bog on an estate with which he was connected.—Lord ASHBOURNII asked if the noble Earl had any reason to doubt that this was an agrarian morder.—The Earl of KilateßLEtt observed that Earl Spencer had said nothing so absurd as that the murder referred to was pre-arranged. Some of the moon- light affairs were pre-arranged.—Lord FITZGERALD pointed out that in all probability the judge before whom the mur- derers would be taken, if any of them were apprehended, would change the venue from Kerry to Cork, in which county in such cases as this there would be no fear of a mis- carriage of justice.—The subject then dropped. RAISING OF THE GREEK BLOCKADE.—The Earl of Rose- sway announced that a telegram had been received from the Duke of Edinburgh stating that the blockade on the Greek coast had been raised, and that the fleet had returned to Sada Bay. (Hear, hear.) Their lordships rose at 5-15. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDaY. The Speaker took the chair at 4.0 PRIYATE BILLS.—The St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Bill was read a third time.—The Nelson Local Board Bill was considered and ordered for third reading. THE ARREST OF SIR T. HESKETH.—Mr. CHILDERS, in answer to Sir Richard Cross, said he had obtained some fur- ther particulars with regard to the action of the Chief Con- stable of Northamptonshire in ordering the arrest of Sir Thomas Hesketb, and was informed that the warrant was signed on the same day as the arrest, and within a few hours after the arrest had been ordered. (Laughter.) He thought the best plan would be or the right hon. gentle- man to move for the letters which the Chief Constable had addressed to the Home Office on the subject. THE RIOTS AT BELFAST —ln reply to Mr. Sexton and Mr. Johnson, Mr. JOHN MORLEY said his information did not enable him to do more than confirm in substance the news- paper reports of the regrettable incident at Belfast. The riot originated in a quarrel between two navvies of different religions, in the couese of which one was struck by the other with a spade, his assailant making a remark to the effect that the other would never be allowed to earn a crust of bread there again. The iniured man reported his injury to some friends in the shipbuilding yard, and the result was an attack was made on the navvies, ending in one being severely injured and one death by drowning. The coroner's and magisLerial inqeiries were proceeding. Four arrests bad been made, and more would probably follow. It was not right, pending these proceedings, that he should ex- press any opinion on the merits of the case. Answering a further question by Mr. Sexton, Mr. Morley said he under- stood the assailants were far superior in numbers to those whom they attacked. He had received a telegram this I afternoon stating that further disturbances might possibly take place, but there was an abundant force of police and a large number of military on the spot. A SUGGESTION TO THE PRIME MINISTER.—Mr. BANNIS- TER FLETCHER asked the Prima Minister whether he would incorporate provisions for the self-government of England, Wales, and Scotland in the Bill he proposed to revise relat- ing to the government of Ireland, instead of introducing separate bills for those objects, and whether he would call such revised bill the Government of Great Britain and Ireland Bill Mr. GLADSTONE said there were two grave objections to the course indicated. One was that an attempt to deal with England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland in respect of self-government in one and the same bill would entail an amount and complication of provisions scarcely possible to manage in a single measure. The other was that the ques- tion implied that the wants and wishes of England, Scot- land, Wales, and Ireland were the same, with respect to which he had no evidence that would enaute him to take that view. THE HOME RULE BILL REJECTED. SPEECHES OF THE POLITICAL LEADERS.—MR.

PARNELL AND THE TORIES. The concluding night of the Home Rule debate drew an unpreeedentedly large audience. At prayer time every available seat was occupied, and when business began the House and the galleries were crowded from floor to roof. Mr. Bright, who took his seat for the first time during the debate, was warmly cheered, as were also Mr. Gladstone and Lord Hirtington. The adjourned debate was resumed by Mr. Grosenere, who began by regretting that the issue had become confused by the events of the last fortnight until scarcely any member knew precisely what he was going to vote on. At the foot of the matter lay the supremacy of Parliament, and be contended that it.was seriously impaired by the bill, and dependent entirely on clauses and condi- tions in the bill which, in all probability, the House of bpuots iht nb loi fe v et dh et bRa to mt haenl r iCs ha tlhaoi tl yi c sw towardswould be a tt the Commons never would assent to. Another important point mwasinortiltlye, Ea rnega ltadn ids aidnvtahnet iarg:setrui ngelbeeiwnig dethtphreiveeldergoyf to ohe geassistance f t r l of education. The fiscal arrangements of the bill were cer- tain to lead to friction; and, in feat, the legislative, com- mercial, and executive friction certain to result from the bill must lead to separation. Mr. PARNELL, who was received with cheers, said that uf all the lost causes which he had ever heard him attempt to defend (loud Ministerial and Irish cheers) during many years, Mt. Goschen was never less effective thin in contending against this bill. (Cheers.) tie condemned the occurrences in Kerry, and agreed with Mr. G-oschen that they ought to be put a stop to. (Irish cheers.) The right hon. gentleman wanted to put a stop to them by the old method of coercion, which had been tried for the last 86 years, and they said with the Prime Minister, "Try the effect of self-government." (Irish cheers.) If Kerry men then resorted to outrages, they would soon find that the rest of Ireland would put a stop to them. (Irish cheers.) Mr. Goschen spoke about the subordination of Parliament. He and his friend knew perfectly the differ- ence between a co-ordinate and a subordinate Parliament. They recognised that the proposed legislature was subordi- nate Parliament. The argument was now against him that he was precluded from accepting this solution as final be- cause he had claimed the restitution of Grattan's Parlia- ment. He wished to point out that there were practical advantages in a statutory body subordinate to the Imperial Parliament which would render it of much nine use to the Irish people than Grattan's Parliament. Grattan's Parlia- ment had many disadvantages. It had a House of Lords. (Laeghter.) They got rid of the House of Lords under the I constitution of this bill. It was true that there would be the first order—a very salutary proposal, although he did not agree with the extent to which it was empowered to hang up bills—but it would tend to prevent rash legislation and immoderate action. It was perfectly understood that the Imperil! Parliament would have the ultimate supremacy and the ultimate sovereignty. In Grattan's Parliament the Executive was divorced from the Legislative body, and one of the most important parte of this bill was that it threw on the Legislature by their'Executive the duty of maintaining order in Ireland. In accepting the bill they placed them- selves under an honourable obligation not to abuse their powers, and the Irish members pledged themselves for the Irish people, as far as they could pledge thern—(Oppostion laughter and loud Irish cheers)—not to abuse those powers, but to use all their energies and abili- ties and influence that they might have to pre- vent such an abuse. In case, however, such abuse occurred, the Imperial Parliament retained the full power to intervene, but only to intervene in case of grave and urgent necessity. The measure had been accepted by the leaders of every section of national opinion not only in Ire- land hut outside Ireland. (Renewed cheers.) Not a single voice had been raised against the bill by any Irishman of Nationalist opinions. So far as was possible for a nation to accept a measure cheerfully, freely, gladly, and, without re- serve, the Irish people had shown that they had so accep- ted it. (Loud Irish and Ministerial cheers.) ,He would re- fer to Mr. Goschen's fears with regard to a possible abuse of power by the Catholic priesthood with regaid to educa- tion. He had not attempted to fan the ft urne of religious discord in Ireland, and the fears he expressed were no doubt sincerely entertained by him. He assured him that the Irish people would be able to tattle this question of educa- tion amongst themselves. (Irish cheers.) There were many Liberal • Nationalists who did not altogether share the views of the Roman Catholic Church on the question of education, and these men were very much influenced in the desire they had to see Ulster remain an integral part of Ireland by the feeling they had in this matter. With Ulster in an Irish Legislature there would not be the slightest risk of the Catholic priesthood using their power unfairly to- wards the Protestant population. Even if they gave a separate legislature to Ulster they would net protect the loyal minority, because there were outside the province of Ulster over 400,000 Protestants who still would be without protection ; and in Ulster the Catholics and Protestants were about equal, and the Nationalists had been successful in returning a majority of the Ulster members. The first thing an Ulster legislature would do would be to unite itself with the Government of Ireland in Dublin. (Cheers.) Driven away from the fiction of Protestant Ulster, the op- ponents of the bill sought refuge on this point in the north- east corner of Ulster, consisting of three counties. But they could not give up a single Irishman. (Cheers.) They wanted the energy, the patriotism, the talent, and the work of every Irishman. This Protestant class would form a most valuable ele- ment in the Irish legislature of the future. (Cheers.) They regarded their presence as vitally necessary to the suc- cessffil trial of this experiment, and they could not admit that thereiwas a single one of them too good to take part in this work. (Cheers.) He bad been reproached that In his speech at Wicklow he had claimed the right of protection for Irish manufactures. and that this bill gave no right of Protection. Undoubtedly he did claim that right, but it was not when a Liberal Government was in power. (Laughter and cheers.) That speech was made when they had reason to know that if the Conservative party had been successful at the polls they would have offered Ireland a stateitory 12gislature with the right to protect her own industries— (loud and prolonged Irish and Liberal cheers)—and that would have been coupled with a settlement of the Irish land question on the basis of purchase en a larger scale than that sow proposed by the Prime Minister. (Beamed cheers.)
