Government—of a free Executive, such as was proposed for Ireland. (Cheers.) They proposed that measure because Ireland wished to make her own laws. It was not enough to say they were prepared to make good laws. The member ' for West Birmingham had proposed alternatives, and plenty of them. He said a dissolution had no terrors for him He did not wonder at it. He did not see how dissolution could have any terrors for him. he had trimmed his vessel and detached his rudder in such a masterly way that whichever wind of Heaven might blow it would fill his sail. (Loud laughter and cheers.). Supposing at an election public opinion should be very strong for the bill, the right hon. gentleman was perfectly prepared to meet that public opinion and to say, "I declared strongly that I adopted the prin- ciple of the bill." Suppose, on the other hand, that public opinion was very adverse, he was again in complete armour, for he could say, "Yes, I voted against the bill!' (Laugh- ter and cheers) Suppose public opinion was in favour of a large plan for Ireland, his right hon. friend was perfectly irepared for that case also, because the plan was not large mough for him, and he proposed in his ..speech on the in- reduction of the bill that he should have a measure on the .of federation. But lastly, suppose that public opinion Add take quite a different Ulm, and instead of wanting iery large measures for Ireland, should demand very small measures, still the resources of the right hon, gentleman were not near exhaustion, because then he Was able to point out that last of all his plan was for provincial councils con- trolled from London. (Loud laughter and cheers.) But those plans were only the visionary creatians of a vivid Imagination born of the hour and perishing with the hour, utterly and absolutely unavailable for the solution of great and difficult problems, the weight of which and the urgency of which the right hon. gentleman himself in other days had seemed to feel. Lord Salisbury said, complaining of the construction which had been put upon his words, that he was not favourable to coercion but only legislative pro- visions for preventing one man interfering with the liberty of another, and for ensuring the regular execution of the law, and that they said was not coercion. ("No, no.") Was that their view six months ago, when the Government proposed to enact clauses against boycotting. "to prevent one man from interfering with another," and to facilitate change of venue "to insure the execution of the ordinary law ? " The late Government proposed a measure of coer- cion, an 4 by this time, if they had proceeded with it, we should have been torn by conflict. Let his hon. friend recol- lect that this was the earliest moment in Parliamentary his- tory when they had the view of Ireland authentically ex- pressed. A practical majority of the Irish people never had been brought together for such a purpose. Could anything stop that nation's demand except its being proved to be im- moderate and unsafe. There were millions upon millions who believed the demand to be neither immoderate nor un- sefe. There was only one question about this demand. That was as to the time and circumstances of granting it. There was no question in their minds that it would be granted. (Ministerial cheers.) The opponents of the measure had wealth, rank, organisation. What had its sun- porters? The people's hearts, the promise of the harvest of the future. (Ministerial cheers.) He believed there was in the breasts of many men who would vote against them that night a profound misgiving that the end would be as they foresaw it, not as his opponents saw it—that the ebb- ing tide was with them, and that the flowing tide was with the Government. (Ministerial cheers.) Ireland stood ex- pectant, hopeful, almost suppliant. Her words were the words of truth and soberness. (" Oh," and Ministerial cheers.) She asked a blessed oblivion of the past; she asked also a boon for the future. Such was her demand. Let them think, then, not for the moment, but for the years to come, before they rejected this bill. (Prolonged cheers.) Mr. Gladstone sat down at five minutes past one o'clock, having spoken about an hour and a half to a full and sym- pathetic House, and the division was then taken in a scene of unexampled excitement. When the Speaker put the question, there was a loud and long-drawn-out "Aye " from the Radical and Nationalist benches, and the response was an equally loud "No "from the Opposition side.

He uhonld never have thought, and did not think, of claim- ing protection from the Liberal party, and he recognised this settlement as final without protection. But there was another stronger argument still. The Prime Minister had shown them that they would gain by the proposed arrange- ment £1,400,000, v.hich he regarded as a very good quid pro quo, as he had already said. With regard to the question of the retention of the Irish members, be tried to keep his mind open upon it, and not to regard it as a vital question. rb• provisions in the bill for terminating the representation of the Irish members had been very vehemently objected to by Mr. Trevelyan, who had said that there was i4o half-way holm between separation and the maintenance of law and order in Ireland by the Imperial authority. Well, in his judgment there was no half-wav house between the conces- sion of legislative autoaomy to Ireland and the disfranzhise- °lent of the country and its government as a Crown colony. (Irish cheers.) But he refused to believe that these evil days must come. He was convinced that there were a suffi- cient number of wise aad just men in the House to cause to disregard the appeals which had been made to passion, and pocket. Let them choose the better way of the Prim, Minister, the way of peace and goodwill amongst nation, and when the numbers in the division lobby were told t( night it would be also told for the admiration of future gene, ations that England and her Parliament were wise enough. brave enough, and generous enough to close the strife of centuries, and give peace, prosperity, and happiness to suf- fering Ireland.. (Loud cheers from the Irish members.) Mr. M. HOWARD argued that tbe commercial prosperity of Ireland had materially increased Since the Union. and maintained that there was no evidence that the industrial Glasses of that country desired Home Rule. Mr. Menzies and Mr. E. R. Ruesell spoke in support of

the bill, and Mr. Muntz opposed it. Mr. J. Cowin's, who was received with loud cheers by the Irish members, spoke in favour of the bill. They did not desire to strap Eagland and Ireland together like a pair of angry hounds, but to weld them together by the magnetism of reconciled interests. Events were stronger than Cabinets. Party combinations would not stop the progress of this bill. The bill might not be a victory, but it was the herald of victory. (Irish cheers.) Sir M. Him-13nm said the history of this bill was re- markable. It did not represent the views of the leaders of the Liberal party, for with one great exception all those leaders were going to vote against it. The bill was the pro- I duction of one man—(Opposition cheers)—the highest, no doubt, in authority and in power in thie country. (Minis- terial cheers.) The member for Cork said that his demand I for power to protect Irish industries was made at a time , when he had reason to suppose that if the Conservative party had been successful at the polls they w uld offer him' a statutory Parliament for Ireland. Mr. PARNELL : With power to protect Irish industries. (Ministerial cheers.) Sir M. HICKS-BELCH : With power to protect Irish Indus- tries. That wauld surely be a more agreeable proposal than! the bill now before the House. (A Voice: "No," and I langhter.) If the Member for Cork really believed that he I could obtain from a Conservative Government a bill that would be more agreeable to him and his party than this I bill, why did they not vote against the measure .now before the House? (" Oh," and laughter.) For himself and his colleagues he entirely and categorically denied that the late Government ever had any such intention. (Loud Opposi- tion cheers.) Mr. PARNELL, rising amid the loud cheers of his friends, said: Does the right hon. baronet deny that that intention was communicated to me by one of his own colleagues, a Minister of the Crown? (Prolonged Ministerial cheers.) Sir M. HICKS-BEACH : Yes, I do—(loud opposit!on cheers, and cries of "Natne " from the Ministerialists)—to the best of my belief and knowledge—(ironical cheers and laugh- ter), and if any such statement was communicated by any- one to the member for Cork I sin certain he had no authority to do so. (Loud Opposition cheers, and renewed cries of "Name.") Will the member for Cork name to the House the member? (Loud Opposition cheers.) Mr. PARNELL : The right hon. baronet .has asked me a question which he knows is a very safe one. (" Oh" from the Opposition, and Ministerial cheers.) I shall he very glad to give the name of his colleague when I receive his colleague's permission. (`. Oh, oh," and Ministerial cheers.) Sir M. HICKS-BEACH said insinuations were easily made —(Opposition cheers)—but proof of them was a very diffi- cult thing, and he had observed that the method of the gentlemen below the gangway stopped at the point when Proof became necessary: (Opposition cheers.) Resuming the thread of his speech, he went on to comment on the unusual prolongation of the debate with the assent of the Government, did the manner in which it had been used to bring persuasion, influence, and intimidation to bear on those Liberals who could not change their minds as rapidly as the Government. For all practical purposes he insisted that the bill did away with the supremacy of the imperial Parliament and handed it over to the Parliament in Dublin. As to the presence of the Irish members, the propea/ d alter-1 ations, while they would irreparably injure the Imperial Parliament, would not remove the main objections to the bill. The Pretestants of the North, he pointed out, were unanimously elat Intel at the bill, because they dreaded not so much legislation as unfair administration. The question of Ulster was the first difficulty, and the Conservative party would decline to give to the Roman Catholic majority a power over the Ulstermen which would be worse than any Coercion Act which had ever been passed. The measure destroyed the advantages of the Union, and did not satisfy the national sentiment, and he prophesied that the decision of the country would be decisive against it. MR. GLADSTONE, on rising at 11-25, was received with loud cheering, which continued for several minutes. He prefaced his remarks by eulogising the speeches of Mr. Parnell and Mr. Cowen. Sir M. Hicks-Beach had stated a series of "simple facts," which were as devoid of founda- tion as if they had been fictions. (Laughter and cheers.) He declared that this was the bill of one mail. (Opposition cheers.) How could anyone know that it was the bid of one man? (Cries of "Mr. Chamberlain.") Mr. Chamber- lain spoke within the cempaes of his own knowledge, and if he said it was the hill of one man, he knew no more about it than the noble lord. He stated the time when this bill came before the Cabinet. But long before that time the subject of the bill and the leading outlines of the bill had been matter of anxious consideration between him and his nearest political. friends. (Ministerial cheers, and cries of "Name.") Sir M. Hicks-Beach said the bill would be rejected by the votes of the majority of English and Scotch members—(Opposition cheers)—and be was cheered by those who above all things were anxious for the maintenance of a Parliament in which the Irish members were to be assimilated with English and Scotch members. It was absolutely beyond dispute that what was to be voted upon was the principle of the bill, as distinct from the particulars. As to the particulars, members voting for the principle cf the bill were entirely and absolutely free. (Ministerial cheers.) The question of Ulster was a ques- tion of principle. As yet no separate plan for Ulster had ,nade any effective progress. On the subject of Irish loyalism, he said the member for Belfast and other gentle- men appeared to be under the pious conviction that loyalty was innate in the Irish Protestant and disloyalty innate in some other persons. (Laughter.) Many gentlemen were greatly enamoured of Federation, and the object they had in view was a noble object. If the means could be de. vised of establishieg a more active connection with our distant possessions the subject was well worthy of the interest of every enlightened man. It was beset with more difficulties than had been examined and brought to light, but this bill was unquestionably a stew in the direction of Federation. (Ministerial cheers.) Federation rested on two essential pre-conditions, first the division of legislatures, and next the division of subjects' and both were among the vital objects of the bill. (Cheers.) As regards supremacy, the debate had cleared the ground on that subject, and the balance of authority established clearly that whether that Parliament was an Imperial Parliament or not, so long as it continued in its legal identity it possessed now, as it possessed before the union and before the time of Grattan's Parliament, a supre- macy absolutely and in the nature of things inalienable (Hear, he.) In constituting a legislature in Ireland they devolved an important portion of powers—a real and prac- tically independent management of her own affairs. That was what the right hon. gentleman opposite objected to do; that was what they desired and hoped and meant to do. (Loud Ministerial and Irish cheers.) How were they to deal with cases where the Imperial Government were com- pelled to interfere ? That question had received a far b-t- -ter solution front the practical ;politics of the past 40 or 50 years than would ever have been given by the definitions of lawyers. As it had been perfectly easy to reconcile the rights of Canada with the supremacy of the Imperial Par- liament, it would not be less easy in practice to reconcile the rights and the autonomy of Ireland with the same authority. He beard constantly the words Unionist and Separatist. Who were the Separatists? (Loud Ministerial cheers.) To describe the bill as a Separation Bill was the merest slang of velgar controversy. (Loud cheers.) Could they give an instance where acknowledgment of local in- depeedeece bad been followed by severance of coun- tries ? (Loud Ministerial cheers, and Opposition cries of " Servia " and "Roumania.") He was just going to refer to them, but be asked were they going to wait till some third power intervened, America for instance. (" Oh," and Irish cheers.) Could they give a single instance where apart from the intervention of a third power, the acknow- ledgment of local independence had been followed by sep- aration? (Loud Ministerial cheers.) He would show where total severance of countries had been the conse- quence of an attempt to tighten the bongs ; in the case of England and America, of Bel- gium and Holland; in the case of Denmark and tbe Duchiee. Having on the otber side mentioned the case of the Islands Crete, Lebanon, and the Island of Samoa, he said: Even Turkey here testimony tbat the principle of local autonomy produced contentment. Then there was the most remarkable case of Norway and Sweden, of Den- mark and Iceland. (Laughter.) There were difficulties between Iceland and the Crown of Denmark, but not with the legislative body of Denmark.' (Cheers.) Fiulend had perfect legislative autonomy, and was contented. The case of Austria was perhaps the most remarkable of all. Galicia,

though part of that unhappy country Poland, was conten- ted with her autonomy ; while Russian Poland was at this moment subject to difficulties. Mr. Chamberlain said that the Legislative Councils were introduced into Canada for the purpose of protecting the minority. Where did lis fi,nl that? (Cheers.) lie read. not long ago the debates in the Parliament of the Legislative Councils in Canada, and from beginning to and there was not a word about their beine appointed for the protection of a minority. (Cheers.) Be- ween 1830 and 1840 Great Britain and Canada bad a most remarkable difference. These differences were completely wed ad • healed by the establishment of a responsible

THE POLITICAL SITUATION. IMPENDING DISSOLUTION. MINISTERIAL MOVEMENTS.

IThe greatest interest centred on Tuesday in ihe movements of the Premier and the Ministers, and from a comparatively early hour there was an un- usual activity noticeable in the neighbourhood of Whitehall. Mr. Gladstone rose somewhat later than usual, and as lie was none the worse for his exertions in the early hours of the morning, he was soon busily engaged in preparing for the Cabinet Council to be held in the afternoon. Sir Henry Pon- sonby, the Keeper of the Queen's Privy Purse and Private Secretary to Her Majesty, had remained in town to acquaint her Majesty of the progress of events, and he called on the Premier during the forenoon. Messengers from the other members of the Cabinet visited Downing-street, and at the Treasury there was unusual bustle and activity. Great interest was attached to Tuesday's meeting of the Cabinet. It lasted from two o'clock until twenty minutes past three, when Lord Rosebery and Mr. Campbell-Bannerman left together, fol- lowed by Mr. Mundella walking alone. Sir Henry Ponsonby, who had been awaiting the result of the Ministerial deliberations, next left the Premier's re- sidence; and Earl Spencer and Mr. John Morley next walked away together engaged in close conver • sation. Mr. Childers, the Earl of Kimberley, and the Marquis of Ripon, who followed, proceeded to their respective offices, and Sir William Harcourt re- mained for some little time at the Treasury before leaving for the Home Office. Lord Rosebery had a long interview early in the forenoon with Mr. Gladstone. _ _

The Press Associatirn says :—We have high au- thority for stating that the decision arrived at by the Cabinet on Tuesday was unanimously in favour of dissolution. We are further informed that her Majesty communicated through Sir H.F. Ponsonby her assent to this course. The Cabinet did not re- solve on an appeal to the country without much de- liberation. The alternative of resignation was dis- cussed, and was at first preferred by more than one Minister, but it having been ascertained that Lord Salisbury would decline to form a Government if sent for, and that Lord Hartington was indisposed to take office unless on the understanding that a dissolution should be the immediate sequel, the idea ' was abandoned. Dissolution was seen to be the ' outcome of the situation, and there being no reason to believe that delay would tend to reunite the ! Liberal party, it was felt that the sooner the ver- dict of the country was ascertained the better. The " dutiful communication" conveying this intelli- gence to the Queen was sent to Balmoral on Tues- day night, the substance of the despatch having ;been telegraphed by ir H. F. ronsouhy immeat- ately after the rising of the Cabinet on Tuesday afternoon. Although no formal decision had been taken previously, afrequent interchange of views on the subject amongst Ministers had rendered the result of the Council a foregone conclusion, and as I soon as the defeat of the bill was assured prepara- tions were set on foot for a general election. On Wednesday Mr. Gladstone received his col- leagues in his private room. In the course of the ! consultation Mr. Arnold Morley, the chief Liberal I, Whip, waslsummoded to lay before the Ministers his report as to the state of feeling amongst Liberals generally in view of the forthcoming contest. The right. hon. gentlemen present were Mr. Childers, Mr. John Morley, Mr. Stansfield, the Marquis of I Ripon, the Lord Chancellor, Mr. Mundella, and Sir I W. Harcourt. The Home Secretary, who was the last to arrive, reached Downing-street at the same time as Mr. Schnadhorst, who had been invited to give his testimony respecting the election pros- pects. The meeting lasted from noon until two o'clock, when most of the Ministers went to their respective offices. Shortly before the proceeding's closed Sir Henry Ponsonby arrived at Downinc,- street. He remained with the Premiei until after 4 o'clock. In the course of the afternoon Lord Rose- bery also called on Mr. G ladstone and remained with him nearly an hour. SCOTCH SELF-GOVERNMENT ASSOCIATION.

At the residence of Mr. Marjoribanks, one of the Government whips, a conference was held of Scotch peers and the Scotch members who voted in favour of the bill. Lord Rosebery presided, and among those present were Lords Elgin, Aberdeen, Dal- housie, and Huntley. It was agreed to form an association called the Scottish Association for Pro- moting Self-Government in Ireland. Lord Rosebery was elected president, and Lord Elgin, Lord Aber- deeu, Lord Dalhousie, and the Marquis of Huntley vice-presidents, and an executive committee was appointed, with power to add to its number, to place itself in communication with a view to pro- mote the One question of self-government in Ire- land, and to carry out Mr. Gladstone's policy in relation thereto. Dr. Clarke, MP., Dr. Cameron, M.P., Mr. Gilbert Beith, M.P., Mr. Duff, M.P., Mr. Marjoribanks, M.P., Mr. Edmund Robertson, M.P., and Mr. Haldane, M.P., were appointed members of , the committee.

including Mr. Caine, with whom he had an inter- view of considerable length, at which they had under discussion the future policy of the right hon. gentleman and his followers, and the extent to which, if any, they should make common canoe with the Liberal Unionists who have followed Lord Hartington. Mr. Chamberlain, it is understood, fa- voured an independent course, and the result wag, we understand, that it was decided immediately to - start a national organisation having its head-guar. ters in Birmingham, in the shape of a Radical Union, having for its object to secure a large e.xten. sion of local self-government to England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland, under the authority of one su- preme Parliament for the United Kingdom. Mr. Chamberlain, it is stated, has agreed to accept the presidency of the new association, and Mr. Jesse Collings will act as hon. secretary. A number of members of Parliament have already expressed a willingness to become vice-presidents of the Union. Wednesday was a tolerably quiet day. at Mr. Chamberlain's. The right hon. gentleman received a few political friends in the forenoon, but it- was tacitly agreed that no active steps should be com- menced until after Mr. Gladstone's public announce- ment of her Majesty's decision. The Premier is ex- pected to issue his manifesto within a. few hours of the official intimation of the, dissolution. Mr. Cham- berlain will probably publish his address on the fol- lowing day, and will visit his constituents as soon as .possible afterwards. Meanwhile the Radical Union for the Promotion of Self-government in Eng- land, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales will be actively engaged in the furtherance of the cause of the Unionist candidates. The association will work quite independently of the Spring Gardens organ- isation, though both will.join in opposing supporters of Mr. Gladstone's policy at the polls. Promises of support to the new bOdy are already coming in freely, and a large number of gentlemen:have inti- mated their desire to have their. names enrolled as members. Home Rule Radical members protest, strongly against the formation of such an organisad. tion.

LORD HARTINGTON AND THE LIBERAL' UNIONISTS. The departure of Lord Hartington for Ascot on Tuesday tempozarily diverted public attention from the doings of the section of the Liberal Unionist& who follow the noble Lord, but on his Lordship's return on Wednesday morning to Devonshire House there was a return of activity to the quarters fre— quented by his supporters. It is understood that ' after a lengthy deliberation a decision was arrived at to oppose the principal Ministerial candidates with the help to a greater or less extent of the Con-. • servative party, with whom, it is stated, an arrange- ment has practically been arrived at on this basis. No Unionist Liberal supported by Lord Hartington's Committee would therefore be opposed by a Con- servative, and on the other hand the Unionist Liberals would not interfere with safe Conservative seats, while each would 1-klp the other by means of electioneering literature and similar assistance. This arrangement, if carried out, is not expected to- extend beyond the general election, and it is under- stood that it does not necessarily indicate a coali- tion for other purposes than the electioneering arrangements of the two parties. After the meet. ing Mr. Goschen returned to the Liberal Union offices in Spring Gardens, and with other members of the Union was busily engaged the remainder of the day in putting the decision of the leaders into operation. Both Mr. Chamberlain's Radical Union and Lord Hartington's Liberal Union will probably have the assistance of the organisation of the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union.

- PREPARATIONS FOR THE ELECTION. 1 Amongst the supporters of the Government there lis an extraordinary activity. Mr. Schnadhorst was at the National Liberal Club early on Tuesday con- ferring with English and Scotch Liberal members I of Parliament on the subject of the selection of candidates and other matters affecting seats which are to be contested on behalf of the Government The 'Government whips are besieged with callers, mostly gentlemen representing Liberal Associa- tions throughout the country, having matters to discuss relating to a possible dissolution, and an almost overwhelming mass of correspondence, due to the same cause, is daily received and despatched 'from the Treasury. In the course of the afternoon Mr. Schnadhorst had a long interview with Mr. Arnold Morley at Downing-street, and amongst other gentlemen who were closeted with the Patron- age Secretary to the Treasury were Mr. Conybeare, M.P., and other persons interested in the organisa- tion of Devon and Cornwall. The labour members. ,_dp not regard a general election with Any apprehen- sion, although they make no secret of the fact that I some financial difficulty will be caused. On Wednesday Mr. Arnold Morley was again busily engaged on electioneering business. Amongst others who called on the Whips were Mr. Illing- worth, M.P., and Mr. Coote, M.P. At the National Liberal Club, which is gradually becoming the recognised centre for provincial Liberal activity, there were frequent conferences throughout the day, Mr. Schnadhorst and other well-known organi- sers being much in request.

A Queen's messenger arrived at Downing-street, on Thursday morning, with despatches from Her Majesty in reply to the recent communication from the Premier. Consent was given to the dissolution of Parliament.

Lord Hampden, the late Speaker of tliß House of Commons—whose son "told" against the Govern— ment in the division—is a warm supporter of Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy. A letter has been received from Mr. F. W. Graf— ton,•M.P., who is present in Austria, intimating that on account of ill-health he is compelled tc.- retire from the representation of the Accrington Division.

It has been resolved by the Liberal Council of the Damen Division to contest this seat against Lord Cranborne. Mr. Potter, the late Liberal candidate for the division, has declared himself against Home Rule, and a new candidate will consequently be chosen. _ . • . .

The Birmingham Home Rule Association have decided to run Home Rule candidates against Mr. Bright, Mr. Chambedain, Mr. Merrick, Mr. Dixon, and Mr. Powell Williams in the event of Mr. Broad- hurst and Mr. Cook being opposed by Liberal Unionists.

It has now, we are informed, been definitely arranged that Mr. Gladstone will visit Midlothian, should there be a dissolution, and deliver, perhaps, a couple of speeches. Mr. Gladstone rose early on Thursday morning and entered vigorously Upon the preparatory work for the coming electoral struggle. The two Ministerial Whips and his secretary, Mr. Primrose, were closeted with him during the morn- ing, but beyond them the Premier received no visi- tors.
Mr. Chamberlain contradicts the statement pub- lished in a London morning paper that he dined with Lord Salisbury on Tuesday evening.

• FUTURE ACTION OF THE CON- SERVATIVES. In the quarters frequented by members of the Conservative party, with the exception of the pure- ly official and working departments, there was not much stirring in the early part of Tuesday, many members having left town for Ascot to attend the races. In the afternoon, however, several leaders of the party, including Sir Michael Hicks-Beach and Lord Randolph Churchill, visited the Carlton Club, and informally discussed the situation with their supporters, among whom were many who were unsuccessful candidates, at the last election, and who, it may be presumed, are ready to fight the battle again. There was a general congratulation on the result of the division, but as to future action, it was understood that no step could be taken of a definite character until after the meeting of the House of Commons. Preparations are, however, being pushed forward, in the full expectation of an immediate dissolution, and the most sanguine pre- dictions as to the issue were indulged in: Lord Salisbury left town fOr Hatfield on _Wed- nesday night, but othen prominent members of the late Government remain in London, and throughout the day there has been a large attendance at the Carlton, St. Stephen's, and other leading Conserva- tive clubs, whilst at the central offices everything points to immediate activity. It is generally under- stood that the Conservative policy will follow the lines marked out in the Marquis of Salisbury's speech at the St. James's Hall meeting, and that no Conservative candidate will be run against those who voted against the Home Rule Bill unless local circumstances demand it in the interests of the party. By adopting this course it is calculated that the Conservatives will win some thirty seats, mainly at the expense of Mr. Gladstone's followers; but at the same time it is admitted that there are constituencies in which seats will be lost by the alienation of Irish support which was given to the Conservatives at the last election. MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S RADICAL UNION.. At Devonshire House there was for a time on Tuesday a rapid arrival of visitors, including Mr. Goschen, who had a lengthy interview with Lord Hartington. His lordship left, however, about noon for Ascot races, and interest was diverted again from thence to Downing-street. Mr. Chamberlain received at Princes-gardens several of his followers,

ALLEGED CONFESSION OF A MURDER AT NEWTON. The following is taken from a Liverpool paper on Wednesday :—" A sensational story is being freely circulated at Lovvton, where an old man named Smith has recently died, having had both legs amputated, the result of an accident whilst working at a neighbouring colliery, it is alleged that in his dying moments Smith confessed to his nurse and doctor to having taken part in a murder in that district many years ago, he and three com- rades, during a spree having quarrelled with a man, taken his life, and afterwards thrown him into an old disused pit, where he is alleged to have been found by a workman the next morning. Accord- ing to the story the man named his three com- panions, all of whom are now dead. Whether the alleged confession be true or not, the inhabitants well remember the three men named, all of whom came to a sad end. One is said to have been killed_ an the railway, another died on the way to his wife's funeral and was carried home on a door, whilst the third died in the workhouse." Inquiries which have been made in refer- ence to this report show that there is some foundation for a portion of the statements made. It has been ascertained as a fact that about 40 years ago the dead body of a man was dragged from an old pit at Lowton, near Newton, and anin- quest was subsequently held. There was no defi- nite evidence as to how the vim got in the pit, but the only marks on the body were a scar on the nose,, and an apparently old wound on one of the legs. The then coroner, it is stated, expressed his belief that the deceased had committed suicide, and the jury returned a verdict to that effect. The matter- has since been forgotten, but the report alluded to has revived consideration of the fact stated, in some of the old residents of the district. Up to the present it is believed the authorities have taken no action in the matter.

div.p: reached in the present Parliament before its dissolution. He should propose that the Government should have precedence on all days for financial business. As to the Whitsuntide recess, the Government proposed to adjourn on Friday rrigin until Wednesday next. Their disposition was to drop bills which conlc! be considered of a contentious character. As to the Railway Rates Bill, it was of a magnitnde that rendered it impossible for the Government to prosecnte it compatibly with their intention of rapidly winding up the business of the session. He did not abandon the hope that the Medical Acts Amendment Bill might pass into law. With respect to Supply, it was proposed that they should go forward with the votes on the Navy Estimates precisely as had been in- tended. The votes for the array would next be taken,and then the Government would propose a vote on account for the Civil Services to carry them on to the 31st of Octo- ber. That would enable the Appropriation Bill to be brought on on Wednesday next, and on the following day the usual statement would be made on the education vote.. The Indian Budget would be taken on Monday week.—Sir M. FlicKs•Baacs moved the adjournment of the House in order to be able to criticise the speech of the Prime Mini- ster.—This having been assented to in the usual manner by 40 members rising, Sir M. flicas-Baecrt wished to know the exact-date at which tbe Prime Minister anticipated that Parliament would he dissolved. He wished to urge that considering the embittered relations of the different political parties in Ireland no time should be lost in dissolving the old Parliament and in summoning the new.—Mr. GLAD.. STONE said be could not give thedate of the dissolution, but he hoped it might take place before the close of the month. —Sir M. limits-Bract,' expressed satisfaction with Mr. Gladstone's statement, and asked leave to withdraw his mo- tion, and this was agreed to. THE NAVY ESTIMATES.—The House then went into COMI tnittee cf Supply on the Navy Estimates. A vote or £2.034,000 for the Admiralty offices was agreed to. Othe votes were taken up and discussed at length. Mr. ACLANE brought in the bill to amend the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Fishing Boats Act, which was read a first time. The House adjourned at 4-G.

t kit. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill is lost II? far as Parliament is concerned; but be- Parliament there is the people, and the have every confidence that an appeal to tte Country will result, in the long run, in illrengthening the hands of those who are th favour of giving Ireland the largest mea- t4"re, of self government consistent with the bsalritenance of the integrity of the empire. 1e majority of thirty against the Govern- it is larger than was generally expected; 4,14 it is not, after all, a large number ; for if wiXteen only of the Liberals who went in the prong lobby had voted with the rest of their C,rtY, the second reading of the bill would r,ve been carried. Perhaps when, in the ti4l`tire, the historian comes to deal with he Home Rule question, the surprise to 1;41 will be that as many-as 3r r members of 4„arllament were found voting in its favour, e'twithstanding the opposition of such emin- Alit Liberal politicians as Lord HARTINGTON, t• CHAMBERLAIN, and Mr. BRIGHT. It IAB impossible, of course, that the present Ql,,Lt Could become law; if it had passed the telllrnons it would certainly have been rejec- 'by the Lords; so that it was merely a tiltlestion of time as to when it should go be-. c're the country. We have always been pre- to admit that there was much force in HARTINGTON'S plea that the present trliament had no express mandate to go e full length of setting up a Parliament r,1)°11 College Green ; and we cannot sup- that such "an old Parliamentary hand" ti) kr. GLADSTONE had the remotest hope it would be possible to carry out the 11c37 of Home Rule for Ireland without an Peal to the country. But with his genies .15'llstructive statesmanship the PRIME MINIS. Was not satisfied to proceed by way of stract resolution; he determined to formu- fte a scheme; hence the Government of freland Bill which, whatever im minor de- hets, proves singularly acceptable to the rc)ople of Ireland, and has so attached itself , the people of this country that, while other oposals have crumbled under criticism, it tl.tllds its own and stands without a rival in Dge field. The rank and file of the Liberal t4rtY have been quick—quicker than many till their leaders—to see and acknowledge e. Wisdom and justice of the demand for jetaislative autonomy for Ireland ; and thus tilaPpens that to-day the country is riper on Als question than the House of Commons. yet it is not to be gainsaid that a dis- t'illtion within the next few weeks will ea great disadvantage to the Liberals. gt house divided against itself cannot an.d though the division in this se is not large, it may prove sufficiently I,rge to give a seat here and there to the ':)tles. It is just possible, indeed, that the Orlservative party, if they are aided through- by the Secessionists, may find themselves a majority in a new House of Commons; th. then what would be the result ? Not enty, but at most two years of coercion- 11ch to the disgust of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN 1,1.1 d his friends, who would feel, we imagine, t they ought to put on sackcloth and :hes. Lord SALISBURY seeks,. after his p°llt, to unsay himself, and would have De°Ple believe that he has not advocated a leY of coercion ; but both Mr. GLAD- and Mr. JOHN MORLEY have so pinned e,141 down to his own words that he cannot alse. Speaking as the guest of the ghty Club," on Tuesday evening, Mr. t)ItLEy asked : did Lord Salisbury say? liesaid in St. 4:ll4es's Hall " The alternative policy is that Tiarlia- hetit should enable the Governmnt of England to ai:ertt Ireland. Apply that recipe honestly, con- th'ently, and resolutely for twenty years, and at e end of that time you will find Ireland will be to accept any gifts in the way ,of local s9lf- 4wiernment or repeal "—of what ?--`. of coercion tpor (Cheers.) Well, but if Lord Salisbury never ke'-e in the sense of coercion, what do those words )411? How can you repeal coercive laws that It never been passed! (Cheers.) t is ridiculous, it is mean, it is cowardly of D?1:d SALISBURY to seek to shuffle out of a 10424 construction of his own language. Not togg since, when the Tories were challenge.d ti,Mate what policy they proposed in opposi- C 4 to that of giving Home Rule for Ireland, itV RANDOLPH CHURCHILL exclaimed— *a he policy of the 26th January." And that It was the policy which the I ries announced on that date through their ,e4d • z er in the House of Commons as that of 4Ppressing the Land League." This was ercion pure and simple, and to deny it is ,pffirm that words have no meaning. th, he Tories have no other policy now, 'ugh there is evidence that they had a dif-
I,

ferent policy in view when they were seek- ing, by the aid of the Parnellites, to dish the Liberals prior to the election. Mr. PARNELL states in the most unequivocal manner that when he made his speech at Wicklow it was 1" made at a time when ,they had every reason to know that the Conservative party, if they were to be successful at the polls, would have offered Ireland a statutory Parliament, with a right to protect her own industries, and that that would have been coupled with a settlement of the Irish Land Question on a basis of purchase on a larger scale than that now proposed by the Prime Minister." It is true Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH denies that the Conservative Cabinet were party to such a proposal ; but that does get rid of the fact that the communication to Mr. PARNELL was, at any rate, made by a colleague of the Tory leader and a Minister of the Crown. But we shall hear more of this, for it is the key that unlocks several mysteries, if it does not quite open the door of the "Cabinet." We know that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and Sir CHARLES DILKE should have gone over to Ireland to advocate a scheme of National Councils, and that their visit was abandoned because, as rumour had it, these gentlemen found that the wind had been taken out of their sails—that, in- other words, the Parnel- lites had made, or believed they had made, better terms with the Tories. We know how the Government of Lord SALISBURY aban- doned the Crimes Act, how Lord CAR- NARVON was sent over to Ireland with what was called a policy of conciliation, and how he resigned his post when, after the General Election, he found that Conciliation was to be followed by Coercion. Can it be that it was Lord CARNARVON, who was the "Minis- ter of the Crown," that communicated with Mr. PARNELL; and that, with some regard for honour and consistency, he sent in his resignation as Viceroy of Ireland when he found that the National League had to be sup- pressed rather than accommodated with a Parliament in Ireland ? What a punishment it will be for the Liberals who oppose Home Rule if they should be forced to the con- clusion that, in falling back von the Tories, they are falling back upon the party that has been the first to enter into communication with Mr. PARNELL with the object of provid- ing a statutory Parliament for Ireland! The Tories, to be sure, lift up their hands just now in pious horror at the thought of Home Rule; but let the Liberals beware. Having put their hands to the plough, let them turn not aside, or their unscrupulous opponents, leaving the Hartingtons and the Chamber- lains lamenting, may yet step in and do the work badly, and then take all the credit to themselves. [Since the above was written, Lord CARNARVON has made an explanation in the House of Lords in which, whilst he admits that an interview took place between himself and Mr. PARNELL, he denies that his action bound the Tory Cabinet of which he was a member. It will be interesting now to see what Mr. PARNELL has further to say. We are getting at the truth at last.)

THE Irishmen of Warrington held a crowded meeting in • the League Hall on Monday evening, with the object of thanking MR. GLADSTONE for his Home Rule Measure, and pledging themselves to give him every suplrt in seeking to make it the law of the land. .M. LOUGHLIN presided, and it was interesting to see how much more at home he seemed to be now that he has turned his back upon the Tories. Irishmen are not a little hurt just now at the way in which the whole of the Conservatives, and a number of Liberals, express themselves as unable to trust them to act fairly in a Parliament of their own. Things go for what they are worth ; and Irishmen in this respect are reaping what they have sown. They turned round upon MR. GLADSTONE and the Liberal party at the last election, and voted, contrary to their con- victions, for their hereditary foes. They may find it irritating, but they can hardly be sur- prised to learn that conduct of this kind is bitterly resented by the more unrelenting of politicians. Fortunately, Liberals as a body, are not bitter at heart ; they have made al- lowance for the extraordinary circumstances of the time; and, as they are now fighting the Irish battle, it would be absurd to supptAe that they would reject Irish help in the con- flict. The best amends for a wrong done ; yesterday is to do right to-day.. The Liberals of Warrington, and St. Helens, of Widnes and of Newton, have a strong feeling that four seats were lost to them in the House of j Commons in consequence of the Irish vote in November; and if the Irishmen of South Lancashire would repair their grave error, they must be up and doing. It is not sufficient that they pledge themselves to support Liberal candidates who, like M. JoHN CROSPIELD, j are in favour of Home Rule; they must work hard in educating those who from ignorance of Irish history are blind to the facts of the situation. They must put it to English Catholics whether, at a great crisis of this kind, any of them are prepared to play into the hands of the fanatical Orangemen of Ulster. If Home Rule is to be obtained, priest and people must work together in Eng- land as they have worked in Ireland. SIR GILBERT GREENALL, SIR RICHARD CROSS, MR. SETON-KARR, and MR. T. C. EDWARDS- MOSS were returned to Parliament by the aid of Irish votes; and they showed their faith in liishmen by voting, on Monday night, against MR. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill. If all or any of these gentlemen should again present themselves to the electors, it is to be hoped that Irish voters will meet them at every side with the most ardent, resolute, and uncompromising opposition. It is a duty they owe to themselves and to their country- men in Ireland; they must make amends for the past by making better provision for the future.
"TOUCH AND GO."

Colonel Gamble having declined to come forward again as the Liberal candidate for St. Helens, the Liberal Council have decided to recommend Mr. Arthur Sinclair, J.P. They are buckling on their armour for the fray, and will march to battle, with the cry of "Gladstone and Home Rule."

Colonel McCorquodale is to be congratula- ted; he has had a daughter and a son hap- pily married within a few weeks of each other. But there is one thing vet lacking; he must consent to be nominated as the Liberal candidate for the Newton Division, and permit the electors to make him an M.P. It can be done this time—if " Barkis is willin."

The Liberals of the Eddesbury Division are returing to their old love in seeking a candidate in the person of Mr. James Tomkinson. They feel the necessity of hav- ing somebody tried and true, and they are on the right track. Mr. Tomkinson is for- tunate in having a better-half who can assist

WHIT-MONDAY AT RUNCORN.—The usual procession et friendly Societies and Sunday school scholars will take place at. Runcorn on Monday. Should the weather be fine, there will be thousands of visitors in the town. A POSTPONED MARZIAGE AT RUNCORN —A. marriage which was fixed to take place on Wednesday morning at Betheedi Congregational Chapel was eorneweat suddenly postponed. Tne minister and registrar awaited the arrival of the perly for some time, where a woman entered the vestry and inforined them that the marriage had been post- poned, and they need wait no longer. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the School Board, on Thursday prosecuted the following per- sons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—John Kinsella, John Tinkler, George Whitley, John Clegg, Samuel Hunt, John Malarkey, William Lee, William Smith (2 cases), Thomas Howls, and William Lee. The usual penalty of 5s was imposed in each case. ACCIDENT TO A FARNWORTH TRADESMAN.—As Mr. Chartes Taylor, butcher, Fern worth, and his son, were driving in a trap towards Liverpool on Mondaay morning, and when descending a brow in the neighbourhood of Knotty Ash, the horse stumbled and fell, and both occn• pants were thrown out. Mr. Taylor was cut on the head andface, but his son received no other injury than a slight shaking. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fort- nightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tues- day, under the presidency of Mr. John Ashton. Present— the Rev. J. Lockwood and Messrs. Aaron, Lewis. Hadfield, Mclntyre, Hewitt, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy cletk.) Mr. Dansey, inepector to the ',peat Government Board, was also present. There was no busi- ness of public 'interest. SUPPOSED ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN. On Saturday morning Dr. Robieson was summoned to attend a married woman named Hancock, living in Regent-street, Rancern, who was suffering from the effects of poison sup- possd to be administered with her own hand. Dr. Robinson applied the stomach pump, and succeeded in obtaining up- wards of two ounces of laudanum from the woman, who had become unconscious. She had quite recovered on Monday. OPEN AIR CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—The first open air concert of the season was given on Wednesday night in the Markeosquare, Runcorn. Although the weather was not very propitious, several hundreds of persons assembled to hear the performances of the Mill Brow Brass Band, and enjoyed a rich treat. A programme comprising many ad- mirable selections from the works of popular composers was gone though in capital style. Mr. Touthwaite was the oosaductor. ACCIDENT AT HALFEANK.—About half-past seven OD Thursday morning a serious accident occurred to Etty Black, about 19 years of age, employed by Mr. Wm. King, farmer. Halebank. She was driving in a milk cart towards Widnes, and when near Ditton Junction Station the springs of the cart gave way, the axle broke, and she was precipi- tated into the road, receiving serious injuries to the head and one of her legs, which was at first thought to babe been broken. She is now progressing favourably. WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, David Woolley, alias Wm. Davies, chemical labourer, of Major Cross-street, was charged with having deserted his wife and child.—Mr. Scannell stated that on the 21st May the Prisoner had a child lying dead in the house. On the pretence that he was going to procure money to bury it, the prisoner went away and never returned. The Union paid the burial dues, and his family had cost the Union altogether £l. 2s 6d.—Tbe prisoner was remanded. RUNCORN CRICKET CLUE.—Tbe Runcorn Club took a strong eleven to Prescot on Thursday to do battle with the capital club of that town. Prescot won the toss, and went to the wickets. The ground was in good condition, and runs came pretty freely, the tenth man being dismissed with the score at 138. This total would have been considerably less but for one or two mistakes in the field. Unfortunately rain descended heavily when the time arrived for Runcorn to hat, and the ground becoming flooded the match had to be abandoned. There is no doubt they would have made a good show against their formidable opponents. GENEROSITY OP MR. H. OASKELL OF WIDNES.—At a meeting of the Chemical Laboratories Building Committee, in connection with University College, Liverpool, held on Tuesday, it was decided to supply fittings for electric bells and for a cable to serve the electric lights. After some dis- cussion upon the advisability of supplying a dynamo ma- chine for bringing the electric lighting system into effec- tive operation, Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, of Widnes settled the matter by generously placing at the disposal of the com- mittee a sum of £5O for supplying and fixing a dynamo suitable for the purpose. This offer was accepted with expressions of gratitude from the chairman (Mr. Isaac Roberts). BOWLING MATCH AT RUNCORN.—An interesting bowl- ing mach took place on Monday afternoon on the green at- tached to the South Bank Hotel. For a small stake Messrs. R. Wright (Runcorn) and W. Dainteth (Ditton), well- known manipulators of the "woods," conceded 15 points to Messrs. W. Anderton and John Sayle (both of Runcorn), in a game of 101 up. The game, which occupi.d about four hours, concluded in favour of Messrs. Wright and Dainteth by 12 poiets. The losers played rather badly at the start. and the game was soon 16 to 20. After this the young uns' held their own, and it stood 51 all, 65 all, but after this point the "old un's " (Messrs. Wright and Dainteth) went ahead and won as stated. Ituncouer BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Lieutenant-Colonel Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dut- ton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present—the Rev. J. Lock- wood, Messrs. Fisher, Taylor, Aaron, Farrell, Stokes, Speak- man, Lewis, Weir, Mclntyre, Hadfield, Smith, Hewitt, Davies, Parr, Brandreth, Forster, Baguley, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). Mr. Dansey„ the inspector to the Local Government Board was present. —The Rev. J. Lockwood moved the payment of accounts amounting to £920 7s 91. This amount included a county rate of £897 Oa lid for the past quarter, being an increase of £272 on the corresponding quarter last year, when, how- ever, there was no charge made for local purposes.— The motion was passed. There was no other business of public interest. CRUEL PARENTS AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court on Mondeet, before Messrs. 11. Gaskell, jun. (in the chair), and T. S. Timmis, a chemical labourer named Wm. McNamara was charged with deserting his family and leav- ing them chargeable to the funds of the Prescot Union.— Mr. Scannel, who appeared on behalf of the Guardians, said that for three 'years the prisoner had 'done very little to- wards the support of his family. In August, 1885, after serving two terms of imprisonment, he deserted his family, and a warrant was taken out for his apprehension. All efforts to find him, however, proved futile until Saturday, when he was apprehended in Widnes. Since August, 1885, the prisoner's children had been maintained in the Work- house at a cost of £32 12s 6d. The children were left in a shocking condition. They were very dirty and naked, and for several daYs lived in an empty house, being supported by neighbours.—The prisoner was font to gaol for three months.—The prisoner's wife was charged at the same time with being drunk on Saturday eight, and was com- mitted to gaol for ten days, in default of paying 7s. 6d. and costs. THUNDEESTORM AT WIDNES AND RDNCORN.—A heavy thunderstorm broke over Widnes and Runcorn on Wednes- nesday evening after a fine but sultry day. The storm 1 commenced about eight o'clock with phenomenal sudden- ness, and continued with great violence for upwards of an hour. Rain, accompanied with large hailstones, poured down in torrents, and peals of thunder were loud and pro- longed. In Victoria and Waterloo roads the cellars were, as usual on a a heavy rainfall, flooded to a depth of several feet, but no damage was done. In Runcorn, water poured down Penketh-lane in a swift stream, and flooded the stables of Messrs. Yarwood to a depth of two or three feet. The Boathouse Inn, being at a low level, suffered consider- ably. The yard behind was covered to a depth of several feet, and in the cellar the barrels were almost lifted from the .stillages. Other houses in the neighbourhood were .also flooded. The house occupied by Richard Eccleston, Percy-street, off Halton-road, was struck with lightning. The electricity removed one of the ridging tiles, split a wooden spout from top to bottom, and passing through the bedroom into the kitchen, damaged the ceiling and ruined several pictures. No one was injured. Under•the railway bridge in the Holloway water accumulated to a depth of four feet.

Mr Brunner, M.P., is, of course, to be the Liberal candidate for the North wich Division. It is said that Mr. W. H. Verdin will creep out of the cocked hat into which he was knocked at the last election, and try his luck again. It is also rumoured that his brother, Mr Robert Verdin, will be brought out as a "Unionist" candidate—not, it need hardly be said, with the hope of winning, but as a sort of "lion's provider." But he will not catch Northwich birds by putting that kind of salt on their tails.

-- . Mr, E. K. Muspratt being unable—from pressure of a great business which he has now entirely on his hands—to accept the invita- tion to become the Liberal candidate, Mr. W. R.. Kennedy, Q.C., has been asked to step into the breach. He is in demand, too, at Birkenhead ; but there is no fear as to a good candidate being found for Widnes. The Irish vote is all powerful, and it will not this time be given to the gentleman who misrepre- sented the Division, on Tuesday morning, by voting against the Home Rule Bill. Mr. Moss may pack up his traps and say—" By-by Westminster."

The Irish electors are wide awake at War- rington. They find Mr. John Crosfield a man after Mr. Gladstone's own heart, and their hearts are therefore already warm to- wards him. They know that he does not use language to conceal his thoughts ; that having pronounced in favour of Mr. Gladstone's Bill he will keep his word. He is as yet under eighty ; his memory is good ; and he still knows, more than half his time, where he is going, and what he is doing.

"Sir," said Dr. Johnson, "let us take a walk down Fleet-street." But" sir, or madam," which if the Sirs is to be the Conservative candidate for Warrington—Sir Gilbert Green- all or Sir A. B. Walker? It must be a brewer, of course—they are very conserva- tive on that point ; but there are two kinds of Warrington ale ; and there are some who say Sir Gilbert has " gone in" astride his beer barrel often enough ; they think the other brewer should have a chance.

The career of Mr. Peter Rylands as a poli- tician is likely to close with the present Par- liament. Concluding his speech to his con- stituents on Wednesday night he said that, "if he was not elected by the Liberals of Burnley at the forthcoming dissolution, he should not stand for any other constituency, and they would close his public career." That he will not be elected by " the Liberals of Burnley" is shown by "the 300" deciding: againsthim by 203 against 67. Has he not been rather rash in staking all upon the hazard of a single die? He has done the State some service, and is yet capable of doing it further service.

The magistrates of St. Helens, who had before them a lad for climbing a tree in the new park, seem to have forgotton that there was a time when they were boys. The lad was sum- moned for wilful damage which was assessed at one penny, and the judgment was that the parents should pay this penny—with a fine of ss. and 7s. costs. The Park should of course be protected, but this is protecting it with a vengeance.

The London police behaved badly in dealing with the crowd that waited on Mon- day night, or rather on Tuesday morning, for the result of the Home Rule division. So afraid were they of an ugly rush that they set to work to beat the people back. To prevent a riot, they proceeded to create one. It is to be hoped that some of those who were as- saulted will bring the police into the Police Court.

Tkie people of Newton have the benefit of cheap gas ; it is 2S. 9d. per 1,000 feet, less 6d. discount ; but Mr. Forster would have it cheaper still. He proposed to reduce the price 3d. per t,OOO at the meeting of the Commissioners on Monday last; but he got no seconder to his motion. Not that the rest of the Commissioners object to having things at cost price; but they are about to spend Lz,+oo on extending the gas works, and, like wise men, they propose to set aside their profits until they are out of debt.

Speaking at Liverpcol, June 3, 1868, Mr. Bright said :--" I have never said that Irish- men are not at liberty to ask for, and if they could accomplish it, to obtain the repeal of the Union. I say that we have no right whatever to insist upon a union between Ire- land and Great Britain upon our terms only." These are " brave words ;" .and they are as true to-day as they were in 186 E, whether Mr. Bright says them or not.

And what can be finer than the following passage from another speech made in Ireland the same year :—" Let us make a new treaty —not written on parchment, not bound with an oath. Its conditions should be these : Justice on the part of Great Britain; forgive- ness on the part of Ireland. It shall be written in the hearts of three nations ; and we will Dray to Him who is the common Father of all peoples, and in whose hands are destinies of all States, that He will make it last for ever and ever inviolate." Amen ! Amen!

MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN —A large number of persons gathered on Wednesday morning at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, to witness the marriage of Mr. W. G. Comes, of Bolton, to Miss Kniveton, eldest daughter of Mr. B. Kniveton, Greenway-road, Runcorn. The officiating minis- ter was the Rev. George Wood, who conducted the cere- mony in a very impressive manner. On the entrance of the bridal party, the choir sang the marriage hymn The voice that breathes o'er Eden." The bride was accompanied by four bridesmaids, viz. :—Misses EmilF Kniveton, Maggie Comes, Polly Kniveton, and Annie Smith, each of whom carried a handsome bouquet of flowers. Mr. John Comes, brother of' the bridegroom, acted as best man, and the bride was given away by her father. The wedding party included Mr. and Mrs Kniveton, Mr. and Mrs Comes, Mr. and Mrs S. Joyneon, Mr. T. Millington, Miss Greaves, Miss Simkin, Miss Jones, Mrs Pleavin, Mrs Dyer, Mr. J. A. Smith, and Mr. Hard. At the close of the ceremony, Mr. W. Once, organist, played Mendelssohn's "Wedding march." The party then returned to the residence of the bride's father, where they partook of breakfast, and subsequently the newly-married pair left Runcorn for a fortnight's sojourn in North Wales. The bride was formerly a teacher in the Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday school, and the large number of presents testified to the respect in which she was held. The carriages were supplied by Messrs. Yarwood and Sen.

THEFT OF WATCHES AT W.A.RILINGTON AND WID- NES.—John Martin Meade (26), painter, was on Tuesday committed to prison for nine months, with hard labour, at Liverpool Quarter Sessions, for hav- ing in July ancl August of last year stolen silver watches, the property of Thomas Yost, at Warring- ton, and of Robert Hicks, at Widnes. Prisoner was committed for trial from Warrington, and particu- lars of the ,case were given in our last issue.

THE NEW RAILWAY AT ST. HELENs.—Prior to the resumption of the great debate on Home Rule in the House of Commons, on Monday, the St. Helens and Wigan Junctions Railway Bill was read a third time and passed. We understand,that the bill will meet with some opposition from a large St. Helens manufacturer when it comes before the Lords; and in view of an early dissolution and a de- sire on the part of the directors to push forward the scheme, a small but certainly not unimportant branch line may have to be abandoned,

Peter Rylands, M.P., addressed the Burnley Liberal Three Hundred on Wednesday evening, and met with a rather lively reception. His observations elicited repeated remarks of disapproval mingled with cheers, while Mr. Gladstone's name was greeted with hearty cheering. The hon. member defended at length the action he had taken against the Home Rule Bill, contending that he had broken no pledge which he had given to the electors, and denying that he had acted inconsistently. The Bill was now dead, and he believed that when Mr. Gladstone again approached the subject it would be on new lines, that the Prime Minister would return to the lines he formerly intended—namely, such a measure of local self-government to Ireland as he would be able to give to Scotland, England, and Wales—a measure which would contain the three provisions, maintaining the unity of the Empire, supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, and the protection of the Protestant minority. To such a measure he (Mr. Rylands) would give a cordial support.—After some OPENING OF NEW SCHOOLS AT discussion, a vote by ballot was taken on the ques- tion " Are you satisfied with Mr. Itylands ?" HIGHWAY COMMITTEE,—Among other matters this com- mittee reported that their attention had been called to a building in course of erection in Church-street, and that the Surveyor's explanation was considered satisfactory ; plans for eight houses, Lower House-lane, for W. Riley, were approved subject to the plan being completed, and the outfall for drainage shown; plan for two houses, Frederick- street, for T. Edwards, was approved subject to the subsoil being drained, to a drain being made in back passage, and to the error in drawing being corrected ; plan for alteration to T. At Iserton's property in Lacey-street was referred back ; plans for two houses. Halton View, for W. Christie, were disapproved, being incomplete; plan for alteration to shop, Halton View, for J. Horrobia, was disapproved ; plan for school in Oakland-street, for United Methodist Free Church, approved, subject, to the drain being connected with Oak- land-street, instead of going under the building into the back passage, to water closets being substituted for privies, and to specification being furnished.—The minutes were ap- proved.without discussion, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Sadler, and it was also decided to accept the tender of It. Lomax (£1,004) for street making in Witt- road and Marsh-street. HEALTH COMMITTEE.—The adoption of the minutes of this Committee was proposed by Dr. O'Keeffe and seconded by Mr. Hayes. The Committee's report stated that there had been one case of smallpox, and the patient was now convalescent. The nightsoil contractor had cleared up all arrears, and the current work was in a satisfactory state. The usual inspection of shops had been made, and the fol- lowing food had been destroyed :-110 lbs onions, 46 pounds apples, and 95 oranges.—ln answer to the Chairman, Dr. O'Keeffe said that he thought the danger of infection from smallpox was now passed; he thought there was no danger of any fresh case arising in the township.—The minutes were confirmed. THE MARKET.—It was reported that the receipts of the market for the month amounted to £43 16s 4d, being a de- crease of £9 12s 61 as compared with May, ISBS. The machines had been tested. The large one required few re- pairs, which would occupy about two days. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.--,The question of the Infectious Diseases Hospital was considered in commit- tee, and it was resolved that the Board should proceed with the construction of the fever ward, but adjourn for the present the work of putting up the administrative buildings. Misceaaaamons.—The minutes of the Finance Commit- tee were adopted on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Wright, and those of the General Purposes Committee on the motion of Mr. Gaskell, seconded by Mr. Handley. This was all the business.

education. Personally, he did not agree with free education, and his reason for not agreeing with it was that he believed parents should be encouraged to assist the development of their children in re- gard to education, and it was their duty to advance their children in every possible way. If that was done for them by other people what was the effect? That they lowered the natural pride which he ap- prehended all parents felt in the advancement of their children. Education was in every way one of the greatest levers by which children might advance in life. Every man who had risen to eminence had risen through the development of those faculties with which he was born, and which without educa- tion would be comparatively useless. It therefore became the paramount duty of every parent—and, as far as that was concerned, of every other person i —to assist as far as they were able n the educa- tion of the young. If they did that they might rest assured that the natural result would be that they would diminish crime, bring through indus- trial pursuits an immense benefit to the nation, and another natural result would, be a lessened payment to the poor rate. He believed that the progress of education must necessarily tend to the doing away with that great incubus which at present rested upon the industry of this coun- try in having to make provision for the poor. By education they improved the tone and morals of the community. (Hear, hear.) He did not believe for one moment that by educating people they made them less inclined to labour. It was true they might suffer for some little time through education giving persons a false notion of their position, but when the mass of the people were raised to the true level of humanity a natural result would be that men would not be afraid to labour. No right thinking and really well educated man was afraid to labour. (Hear, hear.) He sincerely hoped that the result of the building of those schools 'would be the raising of the poor people to a higher level, and that there would be a real and lasting improvement in the direction he referred to. (Applause.) A short entertainment was then given. Mr. Mercer sang" Not very pleasant" and "Far away," for the latter of which he was encored. Mr. Jenkins gave an excellent rendering of "Love's request," and Mr. Dell contributed in his best style "Thou art so

near. Mr. KERFOOT here intimated that the clerk had received the schedules from the Government in- spector who had recently examined the schools, from which it seemed that the result of that examination was very satisfactory. Over 91 per cent. of scholars had passed, and he thought that spoke well for both the Board and teachers. (Applause.) Dancing was then begun and was kept up with much enjoyment till about two o'clock the follow- ing morning. Music was provided by an excellent band under the conductorship of Mr. P. Randall, of Warrington.

div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

RESCUED FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN.—A gallant rescue from drowning took place at Runcorn on Sunday. About half-past three in the afternoon several girls were playing on the canal bank near Doctor's Bridge, when one of their number, named Emma Wynne, living at 11, Cross- street, Runcorn, accidentally fell into the water. The screams of her companions attracted the attention of Mr. J. Parry, of 22, Agnes-street, off Clarendon-road, Cross-lane, Salford, who, seeing the peril in which the child was placed, plunged in the water to her assistance. He brought her to the side with much difficulty, and was assisted out of the canal in an exhausted state by Mr. William Leather- wood, blacksmith, and two other men who had appeared on the scene. The girl was little the worse for her immersion. The conduct of Mr. Parry, who is 58 years of age, and in delicate health, is deserving of all praise. CRUELTY TO HORSES AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. H. Gas- kell and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Philbin, a farm labourer, of Moor-lane, was charged with cruelty to a horse. On the 26th May P.C. Almond saw the defendant in charge of a horse attached to a heavily laden cart, the wheels of which had sunk six inches in the ground. The defendant struck the horse on the head and neck many times with a long stick an inch and a half thick. Defendant alleged that the animal was a. young one with a wicked temper, and that it had bitten him. Mr. Gaskell said such treatment would ruin the tem- per of any horse. A fine of 7s 6d and costs, 7s 6d, was im- posed.—Samuel Higginson. of Appleton, was summonea on a similar charge. P.C. 245 on the Ist inst. went to a field at Appleton, and saw the defendant's horse lying down. The defendant kicked it and struck it with a leather strap on the head. The horse was unable to get up, and it was raised by means of blocks. It could not stand without the aid of four men to steady it. The animal was in very poor condi- tion, and not fit to work.—Mrs Foster corroborated, and said tae horse fell down when drawing a cart. The defendant said the horse was in good condition, and able to work. He did not know why it fell down. They kept it in slings in the stable. He denied kicking the animal. The defendAnt'e father also gave evidence. The Bench did not consider there bad been intentional cruelty, and dismissed the case. •
