div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

, The defeat of the Government on the Irish Bill, which, amid h. scene of profound excitement, took place on Tuesday morning, was, as Mr. Morley said, only the beginning of the end. It left members and the public uncertain as to what course would be taken by the Government—whether they would. resign, or whether they would dissolve. The doubt on the subject was not very determined. Those who had access to Mr. Gladstone were aware that from the very first he has been resolved, if beaten by political combinations in the House of Commons, to appeal to the country. He had made the Queen aware of this intention when he visited her on the eve of her departure for Balmoral, and it was known . to his colleagues that he had convinced Her Majesty that there was no alternative from this procedure. But as I have frequently pointed out, it is high. treason to make known to the public (who after all. are chiefly concerned) any decision come to by the Ministers of the day before it has been communi- cated to Her Majesty, and received her formal ap- proval. Thus throughout Tuesday and yesterday afternoon information was lacking on this impor- tant subject, and members whose hearts were with. their constituents hung about town to await the formal announcement of the decision.

It was made to-night by Mr. Gladstone in the presence of a crowded House. Parliament is to be dissolved as soon as the business of the session can be wound up, and thEyt business is to.be confined to financial affairs. There has been some talk of bringing in the Registration Bill, but with the elec. tion taking place in July such a course would ob- viously be inutile. The Liberal party will, there- fore; among other disadvantages forced upon them by the action of Mr: Chamberlain, be compelled to go to the country on the old regiliter. Cheers and counter cheers greeted the Premier's announcement of the coming dissolution. But that is only cour- ageous make-believe. It is undoubtedly a heavy blow to gentlemen elected to Parliament after the laborious contest of the autumn, to find themselves dispossessed after holding their seats for 'little more than six months. It is cer- tain that few will meet where many part on the day of • the dissolution. Political affairs are so wofully askew that there will be a fearful cutting up of members. In ordinary time's it is enough that Liberals and Conservatives stand up against each other. - At the coming election there will be more than the three-cornered duel in which Midshipman Easy took part. The hand of every man will be against his neigh- hour, and the slaughter will be great. As to the probable issue, it baffles with more than usual success the efforts of the seer. It will be in- teresting to see how the proposed alliance between Conservatives and Unionist Liberals will work. Conservatives are in certain cases to vote for Liberal candidates, and Liberals for Conservatives. This proposal has a roseate hue for gentlemen who have forfeited the confidence of their Liberal constituents. They are buoyed up with the assurance that they shall have Conservative votes. It is probable enough that, in constituencies where the Conservatives have no chance themselves of sneaking in through a fis- sure in the camp of the Liberals, their votes will be given to a man who has flouted Mr. Gladstone. But in many cases, where the balance is more finely drawn, and where the Contervatives believe they have a chance of carrying their own man, the Unionist Liberal will find himself in the lurch. On the whole I find the opinion of experts to be that, whilst there will be a considerable clearance of sitting members, the general result will be to leave matters pretty much as they stand to-day. The Liberals will win seats from the uonservatives, secured for the latter at the General Election in pursuance of the bargain which Mr. Parnell disclosed in the House of Com- mons on Tuesday. On the other hand, the Conser- vatives will gain some seats by Liberal disunion. The Irish members will remain in undisturbed pos- session ot their eighty-five votes. This, on the face of it, does not look very well; but it will be found to improve upon consideration. The Liberal wheat will be separated from the Whig chaff, and the majority of the members returned by Liberal con- stituencies will be commissioned to give a solid vote for the reconstructed Home Rule Bill which Mr, Gladstone will bring in in October. There will still be the Irish vote, and the Conservatives, with the few Whin who have been returned to the House by the assistance of Tory votes, will be impotent , against the measure. There is no doubt about the popularity of Sir Erskine May in the House of Commons, or the es- teem in which he was universally held. Neverthe- less, an attempt to raise a subscription in order to set up a memorial of his work has not proved very successful. It may be because the movement is not sufficiently well known. It may be that the poli- tical excitement of the last few weeks has absorbed the attention of members, or it may be that mem- bers are too poor to spare the guinea for a memorial to their old counsellor and friend. However it be, the subscription list thus far is not overflowing, though its proposal is not more exacting than the placing of a window in St. Margaret's Church. A. curious question has, by the way, risen in connec- tion with the death of Lord Farnborough. The new peer did not live to take the oath and his seat in Parliament. He was therefore scarcely a complete peer when he died. Still'hisitpatent of peerage was made out, and the question is whethes Lady Farn- borough is to be mulct in the money fromages. that attend upon the creation of a new peer. It would. manifestly be a little hard if the uttermost penny were demanded. Communications are, I hear, going forward on the question. The Farnborough peerage is one of the shortest, if not the absolutely most transitory, that ever appeared upon the roll. The first peer died without issue, and the name disap- pears from the roll almost beford the ink with which it was written was dry. It is six years since poor Bernard Becker dis- covered Captain Boycott and Mrs. Boycott tending their flocks in County Mayo. Since then the agent of the Earl of Erne has added a new word to the Eng- lish language, a word in familiar daily use in every continent and island where the English race con- gregate. It came to pass soon after Captain Boy- cott's condition had been made known, and he be- came a central figure in the agrarian warfare, his Irish neighbours began (pate to take to him. He had certainly somewhat at his own expense added a fresh lustre to the neighbourhood-of Lough Mask. He deserved well of Ireland, and Ireland was not behind in acknowledgment of his service. Within the last two or three years he has become actually popular among the tenantry, and anyone who dared to do him injury, or even speak disrespectfully of him, would put himself in danger. This was a pleasant change, but it has not proved sufficient to keep Captain Boycott in the neighbourhood. More- over, Lord Erne' s rents did not come in in a manner necessary to the keeping up of a large establish- ment. An English nobleman offered Captain Boy- cott the position of agent on his estates, and the man whose name will live as long as CEesar's, Napoleon's, or Wellington's, has now settled down in an English county. The passion for floral decoration is growing in London. For those who entertain, flowers form a prominent item in ihe expenditure. For the official receptions at the Foreign Office and else- where the Board of Works supply the necessary flowers, though Lord Rosebery, since he name to the Foreign Office, has been accustomed to supple- ment the supply by liberal drafts from the gardens and hot-houses at Mentmore. As to the cost, a fact has come within my knowledge, which illustrates it. One day last week the P. and 0. Company gave I a magnificent entertainment to the Colonial visi- tors. Luncheon was served on three of their finest ships moored side by side at the Royal Albert Docks. The tables were a blaze of flowers making a display rarely equalled on similar occasions. • When it was determined to have this display, ap- plication was made to a well-known florist for an estimate of the cost. .£l,OOO was asked, at which the directors paused. It was finally arranged that the work should be done for .E3OO, a hundred pounds of flowers in each saloon. This was pretty well. But the margin between the first estimate and the actual cost is wide, and seems to hint at high profits in this department of trade.

DUEL BETWEEN JOURNALISTS. —A duel with swords took place at Paris on Thursday morning between M Soucord, a writer on the " Evenement," and M. Guttinguer. a writer on the "Echo de Paris." The latter was wounded. Strlpme or A CHESHIRE VICAR'S Sos.—A lamentab'e tragedy has taken place. at Baddeley Vicarage. Cheshire, the circumstances of which transpired at the ingest, held on Wednesday, by Dr. Cburton, of Chester. The vicar's son, aged twenty-one. had for &Ma time been engaged in an office in Liverpool. Recently he complained of bolsi; overworked, and returned to his home, where, it is scarcely necessary to add, he was kindly and affectionately treated by his father, the Rev. J. Wilkinson Ricardo, B.A.' On Tu,s- day night the young gentleman went out for a walk, and, as he did not return, his father left to meet him, when he Was horrified to find Mason lying dead in the grounds with a gun alongside him. The gun bad been placed in his mouth and exploded. Death must have been instantaneous. A verdict of "Suicide while suffering from unsound mind" was returned.

RUNCORN V. WINNINGTON.—PIaved at Winnington on Saturday. Tbe home team won the toss, and elected to field, the visitors sending to the wicket Messrs. Wilcockson and Pic!. thall. Two wickets were down for eight, when Mr. Ciokson joined Mr. Wilcockson, and 20 runs were added before the latter was caught in the long field. Mr. Green batted well for his score, and eventually the innings closed for 51. Winnington fared badly at the commencement of their innings, three of their wickets falling for as many runs, and then Messrs. Bickerton and Hughes became as- sociated, the latter hitting out with great vigour. A change of bowling took place at this point, Mr. Cookson bowling vice Woods, and with his second ball he clean bowled Hughes. Four for 25. STEEL'S ELEVEN. —This annual match, which is always looked forward to with great local interest, took place on the ground of the Recreation Club, at Denton's Green-lane, on Saturday. There was a good attendance of interested spectators. The visiting team, which was captained by the well-known D. Q Steel, first went to the wickets, and were dismissed for the total of 135, the brothers Steel batting in fine style. Mr. J. Tatlock was the most successful bowler, taking six wickets at a cornparativelv small number of runs. The home team failed to make a stand against the bowling of Mr. F. L. Steel and Mr. D. Q. Steel, and in their fist effort they were all dismissed for 46. In the second innings they fared a little better, scoring 79 for nine wickets, Watson batting very well for 17. Score :

NOTES BY THE WAY. With the advent of June the weather has been more pro- pitious for outdoor sports, and there has been a correspond- ing improvement in the quality of cricket shown. So far this season the play has been almost phenomenal. For several past years complaints have been frequent that the batsmen had obtained complete mastery over the bowlers, but so far this season the opposite has been the case. Whether or not this change will be maintained remains to be seen. Un- doubtedly much of the success of the bowlers so far has been owing to the heavy ground. In the leading matches at the close of last week the scores went up so that before the end of the season it ispossible that some big scores will be made. In the third day's play at Cambridge on Saturday, in the match between the University and Yorkshire, an exciting game was witnessed. Yorkshire wanted 151 to win, and whilst Ulvett and Hall were together it looked an easy task for the Tykes Five times Ulyett sent the ball to the luundarr, and the score stood at 55 before they were parted. A change from Toppin to Buxton worked the separation. Then there was something sensational. Hall,

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

" Under the Hoof," by Mr. John T. Day (Messrs. Carson and Cainberford), is a stirring story—or rather, a series of stories—bearing on the labour question as it relates to London. It reveals on the face of it special knowledze of the various classes of workmen referred to, and will do much towards awakening a sympathetic interest in the lot of the struggling poor. The characters are life-like, and, as the interest is well sustained, "Under the Hoof " will be much read, and, it is to be hoped, do muck good. "Picturesque Wales" is the title of a capital six- penny hand book of the scenery accessible from the Cambrian Railway.. It is edited by Mr. Godfrey Turner, and is officially published. It commences with the tourist at Whitchurch, and takes him to Oswestry, Aberystwith, Aberdovy, Barmouth, Del- golly, and Portmadocthat is to say into the very heart of "Wild Wales." The hand book gives a full and accurate Account of these and other places of interest en route, and there are excellent engravings of castles, mountains, waterfalls, Sc.c. Indeed, the hand book is well worth the money for the en;.frav- ings. "Picturesque Wales lis a treasure in its way. "The Life and Times of Queen Victoria" is the title of a new work by Messrs. Cassell and Co. which is being issued in monthly parts, sevenpence each. In view of the jubilee of her Majesty's reign, the book is aceedintrly opportune, and is sure to have a large sale. It promises to be a complete history of Eng- land for the present generation; and as it is beauti- fully minted and profusely illustrated, there can be no question that the work will prove a great attraction alike to young and old. With the first number there is a larva presentation plate of the picture, "A Cottage Bedside at Osborne," in which the Queen is represented, with characteristic kindness, reading to a bed ridden old man. As there is but a limite4 num- ber of these plates, those wh*o first come will be first served.

"The Fireside" Summer Number is issue 3 as a "Jubilee Memorial of the Queen." It is tastefully illustrated with portraits of her Majesty and of the various members of the Royal Family; and, along with a brief biographical sketch, there is a chapter de- voted to Rlyal anecdotes and incidents. Cassell's "Magazine of Art" for June is a strong number. • An article on the "Old Charterhouse " talvfn the lead, and it is accompanied by some very- fine illustrations. There is a short sketch, with por- trait, &c., of Basil Peroff, the Russian artist.; and the St. John's River has justice done to it both by text and illustration. The reader will not fail to see and ad- mire the beauty of detail in the "Capital," which illustrates "Some East Indian Wood Engraving it is unique as a specimen of the engraver's art. "A New Rabelais" is striking; and there is a vigorous reproduction of "The Three Witches" by Mr. J. McWhirter, A.R.A. Among the illustrated articles in the current issue of "The Quiver" are "A Moravian Community" and "Sunday on the Yorkshire Moors." Lord Brabazon discourses on The Welfare of Young Men" and Rev. Dr. Macmillan on "The Stones Buried in the Jordan," while Mr. George Weatherly has a pretty poem—" A Hymn of Summer"—which is prettily illustrated. " Cassell's Magszine " has a bright froitispiece— " A Maiden's Dreams." A special correspondent gives an account of "The Dwellings of the London Poor ;" and the Family Doctor has a .paper on "Climate, and its influence on Health." "Beauty in unlikely places" opens the door to some charming railway bits. The serial stories are making headway, and "The Gatherer " furnishes plenty of material. "Little Folks "has for its frontispiece (coloured) "The Box Seat ;" it is very, very pretty, for the right expression of the loving little couple has been caught to a nicety. A new volume commences in July, and there are some specially good things promi6ed. "Gleanings from Popular Authors (part To) maintains its high level; it is so good it ought, like Tennyson's brook, to "go on for ever." " Our Jerusalem Pony," by Mr. James Payne, would make a capital reading; it is full of fun without vulgarity. Part 5 of the "Illustrated Shakespeare" concludes "The Merry Wives of Windsor" and carries the reader on through three acts of " Measure for measure." The current issue of "The Book of Health" treats of ear diseases, and of everything re- lating to the smell, voice, and speech. "The Encyr. elopseiic Dictionary" (part 29) continues the letter E, giving, for instance, an article on electricity which extends to a column and a half. Part Four of "Familiar Wild Flowers" has for its coloured plate illustration the " Scarlet Poppy" and the "Cuckoo Pint." It is interesting to note in con- nection with this work that Messrs. Cassell announce £5O in ten prizes for "the best collection of wild fliwers, consisting of specimens of the flowers figured in the first volume of 'Familiar Wild Flowers.' "

The "National Library" continues to merit and receive the greatest praise. The latest additions to hand are "Voyagers' Tales" from the collection of Richard Hakluyt, and a carefully edited and nicely Printed edition of "Hamlet." - The chief feature of "The English Illustrated Magazine" is Mr. Hugh Thompson's clever illustra- tions of " Mr. Will Wimple," of " Sir Roger de Coverly " fame. There are besides interesting illus- trative papers On " Yaanouth and the Broads," "In Umbria," and "The Singing Voice." The "Young Folks Paper "—the monthly issue of which is to hand—offors plenty in the way of "hair- breadth 'scapes." "Kidnapped "is the title. of the new story begun in the current Dart. "The Season" (Is.) and "La Moniteur de la Mode" (Is.) are aglow with coloured plates of June fashions, while there is distracting variety in the way of "patterns" and "instructions." In the same class we have also to band " Myra's Journal" and " Myra's Threepenny Journal."

Canon Liddon has telegraphed from Constantinople de- clining to accept the Bishopric of Edinburgh. The will of the late Mr. Bartlett, whose death formed the subject of the Pimlico murder trial, has been proved, and the amount of personal estate is sworn at £3,858. The property is bequeathed absolutely to Mrs. Bartlett. ROBBERY AND MURDER.—A young man named Finch entered a district post-office in Kentish Town en Thursday afternoon and snatched up a cash hex. On the attendant, a chemist's assistant named Bowes. interfering, Finch shot him dead, and he afterwards fired at and injured the mis- tress. The desperado was arrested on Thursday night at his home, where be and his plunder were in concealment. TEE UREAT MAIL BAG ROBBERY—At the Old .Bailey, on Friday, a charge against Henry Andrews of being in Possession of three Russian one hundred rouble notes, part of the property stolen from tbe continental mail on April 8, was further proceeded with. The evidence given on the previous day was almost entirely that of witnesses who de- posed to the mail bags being duly delivered at Ostend from the steamer Marie Louise to the railway train, and showing they were not tampered with there. The cross-examination on Friday elicited no new facts. " Heroine " is perhaps as peculiar a word as any in our language; the first two letters of it are male, the three first female, the four first a brave man, and the whole word a brave woman.

ARREST OF A WELL-KNOWN CRICKETER. Mr. W. H. Gilbert, the well-known Gloucestershire cricketer, was ar- rested at Cheltenham, on Saturday. He WU playing for East Gloucestershire against Stroud, and, during the game, went to the dreising-room of the pavilion, where a detPc- tive was secreted, money having been stolen from clothes left there for a considerable time past. Gilbert was caught in the act of tampering with the clothes in which marked money had been placed. On Monday Gilbert was charged with stealidg half a sovereign and a shilling at the East Gloucestershire Cricket Ground. He pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to twenty-eight days' imprisonment with hard labour.

These sports were continued and concluded in splendid weather on Saturday. The attendance of the public was sot so large as in former years, but there were at least 4,000 persons present. The grand stand was well patronised by the local gentry, and ea:ly in the afternoon Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., accompanied by his uncle, Mr. Gil- bert Moss, were upon the field. Mr. Edwards-Moss, who had to perform the duty of distributing the privo, appelreci to take great interest in the various coinDetitiens. The %rrilogonlents of tb, !Ports were Characterised by their usual completeness, and the programme was gone through in admirable time. The chief feature of the afternoon was the running of A. Wharton, of Darlington, who is a Malay. In the 100 yards scratch race be succeeded to the surprise of all in defeating J. Al. Cowie, of London, who is the champion over that distance. Cowie, however, had his revenge in the quarter mile race ; when, after a splendid struggle he reversed the verdict by a yard. Whar- ton had also to put up with a defeat in the 120 yards han- dicap after winning two heats. His conqueror was T. Kerr, of Manchester, who had seven yards start of him, and ran in grand style. An objection was lodged that Kerr was a professional, and the prizes were withheld. Wharton had three and a half yards start. The bicycle handicaps were productive of numerous dangerous tumbles, but luckily none of the riders were seriously injured. In the mile' race J. Clark, Ditton, had a promising chance spoiled by a spill, and in the three miles race Roberts, of Sheffield, appeared to have the first prize within his grasp when he came a crop- per. The most interesting spectacle of the afternoon was the clever performance of about 20 members of the Liver- pool gymnasium, under the direction of Mr. Alexander. During the afternoon the Widnes Soap Works Band played an admirable selection of music. RIOTING IN ULSTER. SEVERAL PERSONS '77:XILLED AND MANY INJURED. After celebrating the rejection of the Home Rule Bill at Monaghan, some Loyalists, in returning home on Tuesday night, fired at and seriously wounded a militiaman named Murphy. Further along the road the Naionftlists attacked and severely beat a Loyal- ist named Crawford, whom they suspected of shoot- ing Murphy. In connection with the demonstration on the de- feat of the Home Rule Bill, a disturbance occurred at Lurgan on Tuesday night. A Nationalist who had been fighting with a Loyalist took shelter in ' the house of Mr. Arthur Donnelly. The mob attack- ed the house, and several shots were fired by Nation- alists, three men being wounded. More police hare been summoned from Portadown. One hundred houses were wrecked in the Belfast rioting on Tuesday night. A large number of rio- ters were wounded with buckshot, and many police officers were also wounded. Two public-houses were wrecked and afterwards burned during the rioting. Effigies of the Premier and Mr. Parnell were burned. Several rioters • were brought before the magistrates, on Wednesday, and committed for trial. The riots arising out of the celebration of the Government defeat were continued in Lurgan till an early hour on Wednesday morning. In addition to the casualties reported, James Rice, a Protestant, has been admitted into the hospital with a bullet wound in the leg, and Thomas Morris, Protestant, also shot in the leg. Further rioting is apprehen- ded. Forty houses have been wrecked, including the residences of Mr. George Haslett, Crown solici- tor, and Dr. Maginnis, and several large business houses. An inquest on the body of Thomas Gallaher was opened on Wednesday, and adjourned. Addi- tional police and military have arrived, and the authorities are making preparations for preserving the peace.

At the adjourned inquest on the man Gallagher, the medical evidence went to show that the de- ceased had received three bullet wounds. The jury returned a verdict of " Died of gunshot wounds re- ceived during a riot," at Ow same time censuring the authorities for not having sufficient police force to preserve the peace. Arthur and Andrew Donnelly, father and son. leading Roman Catholic merchants, have been arrested and conveyed to Armagh Gaol on a charge of shooting from their dwellings and warehouse with intent to do actual bodily harm. A book- keeper in their employ, named O'Higgins, accused of a similar offence, has absconded. The Donnellys were conveyed to the railway station under strong military and police escort, the mob showing an un- mistakeable disposition to lynch them. It is be- lieved that their arrest will tend to restore order, but the town on Wednesday evening was still in a very disturbed state. On Wednesday evening another terrible riot broke out at Belfast. Several persons at least have been shot dead by the constabulary. The constabulary were obliged to take shelter in Bower's Hill Police Barracks, which was then. attacked by the mob. The constabulary afterwards fired out of the build- ing upon the riotous multitude, and two women and three men were killed. A great many are wounded. All the evening the Shankhill-road and district has been in a most disturbed condition. There is a very strong feeling amongst a large sec- tion of the population against the police, who, it is thought, used their batons somewhat too freely. The mobs stoned the police very fiercely. Seeing the formidable shape which the riots were assum- ing, it was deemed desirable to have the military called out. Detachments of the Northum- berland Fusiliers, Highland Light Infantry, and also a troop of the 3rd Dragoon Guards were plan- ted at various commanding points in the riotous neighbourhood, but the streets still continued crowded with tumultuous mobs, who continued to stone the police, and stated that if they were withdrawn they would become quiet and orderly, but not till then. A.district inspector took a detachment of them into Riversdale-street School- house, and matters then became more tranquil. Very large missiles were thrown at the constabu- lary. A boy was shot at the corner of Moscow- street. A woman, who is supposed to have resided on the Crumlin Road, was shot through the cheek. Another boy was shot through the heart. A medi- cal man was promply at hand, but life was quite extinct when lie arrived. The .second woman was looking out of the window of a public-house when she was killed by a bullet. Another man was shot in the Shankhill Road. He survived a short time after he was shot. More houses were wrecked, and some were set on fire. This is the most serious riot- ing which has occurred in Belfast since the riots in 1864. io A telegram from Belfast on Thursday morning reports at least seven persons shot :—Mary barmaid, 32; Minnie APAllister, 16; John Kale, 15; William James Matthews, carter, 18; a young man named M`Cormack, shop assistant; a boy named Gordon, and two men not identified. Sixteen per- sons are in the hospital, one of whom is said to be dying. There are now 700 police in the town. The military have been able to return to the barracks, but the police patrolled the town all night. The town is now somewhat quieter.

div.p: CHARGE AG.AINST A RUN CORN LOCAL
PREACHER.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, Martha Savage, a young woman living at Weston Point, ap- plii d for an affiliation order against William Palin, of 6, Clarence-street. Runcorn. Mr. F. A Lake was for the complainant, and Mr. J. W. Knowles, of Wickes, for the defendant. The complainant deposed that the defendant was agent to the Royal .Liver Friendly Society, and was a local preacher for the Primitive Methodist denomination. 'He came to their house on the 28-h April last year and asked her if she would ',men him company. As he said he was not going with anyone else, she consented to meet him near th Runcorn Cemetery an the evening of that day, and did so. An intimacy commenced on that night, which was renewed on subsequent occasions. A child was horn on the i2th January. When the defendant learnt, that she was enciente he took her a' bottle con- teioitig a colourless liquor, labelled "white wine vine- gar." (The bottle was produced and handed up to the magistrate, who said it smelled like acetic acid.) She said she was afraid of taking it. The defendant told her it would not do her any harm. On a subse- quent occasion he brought her some gunpowder, hut she would not take it. The defendant had promised to marry her, and had admitted paternity by paying her £3 118 since the child was horse. This included 88 she owed for insurance. He had also paid Mr. Lake a guinea, the charge for drawing up the memo- randum of an agreement to pay 2s 6d per week to- wards the child.—ln cross-examination by 11,1 r. Knowles, the complainant said she had an illegitimate child about three years ago. She denied that she was in the habit of frequenting the house of Mrs. Drury in Back Cooper-street, and the public houses in Runzorn. Eliza- beth Cowley, a married woman of Weston Point, said she was present when the defendant promised the complainant to see her right. She-also heard him say that he could not marry her as he would be brought up for a breach of promise.—Jane Drury stated that on asturday night the defendant promised to give her some money if she would swear that she had seen the complainant with other men. She said she would not do so if he gave her £2O. She had never seen the complainant with any young man ex- cept the defendant. The defendant when he left gave her 2d to treat herself —(laughter)—and asked her not to tell anybody.—Mr. William Pownall, junr, proved the payment of a guinea to Mr. Lake.—Mr. Knowles addressed the Bench at length for the defence and the defendant was put into the witness box. He denied that he had over walked with the complainant, or had any intimacy with her whatever. He gave the complainant money, because he had his name as a preacher on the circuit plan, and was also highly re- spected in Runcorn, and he was afraid of the scandal. Not only that, but he had been engaged to a young lady a distance from Runcorn for two years and was 'to be married on Whit Monday, and he knew if she beard of it it would upset all the affair. But the most important reason was that his mother was seri- ously ill, and the scandal would kill her. He had never admitted the paternity of the child, and the statement that he had given the complainant the liquid and the gunpowder (produce) was false. He never saw them until that morning. He did. not at- tempt to bribe Mrs. Drury.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Lake, the defendant admitted that he had offered to pey 25 6d per week towards the child in his office. —The Bench declined to make an order.--On Tuesday morning Mr. Brundrit and Captain Hazle- burst granted the woman a fresh summons against Palin, and the casa will be again heard on the 21et June.

LIBERAL NEF,TING AT FRODSHAM. SPEECHES BY MR. AND MRS. TOMKINSON. On Tuesday evening an enthusiastic and crowded meeting of the electors of the Frodsham Polling Dis- trict was held in Frodsham Town Hall for the pur- pose of bearing an address from Mr. James Tomkin- son, the selected candidate for the Eddisbury Divi- sion. Mr. W. Farish, J.P,, of Helsby, was voted to the chair, and upon the platform were Mr. and Mrs. Tomkinson, Messrs. B. Kniveton (Runcorn), J. S. Rimmer, and Baxter. Amonsrst the audience were Rev. R: P. Borwick, Messrs. W. Handley (Runcorn), W. H. Linaker, and J. Jeffs, and several prominent Conservatives, including Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P. and Lieut.- Colonel Ashton. The Chairman delivered a speech which frequently elicited cheering, in which he gave his reminiscences of the great re- forms passed during the past 50 years. The Liberal party bad I had lots of defeats, but they had always won in the end. (Loud applause.) He remembered Mr. Gladtkone on one occasion when he was defeated said that time was on his side, and with regard to Hems Rule time was on his side. (Applause.) The day was not far distant when his country- men would concede to Ireland the Parliament of which it ought never to have been deprived. (Loud applause.) They would send Mr. Tomkinson to help Mr. Gladstone to carry the measure. (Cheers.) IMr, Tomkinsop, wh9wa greeted most enthusiastically, alluded to the probability of a general election, and said it I behoved all who laved Liberal principles, and desired to support their great leader, to stand shoulder to shoulder and I do their best to aid him in carrying this great measure of ' Justice to Ireland. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone's Horne Rule Bill was a measure not only of justice to Ireland, but i one that would conduce to the happiness and welfare ,of the kingdom at large. (Hear, hear, and applause) He was not there to advocate Home Rule merely because Mr. Gladstone had introduced it. (Hear, hear.) Great as was his respect and admiration for that great man's noble qualities and for his statesmanship, be was there to ad- vocate it because having considered the question and hay- ing studied the history of Ireland, he was convinced that it was right—(applause)--and be was there to support it with I ; all the powers that he had. (Hear, bear.) Mr. Gladstone's I proposal was to give Ireland what was called a statutory I parliament for the management of purely Irish affairs. ; Imperial questions were not to be within the powers of the parliament. The fact was, our endeavour to govern Ireland ! under the present system of " union " bad resulted in noth- ing but failure. During the 85 years of so called union there i had only been 2or 3 years in which Ireland had been governed by the ordinary constitutional law—in which there bad not been some sort of coercion. If they tested that government by the only test which Liberals allowed, namely, whether government had succeeded in gaining the sympathy, the support, and the co-operation of the gov- erned, he said the present system stood condemned. (Hear, I hear.) A maxim held by Liberals was that we must govern with the consent of the governed, and that Home Rule was demanded by 85 representatives chosen by the Irish people was a fact they could net possibly ignore, much less neglect. ; Alluding to the arguments used against the scheme, the speaker warned them not to be frightened by , the long words and big figures of the Tory party. 'The first weapon of the Conservatives I was to frighten people. There had never been a time when a measure of large reform had been proposed that the Con- servatives had not predicted the most fearful disasters. (Ap- plause.) They were told at the present time that the Em- pire was going to suffer disintegration, dismembered, and I disrupted, and that the proposed change would cost the tax- I payers an enormous sum of money—any number of mil- lions they liked. He wished them to 'believe nothing of ; the kind, and he would prove that the predictions were not based upon fact. To bear the Conservatives talk they I would think that Ireland had never had a Parliament until now—(hear, hear)—and as though there was no other Par- liament in the whole of the British elominions than the one at Westminster. The fact was that Ireland had a Par- liament until 1800, and although elected on a very small I suffrage had powers given to it which were infinitely i greater than any Mr. Gladstone proposed to coecede now. (Applause.) The union was brought about by the most I shameless bribery. £1,400,000 was spent in bribing the Irish members to vote for their OWD effacement. There were Do less than 15 Parliaments in the British dominions. Our colonies had their Parliaments, and were not they loyal. But there was an instance nearer home. 'The Isle of Man had got complete independence. (Ap- plause.) Even tae Channel Islands had Home Rule. What was there to he frightened of in this spirit of Home Rule. (Applause.) The opponents of the bill said the Irish would use it to obtain complete separation, and to set up a Catholic tyranny ; and that the lives and pro- petty of the Protestants would not be safe. He wished to mention one remarkable fact that from Ulster the first agi- l-tation for the repeal of the Union came. (Laughter.) As long as they thought that Catholics would* kept under the disabilities which prevented them from voting or sitting in the Parliament, and that the Parliament would be exchi; sively Protestant, the Protestants agitated for repeal. Now I when the Catholics would have equal rights and liberties I the Protestants of Ulster were strenuous opponents of the hilt. (Hear, hear.) The Conservatives made two appeals, one to the religious bigotry of the people and the other to the pockets of the taxpayer, and these were anything but noble appeals. (Hear, hear.) He declared that Home Rule would not cost the English taxpayers one farthing. But if I it were right and just, and it was necessary to call upon the taxpayer to pay, the charge ought to be paid with the same spirit in which we gave 20 millions to the slave owners for the emancipation of their slaves. (Loud applause.) Horne Rule was called for by the national aspirations of the Irish people, and he. ridiculed the statement that the Pro- testants would be persecuted. The Protestants had no reason to fear injustice at the hands of the Catholics, but I very much the reverse. (Applause.) He pointed out the impossibility of Ireland separating from England, and said now we had got division of countries with union of Parlia- ments. He wished to see a division of Parliaments with a real union of the empire, and he conscientiously believed this would result if they gave a Parliament to Ireland. (Applause.) He referred to the injustice and indignities to which the Irish had been subjected in the past; to the ini- quitous land system under which the Irish farmers had groaned. Mr. Tomkinson predicted that as sure as they sat in Hot room, the Bill would become law. (Cheers.) It was for them to say whether it should become law, while we could give it generously and graciously or after an up- heaval of great excitement. (Renewed cheers.) Having described the Land Purchase scheme, and its safeguards, Mr. Tomkinson dealt with English Reform, and declared himself in favour of small holdings, county government, and licensing reform, and invited questions upon matters to which he had not referred.

Mr. Baxter, of Asbton, moved "That this meeting of the electors of Frodsham Polling District of Eddisbnry Divi- slot cordially welcomes their old candidate, James Temkin- son, Dui., of Willington Hall, and having heard the ex- pression of his political views, hereby pledges itself to use all legitimate efforts to secure his triumphant return to Par- liament at the coming election." (Applause.) The motion was seconded by Mr. Joseph Jeffs, of Helsby, who spoke confidently of returning Mr. Tomkinson, and it was supported by Mr. W. H. Linaker, of Frodsham, and Mr. B. Kniveton, of Runcorn.

It was carried with the greatest enthusiasm, about three hands being held up against the resolution. Mrs. Tornkinsoo, who was heartily cheered, delivered a epeech in moving a vote of thanks to the chairman. She said of cburse women were not supposed to meddle much in politics avpresent, but she thought they would very soon meddle more. (Laughter.) It used to be thought it was I the very extreme Radicals that wished to give women votes, but she had noticed that since a certain important society was started which went by the name of a flower that "blooms ill the spring"—(laughter)— that the Conserva- tives had changed their mir ds. She was very much amused wi h several of her Conservative friends in London this summer. They used to talk in the words of an old song that perhaps some there were not old enough to remember, though she did. (Loud laughter and applause.) The sorg was a very clever one about "clever women " and apropos of politics it said. "It's a pity when charming women talk about things they don't understand." (Laughter.) And that used to be her Conservative I friends' opinions. Now she was talking to an Conservative M P.—he was not in the House now—and be told her that they hoped a great deal from the trained intelligence of women in opposing the demoralising tendencies and the brutalising influences of the lower classes. (Laughter and applause.) She thought she had heard him say rather different things, but she held her peace, because she remembered a good old saying about pearls and certain animals. (Loud laughter.) Well, these were some of the reasons why, if they had to fight this electien, she should do her best to talk politics. (Applause.) She could not do much, but she would do what she could, and it every Liberal did the same their Grand Old Man would ko back to Parliament in spite of all the influences that were against him—of Whig, of different sorts of Radicals, or Conservatives—with a swinging good majority- (Applause.) Perhaps some of them did not like Home Rule for Ireland ; perhaps some of them were prejudiced against it; others might think it a bore, and not care much about it one way or the other. She could quite understand all these views, but at the same time she wished them to consider one thing before these , views of Home Rule made them either abstain from voting I for a Liberal or to vote for the Conservative. What would happen if through their dislike of Home Rule they put the Conservatives in power with a good majority at heir , back. They were decent fellows when put in as caretakers for three or four months, with a majority against them, but what were they when they got some power. She I noticed that those present were rather anxious to reform I the House of Lords, if their applause was a g• uide Now, a Conservative House of Commons with a strong majority would be like the House of Lords now. (Hear, bear.) There they had Conservatives ' I with a strong majority accustomed to have their own Iway; and she was sorry to say it was an uncommonly bad one. (Laughter.) They would scarcely find a truly decent measure on the statute book that these noble and hen- ' ourable lords bad not opposed as long as they could. (Hear, hear.) That was very much like what would happen with many iateresting and important measures that they were all anxious to have carried if the Conservatives got into power in the House of Commons again. She, hawever, did not think they would succeed in stopping Home Rule by sending the Conservatives to power. She should like to take a pretty good bet, though it was an improper thing for a lady to do, that if the Conservatives Government into power that they would pass a home rule bill within about

two years time for peace and quietness sake. (APPlaell% They had done similar things before. The Chairman bad told them how on one occasion their opinions altered mate vellously in a few months about the Franchise, and they' then called it "dishing the Whigs." She should not won- der if they dished the Whigs again. (Applause.) The only way to judge people was by the way they had kePt their promises, and the way they bad acted before. Taking that line it was very possible the Conservatives might Pass a Home Rule Bill. She would tell them what would act, pass if the Conservatives got into power with a good majority. The people would not get an allotment b5ll. When in the constituences the Conservatives would saY it was an excellent thing for each man to have his cottage garden, but when they got to London their memories woo't! get rather short on the subject. (Laughter.) They would find it would be the same with other useful and beneficient bills they desired. (Applause.) Mr. Kniveton had said the Grand Old Man had takee off hi 5 coat and would not put it on until he had attained his end. But the end would be I attained sooner if each Liberal took off his coat to do the work, which she thought all of them in their heart of hearts must consider to be a piece of real justice and fair play to Ireland. We had advocated justice and fair play all over the world, and now when the shoe pinched at home were we to let every other nation say "What hYP(''' crites these English are. They will help other nationalities to satisfy their just aspirations, but when a neighbouft: whom they have been trying to govern, says 'ln heave% name give us power to manage our own affairs ; "n interfere in 'evade' matters,' they won't even let them trY they are so afraid of a little bit of liberty." Don't let that be said of Englishmen but take off their coats to aid the grand old man who had worked so nobly. Mrs Torekinsoa resumed her seat amid most enthusiastic cheering. The motion was seconded by the Rev. R. P. Borwick, a° carried unanimously. The meeting then dispersed.

His injuries were found to be ° such a nature that no hopes are he!d out of his recoverY• The man's name is Newton, and he is a miller and corn merchant at Staly bridge. "SOME HINTS ON BEDDING."—This is the title of a little reprint of part of a lecture by 11.1 r. David Adamson, author of " Bed feathers, Bedding materials." &c. Mr. Adamsoo is a member of the well-known firm of Urquhart and , Adamson' cabinet makers and upholsterers, of Bold-street, Liverpool. In its pages are discussed the important Vs' ton 'of the healthy furnishing of those rooms in which is spent a large portion of a lifetime' The attainment of the consummation, 66 men, ear 3 in sano corpore," is demonstrated to depend largely upon the choice, of bedding which is at once whole some and comfortable. The relative merits of feathers, down, hair, flocks, seaweed, and lastly steel springs, are die" missed and weighed in a manner which shows that the author has a thorough grasp and mastery of the subject. The moral of course is that the greatest care should be exercised in choosing reliable goods, and in this connection it may be mentioned that the firm by whom the little pamphlet 15 issued has a first-class reputation in this as well as all other branches ef the business in which it is engaged. &mous Rareway COLLISION.—A serious railway colli- sion occurred at Eclgley Junction, just outside Stockport Station, on Saturday afternoon. The Buxton train and tbe London train left London-road Station, Manchester, within five minutes of each other. While the London train was at etockport Station the Buxton train passed through on the middle line, and was brought to a standstill about two hun- dred yards from the junction, at Edgley. of the Buxton and Lendon lines. Here the Buxton driver was informed that the London train would pass the points first. He moved slowly on towards the junction. In the meantime the Loa' don train came up, and, the signal being clear, went over the points. Half the train was clear of the junction when the Buxton train ran into it, at a speeA of six or seven miles an hour. Several carriages of each train left the line. Mr. Frank Janion, of Manchester, had his leg broken, and other passengers were shaken. Mr. Janion tees removed to the Stockport Infirmary, and the other p issengers were shaken. Mr. Janion was removed to the Stockport Infirmary, and the other passengers left Stockport by later trains. rbe line WAS blocked for more than two hours in the busiest part of the day. It is suggested ttiat the Buxton driver mis-read the signal, which was against him; or that he looked by mistake at the adjoining signal for the London Lain.

DESPERATE ENCOUNTERS IN THE SOUTH SEAS.—Accord' ing to intelligence from New South Wales, the German gun- _ boat Albatross had returned from an eight months' cruise is the South Seas. The object of the cruise was stated to be to punish the natives in various parts of New Britain and New Ireland for various crimes, the murder of traders VW robbery. In every instance the natives refused to give UP the murderers ard other offenders, and in consequence their villages were destroyed by the sailors from the war vessel' The natives in most instances ran away on the arrival of the war vessel and lauding of the sailors. Mach opposition. however, was encountered from the natives of New Irelands where come severe skirmishes took place. In one of these engagements eight of the crew of the Albatross were wounded, some of them severely. Two of the sailors were shot in the shoulder by bullets from Snider rifles, with which many of the natives of both islands were armed. In, the report which was made it was stated that not any of the crew of the Albatre,ss were killed, but it was mentioned that in the various engagements 45 natives lost their BYO, whilst many were wounded. In most instances the houses, canoes, and- plantations of the natives were destroyed as g punishment for their offences. The Germans were some- what surprised at the stubbarness with which the natives fought in Dir,at of the encounters, and they appeared ale() to be in possession of an unlimited supply of ammunition. THE SHOCKING AFFRAY BETWEEN ORANGEMEN AND CATHOLICS.—At the inquest on the body of Janps Cur" ran, one of the navvies who was drowned in endeavouring W evade the attack made by the Orangemen, a brother of de- ceased gave evidence as to the character of the onslaught, but was unable to identify any of the men who took part in it. The inquest was adjourned to enable the police to in- stitute inquiries with a view of discovering the originators of the attack. All the injured persons are doing well with one exception, an old man named James M•lieown, who 10 dreadfully mutilated, and not expected to recover. O°A Monday, Philip Bice, John Beattie, Alex. Stewart, All" I Norman Pirrie were brought before the magistrate in thil Police court charged with participating in the riot °lll Friday, and with the murder of James Curran, who $O5 drowned. After hearing some evidence the prisoners were remanded for a week. An order for bail was made in favogr of Stewart; the others remain in custody. All there prisoner: are employed on Queen's Island. James M'ElvennY, tiring a revolver into a crowd on Sunday, was remanded ti Thursday. The case of Joseph Wilson, for stabbing a 12111). named Hugh Downey with a knife en Sunday, has not Sir Vet been taken up! The court was crowded to excess, all great excitement prevailed in and around the building' The authorities on Monday had 200 constables under sill and about 300 soldiers belonging to the Northumberla.n Fusiliers and Highland Light Infantry in the viciniti of Messrs. Harland and Wolff's works, both at dinner' hour and also at the leaving-off work time in the evenings. lest the shipwrights might again attack the navvi" No attempt of the kind was made, and all passed off peaer fully. Why is a woman deformed when she is mending her stocking ?—Because her hands are where her feet ought to be. "Composer: "How do you like my new opera?" Musical critic: "Oh, very much indeed! I meet in it se many old musical friends, you know." Diffident lover—" I know that I am a perfect bear in my manner." She—" Sheep, you mean; bears hug people— yore do nothing but bleat." The family cat never cares for applause when he is warbling his woodnotes wild on the back fence where the shot gun never troubles and the boot jack is at rest. "Father," said Bobby, "what is meant by the intoxication of wealth ?" "It means that money is tight," replied Bob- by's father' who had been trying all day to find a friend to back a bill far him. Jones, having read a Tory pamphlet the other day on "Radical Hypocrisy," consigned it to the flames. "flow well that barns" remarked a friend of his. "0 yes! don't you know that it b full of combustible matter ?'! replied Jones. Livtre SHLOOB'S Lova —Moss Schaumburg was romp- ing with his youngest offspring the other day. In order to test the child's affection, he asked. " Shacob, 'rich does you love most, me or your madder?" "I loves you most by twenty-five per shout," answered the child. Nica ron THE " Heams."—A distinguished professor recently asked the daughter of a wealthy brewer who em- ploys a little army of workmen if she ever did anything for the improvement of her father's hands. She replied thought- fully that she did not, but that she used to rub her own with a preparation of glycerine and oatmeal every night before retiring to rest. OMNIBUS PHILOSOPSIT.—CaIm conductor : "Can't take that threepenby-bit, sir !" Indginant passenger: "I'd like to know why not Calm conductor "It's too smooth." Indignant passenger: "Well, that's cool! You gave me that very threepenny-bit as I came into town this morning —I took it from you in change." Calm conductor: "Well, you see, we are more particular than you." A traveller by mistake left an under-garment at a coun- try inn where he had passed a night. He wrote to the land- lady to forward to him the missing article, whereupon he received the following reply—" My gentle sir, pray don't feel hurt; I'll frankly tell you all about it. I've made a shift of your old shirt, and you must make a shift without it." THE INDEPENDENT SPIRIT.—" Why ain't you at work, Jemmy ?" "Cause we're out on strike." "What's the trouble ?" "1 don't know." "What are you striking for ?" "For our rights." "Who has wronged you ?" "Tne corn- pany." "What company ?" 'I don't know." "What has I it done?" "1 don't knew." "Then bow do you know what you are striking for ?" -"Well, we're strikin' for our rights, and we're goin' to have 'em. There! We're goin' to have 'em!" Country visitor addressing school in New York: In the year 1825, my dear young friends, several boys walked from Salem to Boston and back, a distance of thirty miles, to hear Daniel Webster speak. If there were no railroads or means of transportation to-day, would the boys of the present generation undertake such a journey, do you think? —Small boy, after a long silence: No, sir.—Visitor: Ah ! And why ?—Small boy: because Mr. Webster is dead! HE DOES NOT NOW QUOTE, "Os, WAD SORE POWER THE Girria GIE US TO SEE OURSELS," &c.—A member of Par- liament engaged an agency which does such things to fur- nish him with clippings of all the derogatory things which the newspapers should say about him for a month. 'the return was enormous, and cost the member thirty pounds. For the following month he bespoke clippings of all that was printed in his favour, and his bill amounted only to seven shillings and sixpence. THEY 'WERE BOTH CANDID.—King Frederick VI. of Den- mark, while travelling through Jutland, one day entered a village school and found the children in it lively and intelli- gent and quite ready to answer his questions. "Well, youngsters,' he said, "what are the names of the greatest kings of Denmark?" With one accord they cried out, "Canute the Great, Waldemar, and Christian IV." Just then a little girl to whom the schoolmaster had . whispered something stood up and raised her hand. "Do you know another ?" asked the king. "Yes—Frederick VI. !" " What great acts did he perform ?" The girl hung her head and stammered out, "I don't know." "Be comforted, my child," said the king, "I don't know either!" A lady has a pony of which she is very fond; but not long since she thought that he was a little "dull;" so she called in a veterinary surgeon, who prescribed a powder for the equine favourite. The next morning she said to her man-of-all-work," Pat, did you give the pony his medicine ?" "Faith, mum," answered Pat rather ruefully, "I got a big glass pipe, an' I put the medicine in it, an' I backed the pony up in the corner. I put the pipe in his month, an' was , just pin' to blow it down into him, but he breathed first, an' I have the powther in me instead of him!" HE FELT IT.—Mr. Coldcash "Say, have you heard the I news ?" Smithers : "No, what is it ?" Coldcash : " Why, the Argentine Bank has gone up." Smithers " Oh, the scoundrels! I might have known such a rascally set of hank directors would rob the depositors." Coldcash : " Why, I have you any money in it ?" Smithers : "Every cent I made over to my wife before I failed the first time. Oh, the scoundrels !" A teacher in one of the American Indian schools gives the following illustration of an Indian boy's quick thought— He had a,ked the meaning of the word miss." "To miss," I told him, "is the same as to fail. You shoot at a bird or at a mark, and do not hit it; you miss it. You go to a , tailor's for a coat, and your coat fits badly; it is a misfit. You hope to enter the middle class next year, but you can- not pass your examinations, and so you miss the promo- tion." His face wore a puzzled air, and he shook his head. " Then," said I, " there is another meaning of miss.' We call a married woman madam,' but an unmarried woman miss.'" His face brightened; he smiled and nodded. " Ah, I see said he. "She has missed her man." A 'PARROT THAT COULD BEAT GLADSTONE AND RAN- I DOLYR CHURCHILL —"Some time age when Patti was walking down Fourth Avenue, New York, escorted by Nico- lini and Franchi, she expressed," an American writer tells us, "a desire to sample parrots, and went into a bird-fan- cier's rear Fourteenth Street. The fowl she now owns was asleep in a cage. 'This seems to be a beauty; please wake it up,' said the diva to the proprietor. 'Can it talk ? ' ' Talk ! It can beat Gladstone and Randolph Churchill to- gether! "Indeed ! Let us hear it, please.' The boss tickled Polly with a piece of lunar caustic, and the bird awoke, yelled, and waited for instructions. 'Talk, Polly— show your talents. This is Patti, who has come to see you.' 'lndeed,' said the bird; 'is this Adelina ? Truly it seems to me that her visage is resplendent with radiant beauty.' Why, this is marvellous ! ' cried the cantatrice. 'Can he say more?' Indeed he can. He speaks eight languages fluently ;heis a gay old bird.' 'Folly wants a cracker' (biscuit). Crackers be hanged ! " Sing me a song. I have heard that the foriture you introduce in The Barber are dazzling. Let's have them.' Patti complied with the I fowl's request, and, when she had finished, the ci itic in ' feathers remarked, 'Very good indeed; you remind me of Bosio. That re was pearly and altogether excellent, the sustained G altogether good. Before passing judgment, sing •na, " Ah, non giunge" from the Sonnambula, and then we will sing the .duet. Linda. I can take the shine out of Scalchi easily.' 'ROW much is the bird?' asked Patti. Two hundred pounds, madame.' Nicolini handed over the money, and the bird, after talking learnedly about consecu- tive fifths, was carried off in triumph to the Windsor Hotel. When Patti got it safely home, she invited her friends to call, and, addressing the bird, said, Now talk again, pretty Polly." What de yer say?' said Polly. 'Oh, the horrid thing—it is vulgat! "Carramba ! ' murmured the biped. And, oh, it swears in Spanish! The metamorphosis was complete. Polly swore, and sang naughty naughty songs, but spoke no more. The next day the diva discovered that when she was in the shop a hired ventriloquist had spoken for the bird."

A smart shock of earthquake was felt in Guernsey on island were morning. Buildings in different parts of the were shaken. STRANGE DEATH Ora HORSE DEALER.—William Spencer, a horse dealer, has met with his death under singular cir- cumstances at Oldham. 'He was seated in a dog-cart break- ing in a young horse, when the animal kicked through the bottom of the vehicle and sent Spencer into the air. He alighted on his bead, and when picked up was unconscious, and died shortly afterwards. EXCITING ADVENTIJRII.---Abont two o'clock on Monday morning, a flat, coal laden, sank in Collingwood Dock, Liverpool, under mysterious circuenstancer. Joseph Rod- gers, the master, who was asleep in the calm], was awoke by the inrush of water, and, finding the cabin flooded, forced up the hatoa and cot on deck, just in time to escape an awful death. The flat almost immediately sank beneath him, and he was left struggling in the water. His cries for assistance attracted the attention of a sailer on board the steamer Bessbrook. A lifebuoy was thrown out to him, and Rodgers was eventually hauled on board the steamer. He was taken to the receiving-house, and owing to the prompt attention paid to him there he soon recovered from the effects of his immersion. Rodgers is the famous seaman who signally distinguished himself on the occasion of the wreck of the Royal Charter, off Moe Hrs. Head, in Red Wharf Bay, on the Anglesea coast. on October 25th, 1859. The ill-fated steamer was homeward bound from Australia, carrying about 500 passangers and crew and a valuable cargo, with gold to the amount of £400,000, and was driven by a terrific nor- therly gale during the night upon the rock-bound coast, where no assistance could be rendered. Rodgers, who was one of the crew, gallantly swam ashore with a line round his body, and mainly through his heroic efforts some 35 person!—all that survived—were saved. He received a gold medal in recognition of his bravery. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATUR LIVERPOOL INTERNATIONAL EX- HIBITION. LOCAL EXHIBITS (No. 3). Large and well-stocked as are the departments of the exhibition set apart for exhibits to illustrate the great iron industries of the country, it may safely be affirmed that the stall of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, of Warrington, will be found to be one of the most interesting and best selected. The chief item of these exhibits is a massive wrought-iron cheffonnier, into the frame- work and embellishment of which are introdueed the different descriptions of iron and steel manu- factured in the company's works. In the centre, at the back of this cheffonnier, is a "buckled plate" pressed into shape by hydraulic machinery. These plates, it is said, are used extensively for bridge- work and fireproof flooring. The cabinets are framed in square bar iron, twisted cold as a torsion test, united at the corners with turned wrought iron and having glass fronts to protect samples. The table consists of a single boiler plate with a chamfered bar and angle-iron riveted on by hy- draulic machine as a sample of boiler and bridge riveting. From this is suspended an ornamental design in twisted wire rods, and upon it are placed specimens of iron and steel in bars, angles, boiler plates, sheets, hoops, and wire rods, worked hot and cold to satisfy the governntent, admiralty and engineering tests. The table is supported on legs made of round and I square bars, bent and twisted, strengthened with I brackets of special sections for fencing standards, &c. These are secured to circular frames formed by four patent welded carriage and cart tyres, which, in the front, encircle ornamental Greek borders made of hoop iron; inside these are, on the left hand, a single coil of No. 4 steel wire rod rolled without weld or joint, weighingls4lbs., and mea- suring about a quarter of a mile in length, and on the right hand side, a coil of No. 8 rolled steel wire rod, measuring about half a mile in length. The centrepieces at each end are made of hoop iron, ma- chine spayed and riveted, ready for coopers' use, in barrel-making. In this cheffionier specimens are thus presented of the five leading articles in the merchant iron trade—bars, hoops, plate, sheets, and wire rods. On the table of this remarkable cheffion- i ier are numerous specimens of iron wrought into various shapes and forms, and illustrating the great and varied resources of the firm's establishment. Amongst these specimens there is a full sized " billy- cock ' hat made out of a single boiler plate, and an iron book, the leaves of which are formed of very flexible iron plates thinner than ordinary note paper. On each side of the cabinets of the cheffion- ier there are splendidly executed photographs of engineering works erected by the firm, these photo- graphs being the work of Mr. Birtles, of Warring- ton. By the side of the mum n exhibit there are other notable examples of ironwork, including a double-acting steam forcepump ; a huge railway axle, which, to show the quality of the iron had been bentdouble whilst cold; and large iron bars which have been tied in knots whilst cold by hy- draulic machinery. Amongst the numerous other exhibitors in this department of the exhibition are Mr. James Smethurst of the Old Foundry, Foundry-street, Warrington, and Messrs. J. and T. Jolley and Co., of the Excelsior File and Tool Works, of this town. Smethurst is exhibiting his improved water tube irons which are extensively used in connection with blacksmiths' cisterns ; patent cart and lurry bushes ; ornamental grids for parks ; ring bushes and truck bushes for handcarts, &c. Although not a pretentious exhibit, there is a good deal about Mr. Smethursfs stand which will merit an inspection, especially by those whose business require the use of the objects dis- played. Messrs. Jolley and Co. exhibit a variety of tools, some sorts of which have won a high reputa- tion for their durability and other excellent quali- ties. The files, of which there is an admirable dis- play, are well finished, and will be favourably regarded by people who are accustomed to using things of this kind. In addition to the local ex- hibitors in other sections of the exhibition to whom we have referred in previous articles there are also Mr. Edward Bolton, of the Orford-lane glass works, and Messrs. lifaskery and Co., coach builders, of Rylands-street. Mr. Bolton makes an interesting ,display, there being amongst the articles he has contributed a working model of improved lift aque- duct and self-acting lock, with india rubber water- tight fittings, for canals, ship and otherwise, roads, railway works, &c. There are a number of flint- glass bottles, artistically engraved, cut flint dishes, and a number of other highly-finished vessels of similar materials and in various colours. The collec- tion of vehicles, ancient and modern, isa very large ()lie, and amongst the latter two very elegant pro- ductions in the shape of dog carts are exhil4ted by Messrs. Maskery and Co. These are elaborately and handsomely finished, and give a favourable impress sion as to the quality of the workmanship of this old-established firm. We understand that in addition to the Warring- ton firms whose exhibits have been referred to in -these columns a considereable number of others in- tended to exhibit had they been able to obtain the necessary space in the exhibition, but ;this, owing to the large number of applications, they were un- able to do.

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES DIVISION.
div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES DIVISION.

The Liberal Executive Council have decided, without dissent, that the candidate for the Widnes Division at the impending; election must be a supporter of Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy. There were, however, several gentlemen who refrained from voting. The announcement that Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Who made a gallant fight under very ad- verse circumstances at the General Election, would not again offer himself as a candidate, was received with much regret. Mr. Muspratt's reasons for de- clining to place his services at the command of his Liberal friends are, we believe, purely of a business character. He is now the sole proprietor of the Widnes Chemical Works, in the management of which his brothers had formerly a share, and this in- 'creased responsibility h as decided him to refrain from seeking Parliamentary honours. There is a great desire that a gentleman intimately connected with the town should contest the seat, and deputations from the Council waited upon Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., and Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P., to ascertain if either of these gentlemen would relieve the party from their difficulty. Both gentlemen, however, declined the proffered honour on the ground that business motives engrossed all their attentions. Failing in this respect, a deputation, consisting of Messrs. E. K. Muspratt, T. S. Timmis, and E. Carey, accompanied by Mr. H. B. Shores, went to London to interview Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C. They saw that gentleman on Thursday, and acting under the directions of the Council, invited him to contest the division. He replied that, before giving a definite reply. he should wish to see what steps the Birkenhead Liberals, whose cause he championed six months ago, would take. On Thursday evening the Liberal 300 at Birkenhead selected Mr. Kennedy as their candidate, and what his answer will be to the Widnes requisition is a matter of conjecture. He will acquaint the depu- tation with his decision to-day (Saturday.) Mr. Kennedy is a staunch supporter of Mr. Gladstone's Irish scheme, and an eloquent platform speakei, and he would make an admirable candidate. The Conservative candidate will without doubt be the present member, Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss. His ma- jority at the last election was the large number of 1,677, but it is fully accounted for by the Irish Tote, which would be given en bloc to a Gladstone candi- date, and the seat is looked upon as a safe one for the Liberal nominee.

BUCKLEY-STREET GLUE WORKS.

Sir,—Will yon kindly find space in your valuable paper for the following complaint. A few years ago the people were not allowed to keep pigs on account of the smell affect- ing public 11,?.alth, but we afflicted ones in Erwood-street are daily and almost hourly suLjected to horrible stenches which proceed from the adjoining glue works, causing sick- ness. The nuisance is getting more unbearable every day, especially on Sunday.—Yours,
ONE OF THE AFFLICTED.

THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION. Sir,—lt is sometimes urged as an obj,ction to the free lending of books that it leads to volumes being put in the hands of people about whom very little is known, and that consequently there is great risk ef these volumes never be- ing seen again. The only way that one can tell whether there is anything in this objection or not is by consulting the experience of free lending libraries already established, and I was, therefore, rather interested in reading the report of the chief librarian of the very large free library of New- castle-on-Tyne. From this report it seemed that during the past twelve months not a single book had been lost, and during the past five years only something like a dozen had been unaccounted for, although in that time there bad been between pne and two million issues. I think this speaks " volumes" for the honesty of book-readers. W. T.

div.head: WALKING DAY.-THE SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: WALKING DAY.-THE SALVATION ARMY.

Sir,—Thee is one little matter in connection with the above long looked-for day that I wish to bring before the public. I understand that an effort Is being made by the Salvation Army peciple to provide all the poor negleeted children of the town—those who are despised by all the other schools—with a dinner and tea on Walking Day. Now while all other schools no doubt have their regular sub- scribers to their annual treat on this day, these people who, I am afraid, are often slighted, are left to battle with the "cast-off "-children of our town, and wholly depending upon the generous amongst us for assistance. It is no easy task they have undertaken, and as there is still a great amount of distress amongst, us, I think they are deserving of all the support they can get. Having had one of their collecting books placed in my bands asking for my subscription, and seeing so many small subscriptions, I now as au outsider earnestly plead for these neglected little ones in order that they may have the day's enjoyment as well as the rest of school children. I have been an eye witness of their pro- ceedings on former Walking Days; so also have our respected Mayes and Mayoress and others, and I think they will admit with me that kindness and care for these little ones have been admirably shown by the Salvation Army people. It may be truly said in this case "that he who riveth to the peor lendeth to the Lord."—Yours respect- S.D. - fully,
Warrington, Jane 11, 1886. THE HOME RULE DEFEAT.

Sir,—The in-11-u-enc-e iir-a-d-p-;;;-of-:cla-s;;;.have, for the time being, triumphed, and the message ef peace to Ireland has been frustrated. Well, I imagine this triumph will be of short duration. Thanks to the glorious old man, whose efforts during a long life in the cause of freedom have earned for him the gratitude of civilised mankind, the right of the Irish people to condact their own affairs will be con- ceded sooner orbiter. It was to be expected that the great measure of Mr. Gladstone would receive the strenuous eppomition of dukes and their dependents; but, if I mistake not, the attitude taken up by such professed friends of the People as Mr. Chamberlain stet Mr. Peter Rylands will be resented by the working-men of this cannery, and I trust that in the coming appeal to the people these political Othello, will find their "occupation gone." During the Bulgarianatrocitiee, these men's voices were raised in condemnation of oppression, and now, when Ire- land with outstretched hands appeals to us for justice, these lovers of freedom turn their backs upon her, and join with her enemies in refusing to grant her just demands. I am firmly convinced in my heart that the intelligent work- jeg-menof this country are desirous that the Irish race should be our friends--"a consummation devoutly to be wished," a result only obtainable by giving them what they are perfectly entitled to. This is a question of freedom against oppression; of right against wrong. To Irishmen I would say be patient; time is on your aide. The innate love of justice in the English heart will rally to your aid. The result of granting Ireland's praytr will be one fur- ther step in the direction of that principle for which our forefathers fought and suffered. "0 liberty, float not for ever in the far horizon—remain not for ever in the dream of the enthusiast, the philosopher, and poet, but came t and make thy home among the children of men," FELIX HOLT. Yours, &c., June 10, 1888.

FRODSH AM. VVFSLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY—On Sun- day morning and evening special sermons were preached in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, by the Rev. Walter Vercoe, of Rochdale. and in the afternoon special flower service for scholars and their friends was conducted by the same gen- tleman. A collection was made at each service in aid of the school fund, and realized nearly £lB. IN OLD WOMAN BURN!!) TO DEATH....-AD inquest was held before Mr. H. Churton, on Monday, at the Ring o' Bells; Overton, on the body of Charlotte Proms, 71 years of age, who died from the effects of burns received on the sth inst. At three o'clock in the morning of the day in question, the deceased got oat of bed, and in striking a 1 match for the purpose of lighting a candle, she set her nightdress on fire. She was severely burned before the flames ceuld be extinguished, and she died shortly afterwards. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

WARRTNGTON COUNTY COURT. Tarnsnay.—Before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes. APPLICATION.-Mr. J. T. Backton made an application in reference to an action heard in the Court in 1877, it being one brought by Pierpoint and others against Cassidy and others. It was a friendly and equitable action for the sale of land in Warrington, the property was sold, and the money afterwards paid into Court. The present application was for payment out of such money to James Cassidy, the executor of the tenant for the life, and to other benefici- aries mentioned in an affidavit. After hearing particulars of the matter, his Honour said he thought an order might be made as far as the shares of those who were of age were concerned.

A CATALOGUE OF MISFORITIIIES.—A man named William Lamb, an engine driver, at plied to his Honour for an ad- ministration order. Applicant said that he was now earn- ing £1 a week. He had, he said, an illness, after which he was out of employment for six weeps, and two of his chil- dren had been down with fever. One of his two sons had bad his arm broken, and his wife had, unknown to him, contracted debts. In examination by creditors, he said that two of his daughters had dressed extravagantly, but they were now living away from home. He had only one son working. For his wages ot £1 he worked at the "Guar- dian " office sixty hours a week. His Honour granted an order, Lamb to pay 123 a month, and told him that so long as he kept his payments up he would be protected from exe- cutions and judgment summonses; he must, however, be careful not to contract fresh deb!s. CLAIM FOR DAMAGES FOR INJURIES SUSTAINED.—Thos. Glynn, labourer, Dallam•lane sued Mr. S. Horton, of the firm of Messrs. W. J. Horton, Dallam-lane, for injuries alleged to have been sustained by his daughter, in conse- quence of carters in the employ of the defendant. Glynn sued as next friend to his son, a minor. Mr. Langton ap- peared for plaintiff. and Mr. H. Woods (Ashton and Woods) appeared for the defence. The case for the plaintiff was that on New Year's Day, Michael Glynn, aged five, was playing with his sister on the footpath in Dallam-lane, when three horses and carts belonging to the defendant passed. The child was run over and sustained an injury to its hand, and it was alleged that the carters of the two first carts were walking behind with the driver of third, instead of each attending to his horse. For the defence witnesses were called to say that each of the three carters was at the head of the horse of which he was in charge, and could not have foreseen or prevented the accident. his Honour said that he was satisfied the injury had been caused by an acci- dent, or that by his carelessness the boy had contributed to it himself, and gave a verdict for the defendant, with costs. Mr. Woods intimated that his client would not ask for any Costs.
