div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 12, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 12, 1886.
THE REPRFSENTATION OF THE NORTH WICII DIVISION.

The approaching dissolution will find the Liberal party in the Northwich Division fully prepared for the election. The great preponderance of Liberal feeling is in favour of Home Rule for Ireland. Dur- ing his brief Parliamentary career, Mr. Brunner's opinions have coincided with those of the majority of his constituents, and his votes have always been "straight." His name aopeared amongst the " ayes " when the Government was defeated on Monday night. Although not yet selected as the candidate for the forthcoming election, this form- ality will be gone through by the Liberal Council at a meeting to be held at Winsford on 'Saturday next. His opponent will be Mr. W. H. Verdin, who contested for the honour six months ago, and who was so signally defeated. Mr. Brunner's prospects are of the brightest, but the heads of the party will not allow confidence to displace the as- siduous work by which only can success be assured. The majority on the last occasion was 1,028, and al- though there are "Liberal Unionists" in the Divi- sion, their numbers could be easily counted, and a decisive victory for Mr. Brunner is again antici- pated. It is expected that he will address the Liberal Council on Saturday next.

BOWLING MATCH AT BLACKPOOL FOR £lOO.- On Tuesday afternoon, one of the most important matches that has taken place for some time, so far as the amount of money is concerned, was brought off on the green attached t) the Queen's Hotel, Blackpool. The men engaged, namely, John Bromi- low, of Bickershaw, near Wigan, and George Ball, of Warrington, are well known as professional bowlers, but this is the first occasion on which the former has aspired to get in the front rank, whilst the latter has several times beaten James Green (the Blackburn champion), and also Tom Hart (champion of England). The conditions were to play 101 up, for £5O aside. Ball got two in at the first end, then Bromilow made a run of four. The latter totalled 10 to 5, 21 to 17, 38 to 32, but subsequently the game was called "46 all." Bromi- low again, however, went ahead, and at the inter- val had scored 51 to 46. On resuming Bromilow scored 70 to 61, 86 to 69, 90 to 71, N to 72, and eventually won easily, the score at the conclusion being—Bromilow, 101; Ball, 72.

SLATER said it was very good of them to come there that night to hear the committee of St. James's schools deliver their souls. He was sure he was speaking the feelings of the committee when he said they desired to face, as it were, the Warring- ton public, and to tell them that at any rate the great work they had had in hand was completed. They had built schools in St. James' parish, thanks to the general public of Warrington, and to one or two gentlemen in particular, for the wonderful help they had given to enable them to do that which at first seemed quite impossible. There were several gentlemen not present that night he wished were present, and one especially he thanked first, because that school was built upon his land, and that was Mr. Lyon. (Applause.) Mr. Lyon gave that mag- nificent site which extended from the door in which they entered down to the railway, and if they looked outside at their playgrounds he believed they would find them second to none in Warring- ton, in size at any rate. They had to thank another gentleman, Mr. Rowe, their architect—(applause) —who, they might say, had been the dem ex machina, because he had been making those schools but they had not seen him. It was, of course, not easy for a gentleman whose work lay in Cambridge to come ts Warrington; he, however, intended to be present that night, but at the last moment he had to tele- graph that he could not come because he was too ill. Mr. Rowe had done all the architect's work for those schools quite gratuitously. (Applause.) Having referred to the defects of the old school Mr. Slater went on to say that the foundation of those new schools were laid by Sir Gilbert Greenall, but he also laid the foundation stone in a very different'Sense for he (Mr. Slitter) believed that had Sir Gilbert Greenall not taken them in hand those magnificent schools-would not have been built. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They all felt the great kindness of Sir Gilbert Greenall in coming there at such a time and at such personal inconvenience to open their schools. (Applause.) Everybody knew that Sir Gilbert Greenall had not had a very long night as he had been very well engaged in the small hours of the morning, and he had travelled almost in post haste to get there in time. (Applause). Mr. C. S. BURGESS (hon. treasurer of the school building fund) said he was deputed to say that the amount of subscriptions that they had received or promised, and other receipts in connection with the building of the schools, amounted to £2,750, exclu- sive of the architect's work and the site which Mr. Lyon had given. They estimated the whole cost of building those schools would be £2,950, so they would see from that that they would have a defici- ency of something like £2OO. He did not know that he could offer any suggestions as to the manner in which that sum could be raised, but they would be glad to receive suggestions as to the way in which that might be done. (Hear, hear.) Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who WAS received with applause, said he was very glad and very willing to take the part which devolved upon him that even- ing. His first thought was to congratulate himself that he was able to be present that evening, and to see a school, so gifted with accommodation, which would belong to the poorer classes in that parish. The subject of a school in Latchford had long been in his mind, and he had often thought it was a matter to be regretted that there was no school, for he did not call the old building a school. (Hear, hear.) They had had a statement of accounts read. and there was a balance at the end. Hs should like to ask his friend, Mr. Burgess, whether £2OO would entirely cover that adverse balance? (Mr. Burgess: Yes.) Well, as Mr. Burgess had engaged to finish the schools if he had £2OO, if God preserved his (Sir Gilbert's) life upon the day on which Mr. Burgess came to tell him that the school was finished, he would give him £2OO. (L md applause.) He re- joiced to see those schools opened, because he did not love a school board. (Hear, hear.) He disliked a school board thoroughly and entirely, and he dis- liked it for this reason. He thought a school board at its foundation and at its base was irreligious. Now, why did he say so? He said so because what did occur in Birmingham might occur anywhere else. A school board might be so constituted and be so unfortunate as to those who were elected upon it, that the Bible and all scriptural or religion, teaching might be utterly excluded. (Hear, hear.) He was quite sure when he said that he spoke within the law, and he should bitterly regret for the reason he had expressed if they had a school board in the town of Warrington. (Applause.) He then formally declared the school open. Mr. W. BEAMONT then gave a short but interest- ing address as to the history of Latchford. He dare i say they had heard that n ancient times a road passed through Latchford, and there was no doubt that the great Roman general Agricola passed along it to Wildersnool. This road weht straight to Wil- derspool they knew perfectly well, and he had found Roman coins there not above two years ago in a Igood state of preservation. On a map he could point out almost every inch of that Roman road all the way to Northwich. There were two roads to Northwich ; one was a Roman read, and the other was made because it was sought to exact a toll. One road was tollable and the other was not. In the Roman period there was a station at Wilders- pool, and the site of that station contained plenty of remains that anybody miiht 'see who went into the Warrington Museum. They did not hear of Latchford even in the Dooms Day book. Grappen- hall was mentioned but Latchford was not men-

It is expected that Mr. Gladstone's manifesto will be issued to-day. St. Andrews's Hall, Glasgow, which is the largest in the city, has been engaged for the 28th inst., when Mr. Gladstone will deliver an ad- dress under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation of Scotland.

Lord llartington was engaged all Friday morning with his private secretary at Devonshire House. It is expected his lordship will issue his address for Rossendale early next week. Captain O'Shea has accepted the Chiltern Hun- dreds, but in view of the near approach of the general election it is not probable that a new writ will be moved.

There will be a mass meeting at Hatfield to-day at 5-30. Lord Salisbury, Lord John Manners and Mr. Marriott will speak. The political agents of all parties were extremely busy yesterday morning, the most apparent acti- vity being at the Premier's residence, where the Liberal Whips ryceiyed a large number of candi7 dates their agents, and arranging programme of election. Complete accord at present exists be- tween the Liberal Unionists, whose seats are, as far as Possible, being made secure by the Conservative party.

NEWTON LIBERAL '300." MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. • A meeting of the Earlestown, Vulcan, and New- ton portions of the Liberal " 300 " for the Newton Parliamentary Division, was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Earle-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening, for the purpose of electing local officers , for the ensuing year. The chair was occupied by Mr. Rawlinson, of Newton, and among those present were Messrs. P. Hall, B. llarrison, G. Ratcliffe, W. D. Burdis, W. Urquhart, L. T. Foulkes, M. Birkhead, C. A. Luffman, J. Prescot, W. Younger, Mr. T. Mor- ris, and others. The Chairman briefly stated the object cf the meeting, after which some discussion took place as to the advisability of electing separate officers for Earlestown and Newton, and a general feeling was expressed that it would be best for Earlestown and Vulcan to be considered one district and Newton as another district. —Mr. Prescot said the question for them to consider was how best to accomplish the task the Liberals had in hand, and he thought the suggested division was a good one. —The Chairinan observed that they meant to win the election in that division, and it could be given out that the election was almost already won for the Liberals, as it was the determination of the Liberals of the Division, high and low, to win.l There was no mistake they were in earnest— all were determined. The large number that had come there through • the storm that night showed that they were all workers, and that they meant to have the work , done thoroughly and well. (Applause.) They wanted to have the district worked thoroughly and vigourously.—Mt. W. McEvoy moved that Mr. L. T. Foulkes be secretary for Earlestown and New- ton, and Mr. T. Morris, in seconding, paid a high compliment to Mr. Foulkes for his good work in the past, his touch and intimacy with all parties, and his hard work for the Liberal party at all times. The motion was passed unanimously. —Mr. Foulkes, in thanking the meeting, said he hoped to put forth every endeavour to carry out the duties to the best of his ability. That would be his wish, and he hoped to have the sympathy and help of all those whose duty it would be to work with him.— Mr. John Prescott, in moving Mr. B. Harrison as chairman for the district, pointed out that he was a vice-president of the Liberal Association, he was well known, and had been a good worker for the Liberal cause all his lifetime. (Applause.)—Mr. George Ratcliffe seconded the resolution, which was supported in complimentary terms by Mr. Foulkes and Mr. Morris, and carried enthusiastically.—On the motion of Mr. William Davies, seconded by Mr. D. Owen, and supported by Mr. P. Hall, Mr. John Prescott was elected doputy-chairman.—lt was then decided to elect similar officers for Newton.—Mr. Burdis, in moving the appointment of Mr. C. A. Luffman as secretary, said he had formerly per- formed the duties efficiently, and had worked night and day for the good of Liberalism in that division. —Mr. Lennox had great pleasure in seconding the motion, which was passed unanimously, and Mr. Luffman acknowledged the compliment.— Mr. John Prescott moved the appointment of Mr. William Urquhart as chairman, and Mr. Burdis, in seconding the motion, said he was sure there was not a more enthusiastic Liberal in Newton or Eariestown.—The motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. Urquhart returned thanks.—Mr. EcEvoy moved, Mr. Lennox seconded, and it was unani- mously passed that Mr. W. D. Burdis be appointed deputy chairman.—The Chairman stated that the next question was the appointment of Committees for the two districts.—Mr. Hall said if they got a good working committee the question, often asked, "What are the Liberals of Earlestown doing ?" would be easily answet ed.—The Chairman: So far our returns are 'very satisfactory.—Mr. Ratcliffe: I think every Liberal in this district will vote for Mr. Gladstone. We dont know definitely that we have any sece- ders, and if there are any we must try and persuade them to be different. —3lr.Birkhead•said he thought they ought to have among them some Irish Home Rulers to the backbone. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Pres- cott believed the Irishmen were anxious to start the fray. They were waiting for the candidate to appear in the Aeld.—After some further discussion,
the election of committees anCl other council busi- ness was transacted.
WARRINGTON.

DEATH OF AN EX-POLICEMAN.—Ex-policernan William Hitchmough died on Wednesday night from consumption. Deceased was 28 years of age, had been about eight years in the police force, and retired a short time since through ill-health. Ile leaves a widow and three children.

LOCAL MUSICAL EXAMINA-TI-O-N. B.—III the pass lists just published of the examinations in connec- tion with the Royal Academy of Music, held at the Liverpool and manchester centres, appear the names of Miss Florence A. Toft (Museum-street), senior division pianoforte, and Miss Marion Chandley (Latchford), junior division pianoforte, both pupils of Mr. W. S. Woods. BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL—OR Sunday, the 100th anniversary of these schools was celebrated. In the morning and evening there were services at which the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. E. 0. Coleman, of Newport, a gentleman who was formerly connected with this circuit; and in the afternoon a children's service was conducted by Mr. Andrew Powlson, of Widnes. The collections of the day amounted to over £42. THE THEFT BY A CARD SHARPER.—At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, Joseph Cor- i corran (27), labourer, was indicted for having at ' Warrington, on the 31st ult., stolen 12s. from the person of William Johnson, and was sentenced to 112 months' imprisonment with hard labour. Pri- soner was committed for trial by the borough magi- strates last week, and was then described by Chief Constable Hunt as a card sharper and thimble rigger. The prosecutor is a farm labourer, of Sut- ton Weaver, Cheshire, and the offence was commit- ted at the Gun Inn, Scotland-road.

FOOTBALL CLUB.—On Monday evening a special general meeting of the members of the Warrington Football Club was held in the Workmen's Club- room, Market-place. The President (Mr. Councillor Francomb) occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance. The Chairman said that the meet- ing had been called at the request of several mem- bers who had signed a requisition and forwarded it to the secretary (Mr. J. E. Warren) in accordance with the rules of the club. This was done in order that the question of the election of officers at the previous meeting might be considered, as a good many members had been dissatisfied with the mode of that election. It was then agreed, on the motion of Mr. H. Ashton, that all that had been done at the previous meeting should be rescinded, and after-' wards the following officers were elected mien," mously, viz. :—Captain, Ist team, Mr. H. Ashtc.a.n..; vice-captain, Mr. E. Gilbert; captain, A team, -o.l— ; umpire, Ist team, 111 r. J. Barnes; cePj: tam, 2nd team, Mr. W. Dumbell ; secretary, Mr. E. Warren. For the post of treasurer there weref three candidates, Mr. T. Pemberton, the treasurerpt last year, being ultimately appointed. Mr. Wrign was elected umpire of A team, and Mr. H. Boardman vice-captain of A team. The committee was coke: stituted as follows :—Messrs. G. Smith, W. SPeavr. man, J. Evans, J. Isherwood, J. C. B. Savage, T.; Dillon, Fair. Turner, and J. H. Calvert. Messrs, , Webster and Winstanley were appointed auditre o and Messrs. J. Evans and G. Smith trustees.

A VOLUNTEER'S 'FUNERAL.—On• Saturday after- noon the remains of the late Sergeant A. Hill, of D company, 9th L.R.V. (Warrington) were interred with military honours at the cemetery. The vol- unteers assembled at headquarters and thence marched to Orford-lane, where deceased had lived. The funeral procession then walked to the cemetery, passing through Horsemarket, Buttermarket, and Church-streets. The band of the corps played the Dead March. The firing party consisted of Sergeant Cliffe and 18 men, and the coffin was borne from the church to the graveside by six sergeants. THE LATE Mits. J. LEACH.--On Sunday morning the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton preached in Holy Trinity Church, and in the course of his sermon he said they were all mourners upon that occasion, in the loss of one so well known in that parish as the widow of his predecessor in the incumbency of that church, the late Rev. J. Leach. She had indeed reached her full term of years, and it was only to have been expected that ere long she would be taken away. Her loss would be deeply felt by those to whom she was endeared by the strongest ties of affection and love, and by all to whom her kind- ness of heart had been extended. The preacher also referred in touching terms to the late Mr. Richard Hatton, who for many years had been officially con- nected with the church. Special hymns were sung by the choir during the service, and at.the conclu- sion the organist, Mr. Wm. Johnson, played the "Dead march."

ROBBING A LABOUREIL-At the Borough Court on Monday, two women named Annie Hodgson and Ellen Connor, the former described as a factory hand, and the latter as a fustian cutter, were to- gether charged on remand from Saturday with being concerned together in stealing a purse con- taining £5 10s. from the person of Matthew Speed, a farm labourer, who lives at Merton, near Black- pool. From the evidence it appeared that on Thurs- day in last week Speed came to Warrington, and after strolling about the town for a time, got into company with the prisoners early in the evening. With them he went to the Gun Inn, Scotland-road, where he paid for some beer. Afterwards the trio went to the house of the prisoner Connor, where complainant gave that female 2s with which to buy some eatables. When Connor was in the back kit- chen Hodgson, who w.as sitting near the complain- ant, put her hand in his pocket and abstracted his purse. She then ran away, and Connor followed. Prosecutor, being lame, was unable to prevent their escape. Information of the matter came to the ears of the police, and Constable Cheeney appre- hended Hodgson, who was in company with some other Warrington people, at Salford. Connor was afterwards arrested, and it transpired that the women had shared the proceeds of the robbery. They were both committed for trial. At the Quar- ter Sessions at Liverpool on Tuesday, prisoners were each sentenced to six months' hard labour.

THE WARItINGTON FEELD' Cla—The Warring; ton Field Club had their summer programme sup- plemented by a noteworthy "extra " on Saturday last, when, at the invitation of Mr. Robert Davies, they were entertained at his residence, Birchdale, Stockton Heath. Under a glorious summer sky, unsullied, as it happened, by the faintest suspicion of a rain-cloud—conditions unhappily not too often realised of late—the five and twenty members who managed to avail themselves of the opportunity spent, in physical as well as intellectual enjoyment, an afternoon and evening such as we think will en- title the event to a red letter in the annals of the club. Assembling at four o'clock at Birchdale, the club was joined by a number of Mr. Davies's friends, amongst whom were the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Rev. Morley Stewnson, Mr. John Cros- field, J.P., Mr. William Sharp, and Mr. William Owen. Having been accorded a kindly reception, the party rambled, in company with Mr. Davies as circerone, and his son, Mr. Vere B. Davies, into the adjoining grounds at Prospect Hill. Here they were met and welcomed by Mr. James Marson and personally conducted by him through the gardens, greenhouse. &c., the many rare and beautiful speci- mens of plants and flowers -being noted and ad- mired. Leaving here and passing across the high- way, Appleton Hall, the seat of Mr. T. H. Lyon, was next visited, a stroll in the spacious park and through the conservatories being gteatly enjoyed. Returning to Mr. Davies's residence, an excellent repast was found to be awaiting the refreshment of the inner man, the table being graced with the presence of Mrs. Davies. A hearty tea having been partaken of, the visitors found themselves free to ' explore the quaint recesses and cosy "corners of Birchdale itself a picturesque specimen of old Cheshire architecture—or to betake themselves to such al fresco enjoyments as the trim tennis grounds, the velvety lawns, and the lovely flower beds afforded. Before leaving, Mr.. Woodcock, the club secretary, took an opportunity of expressing to Mr., Mrs., and Mr. Vere Davies the unfeigned thanks of the members for the genial and hospitable manner in which they had been entertained. ALL SAtirrrs' SUNDAY SCHOOL.—On Sunday after- noon a distribution of prizes to the scholars of the 'above school, which is situated in Hoyle-street, and connected with St. Paul's Church, took place. Amongst those present were Mr. and 'Mrs, Thomas Morris, Mrs. John Chorley, Miss Wilkinson, and Mr. Wm. Smith (superintendent). About 60 books were distributed—to the girls by Mrs. Morris and to the boys by Mr. Morris. Mr. Smith-Said the school was opened on Februart22nd, 1885, with 32 children in i the morning, while n the afternoon the room was crowded. The mission-house was far too small for their classes, 'and their great wish was to build 4 substantial school in Bewsey ultimately. On Sun- day afternoon, May 30th, they had in the infants' room, 67; mission-room, 62; -boys' room, 70; and girls' select room, 16, with ten teachers, making a total of 225, exclusive of a secretary and superin- tendent. He was proud to say that the children who came to them first were with them still, and would receive their prizes that day for regular attendance and good behaviour. The presents to be given that day were the first since they. com- menced the Sunday. school, 15 months ago, in the Fission-room, Catherine-street.—Mr. Thomas Mori* in distributing the prizes, said that to have books and not read them was, mentally speaking, as al>. surd as having bread in the house and not eating it, and he trusted there was no one who would receive a book that afternoon who would not read every page and think overit while doing so. He had no doubt that that was the ',first time some of them had be- come the owner of a book, and he would suggest a method by which they might multiply one volume into 20 or more. His suggestion was that each one should have his name 'legibly written in the book, and when he had read it make an exchange with his schoolmate or playmate, so that they might read each other's books. Carrying the suggestion fur- ther, they alight establish a sort of changing library, the nussion woman to carry out the work in the mission room at some specified hour during each week with the books they had had that day handed to them. He saw no reason why a free lending library should not develop out of that exchange. t Once start that scheme, and solicit the gentlemen of the town to present them with a few books they did not read now, and the library was complete for the teeming population of the district. (Applause.) If the Rev. 8, Wilkinson would take the matter up, he (Mr. Morris) would start it with a gift of a large 1 number of books, and wish them every. success. (Applause.)—After singing and prayer, the proceedl jugs were brought to &conclusion.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Server Pasha, the Turkish Ministar of Justice, died on Friday morning. The Australian first innings closed yesterday for 222, the Cambridge 51, and no wickets down. _

THE tiTICE OF WESTMINSTER'S GENEROSITY.—The Duke of Westminster has intimated his intention of giving a peal of bells and to till the five light east window and the rose window in the tower of the new church of St. Mary, Ches- ter, with stained glass. His Grace also gave the sites, awl has built at hi fi sole expense a new vicarage and the new church of St. Mary. This noble gift to the Church has cost the Duke of Westminster £30,000.

LORD CARNARTON AND Mn. PARNSLL.—The London correspondent of the "Freeman's Journal." on Friday, re- ferringito Lord Carnarvon's statement as to his interview with Mr. Parnell, says Lord Carnarvon acted throughout this matter in a perfectly honourable manner. There were two interviews with Mr. Parnell, both of them at Lord Car- narvon's express solicitation, through another member of the Irish Party. On both occasions Lord Carnarvon came over from Dublin to see Mr. Parnell.

THE CHLWFORD•DIIICE CASE—In the Divorce Division, on Friday, before Sir James Hannen, Mr. Inderwick, Q C., made an application on behalf of Mr. Donald Crawford, M.P., to strike out the plea of the Queen's Proctor, in the case of Crawford v. Crawford, on the ground that the plea and the particulars together did not show any ground for interventi.n. Sir James Hannen, without calling upon Sir Walter PhillimorP, Q C., who represented the Queen's Proc- tor, granted permission for intervention, but directed the Queen's Proctor to furnish fuller particulars as to the material evidence to be adduced. Sir Henry James thou applied, on behalf of Sir Charles Dilke, that be might be allowed to appear at the forthcoming trial, but this ap- plication was refused with costs.

div.head: RIOTING AT BELFAST.
div.p: THE RIOTING AT BELFAST.

Belfast, at six o'clock on Friday morning, appeared to be fairly quiet, the rioters haying shortly after two dispersed to their homes. The disturbances on Thursday night in York-street and the Ormean and Sandy Bow districts, al- theugh not attended by the loss of life which marked the previous rioting, were of such a character as to cause very' serious alarm throw...gloat the town, a considerable number being wounded and several houses wrecked and burned. On Friday morning Mr. Johr. Morley, Chief Secretary for Ire- land, arrived in Dublin to inquire into the circumstances connected with the riots in Belfast. He will spend the day at Dublin Castle with the Inch law officers and Sir Robert Hamilton, Under Secretary, and Mr. Reed, Innrctor General of Constabulary. He will probably return to Lon- don on Sunday.

div.head: VOLC.,INT DISASTER IN NEW ZEALAND.
div.p: THE VOLC.,INT DISASTER IN NEW ZEALAND.

WELLINGTON, FRIDAY. - The volcanic eruption in the Tarawera dieirict was of so violent a nature that whole vi lagtes are buried in ashes. The surface of the country is in a disturbed condition for miles round. Twentv•six bodies have been recovered, but the total loss of life is up to the present unknown._______

div.head: FIGHTING IN BURMAH.
div.p: FIGHTING IN BURMAH.

A telegram dated Rangoon, Thursday, states: Mr. Phavre Deputy Commissioner of Upper Barmah, the son of Sir Robert Pbayre, was shot on the Bth inst. while attack- sng a gang of dacoits under the notorious chief Boh Sway, who occupied an entrenched position at Ugapeh. His body was carried away by the dacoits. An expedition will set out immediately to punish the rebels.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. RAILWAY BILL.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. RAILWAY BILL.

On the motion for the second reading of the Hull, Barns- ley, and West Riding Junction Railway and Docks' Bill, Mr. CODDINGTON opposed and moved its rejection. The object of the bill was to raise five hundred thousand pounds on preference shares, and the company was in a state of bankruptcy as they were paying large discount on monies borrowed.—Sir E. TEMPLE seconded the rejection ; but after some discussion the bill was read a second time.

TEE BELFAST RIOTS -Mr. CHILDERS, replying to Mr. de Cobain on the subject of the Belfast riots, said they bad no !information of misconduct on the part of the county 'police. He read telegrams which stated that rioting was doing on in Belfast on Thursday night. The police had fired; one man was shot in the face, and others were wounded. One thousand six hundred constabulary were in the town, and the military force was augmented by 250 men from Dublin. The disturbances were principally wreck- ing public-houses.
Ta Eracrio GLIDSTONI3 intimated that if, after the general election, it was found the country disap- proved of the Irish policy of the Government, Parliament would assemble forthwitb.

THE COURSE OF BUSINESS.—MT. GLADSTONE moved, for the remainder of the session, that money hills have prece- dence over other bills.—Some discussion ensued with regard to private members' bills, but ultimately Mr. Glad- stone's motion was agreed to. THE CROFTERS' ACT.—Dr. MACDONALD obtained leave to move the adjournment in order to discuss a matter of public importance, namely, the appointment of Commissioners under the Crofters' Act of the present sessien. He said the Commissioners appointed were nominees of the landlords unsuccessful at last election.—The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for Scorrami defended the selection that had been made, and the motion for adjournment was withdrawn. SUPPLY.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply on the army estimates, Mr. SCL ATER BOOTH called attention to the management of regimental canteens as re- garded the purchase of supplies.—A vote of £l,OOO as a gratuity to Lady Gossett, widow of the late Sergeant at Arms, was agreed to.—On the vote for £6,879,779 being proposed on account of the civil service and revenue de- partments, Mr. PICKERSGILL called attention to the appoint- ment of Mr. Graham as clerk of the Parliaments of the House of Lords. He condemned passing over an old and valued public servant in order that Mr. Graham should be appointed.—Mr. LABOUCHERB condemned the appointment as a Foandalous job. Mr. Graham's principle qualification was his relationship to a Tory nobleman.—Mr. COSTiati said Mr. Graham got the appointment because he was a re- lative of Lord Cranbrook. Mr. SMITH defended the appointment as a good one.—The vote was agreed to.—On the vote of £5.000,000 on account of army services being pro- posed, Mr. WOODALL, in reply to Sir W. Bartellot, said the new rifle had succeeded satisfactorily. In Com- mittee of Ways and Means, the sum of £26,992,652 was voted for the service of the year. • [LEFT SITTING.]

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. NOTICE TO DAIRYMEN, COVVKEEPERS, AND PURVEYORS OF MILK. The DAIRIES, COWSHEDS, AND MILKSHOPS ORDER of 1885. Pursuant to the above-mentioned order of the Privy,Conneil, under the Contagions Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878‘. We, the Mayor, Aldermen, and Bisrgesses of the Borough of Warrington, being the Local Authority for the said borough, do hereby give public notice, that a Register is now open for the Registration, under the said order, of all persons from time to time carrying on within the said borough the trades of Cowkeepers, Dsirynier, or Purveyors of Milk. The mode of Registration is es follows :—Every Dairyman, Cowkeeper, and Purveyor of Milk, shall make written ap- plication to the Town Clerk, to be Registered, and shall des- cribe in such application, his trade, and the situation, number and dimen,ions of the buildings and premises in respect of which he applies to be Registered. When the application is filled up in the prescribed manner, it must be forwarded to the Town Clerk, at his offices in Lyme. street, Warrington, and npcn the Town Clerk being satisfied that the requirements of the order and of the notice of the Local Authority have been complied with, he shall forthwith register the same in the Register kept by him for the purpose, and shalt transmit to the applicant a certificate of the Regis tration thereof. Forms of application will be supplied free of charge to any applicant, and may be obtained at the Office of the Town Clerk. AND NOTICE IS ALSO HEREBY OfvEif that it will not be law- ful for any person to carry on in the said borough the trade of a Cowkeeper. Dairyman, or Purveyor of Milk, unless he is resistered as such under the said order. rated this Tenth day of June, 1886. WM. fly. BROOK, Town Clerk. CAUTION. By secs. 60 and 61 of the above-named Act, it is provided that if any person dees anything in contravention qf the said Act, or of an order of Council, or of a Regulation of a Local Authority, be renders himself liable to a penalty not exceeding TWENTY POUNDS.

The Lancaebire and Notts teams met again after two years separation at Trent Bridge last week, with the result that the County Palatine representatives received the best drubbing tbey have experienced for a long time past. The Derbyshire eleven played far better cricket against the Australians at Derby on Tuesday than on M.nday. But the Colonists had gained so strong an advantage at the start that the county could not retrieve the game, and at half-past six in the evening the Australians had gained a victory with six wickets to spare. As far as the actual day's cricket was concerned, the home team did far better than their formidable antagonists, scoring 144 for ten wickets, while the visitors lost seven wickets and made 71 runs.
